Robert De Niro</h3></a></div><div class="sc-7c95f518-6 iDkHPP"><ul class="ipc-inline-list ipc-inline-list--show-dividers sc-7c95f518-4 lolxqE base" role="presentation" data-testid="nlib-professions"><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Actor</li><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Producer</li><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Director</li></ul><a class="ipc-link ipc-link--base sc-ab9eb9db-0 iRQWod" tabindex="0" aria-disabled="false" data-testid="nlib-known-for-title" href="/title/tt0101540/?ref_=ls_knf_1">Cape Fear (1991)</a></div></div></div><div><button data-testid="dli-add-to-list-button" class="ipc-icon-button ipc-icon-button--base ipc-icon-button--onAccent2" title="Add to list" tabindex="0" aria-label="Add to list" aria-disabled="false"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="24" height="24" class="ipc-icon ipc-icon--add" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="currentColor" role="presentation"><path d="M18 13h-5v5c0 .55-.45 1-1 1s-1-.45-1-1v-5H6c-.55 0-1-.45-1-1s.45-1 1-1h5V6c0-.55.45-1 1-1s1 .45 1 1v5h5c.55 0 1 .45 1 1s-.45 1-1 1z"></path></svg></button></div></div><div data-testid="dli-bio" class="sc-77f37b3d-2 dpXpaE"><div class="ipc-html-content ipc-html-content--base sc-77f37b3d-3 huKIYr" role="presentation"><div class="ipc-html-content-inner-div" role="presentation">One of the greatest actors of all time, Robert De Niro was born in 1943, in Manhattan, New York City, to artists Virginia (Admiral) and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm3902582/?ls">Robert De Niro Sr.</a>. His paternal grandfather was of Italian descent, and his other ancestry is Irish, English, Dutch, German, and French. He was trained at the <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0012245/?ls">Stella Adler</a> Conservatory and the American Workshop. De Niro first gained fame for his role in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0069765/?ls">Bang the Drum Slowly (1973)</a>, but he gained his reputation as a volatile actor in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0070379/?ls">Mean Streets (1973)</a>, which was his first film with director <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000217/?ls">Martin Scorsese</a>. He received an Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for his role in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0071562/?ls">The Godfather: Part II (1974)</a> and received Academy Award nominations for best actor in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0075314/?ls">Taxi Driver (1976)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0077416/?ls">The Deer Hunter (1978)</a> and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0101540/?ls">Cape Fear (1991)</a>. He received the Academy Award for Best Actor for his role as <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0483766/?ls">Jake LaMotta</a> in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0081398/?ls">Raging Bull (1980)</a>.<br/><br/>De Niro has earned four Golden Globe Award nominations for Best Actor - Motion Picture Musical or Comedy for his work in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0076451/?ls">New york new york (1977)</a>, opposite <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0591485/?ls">Liza Minnelli</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0095631/?ls">Midnight Run (1988)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0122933/?ls">Analyze This (1999)</a>, and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0212338/?ls">Meet the Parents (2000)</a>. Other notable performances include <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0088846/?ls">Brazil (1985)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0094226/?ls">The Untouchables (1987)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0101393/?ls">Backdraft (1991)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0109836/?ls">Frankenstein (1994)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0113277/?ls">Heat (1995)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0112641/?ls">Casino (1995)</a>, and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0119396/?ls">Jackie Brown (1997)</a>. At the same time, he also directed and starred in such films as <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0106489/?ls">A Bronx Tale (1993)</a> and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0343737/?ls">The Good Shepherd (2006)</a>. De Niro has also received the AFI Lifetime Achievement Award in 2003 and the Golden Globe Cecil B. DeMille Award in 2010.<br/><br/>As of 2024, De Niro is 81 years-old. He has never retired from acting, and continues to work regularly in mostly film.</div></div></div></div></div></div></li><li class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item"><div class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__c"><div class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__tc"><span class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__t" aria-disabled="false"></span><div class="sc-77f37b3d-0 jCbCZO dli-parent"><div class="sc-77f37b3d-1 gJmTWZ"><div class="sc-7c95f518-0 cDAKkN"><div data-testid="nlib-img-container" class="sc-7c95f518-1 iorieb"><div class="ipc-avatar ipc-avatar--base" role="group"><div class="ipc-media ipc-media--avatar ipc-image-media-ratio--avatar ipc-media--circle-radius ipc-media--base ipc-media--custom ipc-avatar__avatar-image ipc-media__img" style="width:60px"><img alt="Jack Nicholson at an event for The Bucket List (2007)" class="ipc-image" loading="lazy" src="https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMTQ3OTY0ODk0M15BMl5BanBnXkFtZTYwNzE4Njc4._V1_QL75_UX60_CR0,0,60,60_.jpg" srcSet="https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMTQ3OTY0ODk0M15BMl5BanBnXkFtZTYwNzE4Njc4._V1_QL75_UX60_CR0,0,60,60_.jpg 60w, https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMTQ3OTY0ODk0M15BMl5BanBnXkFtZTYwNzE4Njc4._V1_QL75_UX90_CR0,0,90,90_.jpg 90w, https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMTQ3OTY0ODk0M15BMl5BanBnXkFtZTYwNzE4Njc4._V1_QL75_UX120_CR0,0,120,120_.jpg 120w" sizes="50vw, (min-width: 480px) 34vw, (min-width: 600px) 26vw, (min-width: 1024px) 16vw, (min-width: 1280px) 16vw" width="60"/></div><a class="ipc-lockup-overlay ipc-focusable" href="/name/nm0000197/?ref_=ls_i_2" aria-label="Jack Nicholson"><div class="ipc-lockup-overlay__screen"></div></a></div></div><div class="sc-7c95f518-3 krmPLY"><div data-testid="nlib-meter-const-container"></div><div class="ipc-title ipc-title--base ipc-title--title ipc-title-link-no-icon ipc-title--on-textPrimary sc-7c95f518-2 ghWujX" data-testid="nlib-title"><a href="/name/nm0000197/?ref_=ls_t_2" class="ipc-title-link-wrapper" tabindex="0"><h3 class="ipc-title__text">2. Jack Nicholson</h3></a></div><div class="sc-7c95f518-6 iDkHPP"><ul class="ipc-inline-list ipc-inline-list--show-dividers sc-7c95f518-4 lolxqE base" role="presentation" data-testid="nlib-professions"><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Actor</li><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Producer</li><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Writer</li></ul><a class="ipc-link ipc-link--base sc-ab9eb9db-0 iRQWod" tabindex="0" aria-disabled="false" data-testid="nlib-known-for-title" href="/title/tt0071315/?ref_=ls_knf_2">Chinatown (1974)</a></div></div></div><div><button data-testid="dli-add-to-list-button" class="ipc-icon-button ipc-icon-button--base ipc-icon-button--onAccent2" title="Add to list" tabindex="0" aria-label="Add to list" aria-disabled="false"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="24" height="24" class="ipc-icon ipc-icon--add" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="currentColor" role="presentation"><path d="M18 13h-5v5c0 .55-.45 1-1 1s-1-.45-1-1v-5H6c-.55 0-1-.45-1-1s.45-1 1-1h5V6c0-.55.45-1 1-1s1 .45 1 1v5h5c.55 0 1 .45 1 1s-.45 1-1 1z"></path></svg></button></div></div><div data-testid="dli-bio" class="sc-77f37b3d-2 dpXpaE"><div class="ipc-html-content ipc-html-content--base sc-77f37b3d-3 huKIYr" role="presentation"><div class="ipc-html-content-inner-div" role="presentation">Jack Nicholson, an American actor, producer, director and screenwriter, is a three-time Academy Award winner and twelve-time nominee. Nicholson is also notable for being one of two actors - the other being <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000323/?ls">Michael Caine</a> - who have received an Oscar nomination in every decade from the &#39;60s through the &#39;00s.<br/><br/>Nicholson was born on April 22, 1937, in Neptune, New Jersey. He was raised believing that his grandmother was his mother, and that his mother, June Frances Nicholson, a showgirl, was his older sister. He discovered the truth in 1975 from a Time magazine journalist who was researching a profile on him. His real father is believed to have been either Donald Furcillo, an Italian American showman, or Eddie King (Edgar Kirschfeld), born in Latvia and also in show business. Jack&#39;s mother&#39;s ancestry was Irish, and smaller amounts of English, German, Scottish, and Welsh.<br/><br/>Nicholson made his film debut in a B-movie titled <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0051500/?ls">The Cry Baby Killer (1958)</a>. His rise in Hollywood was far from meteoric, and for years, he sustained his career with guest spots in television series and a number of <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000339/?ls">Roger Corman</a> films, including <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0054033/?ls">The Little Shop of Horrors (1960)</a>.<br/><br/>Nicholson&#39;s first turn in the director&#39;s chair was for <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0068509/?ls">Drive, He Said (1971)</a>. Before that, he wrote the screenplay for <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0062395/?ls">The Trip (1967)</a>, and co-wrote <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0063049/?ls">Head (1968)</a>, a vehicle for The Monkees. His big break came with <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0064276/?ls">Easy Rider (1969)</a> and his portrayal of liquor-soaked attorney George Hanson, which earned Nicholson his first Oscar nomination. Nicholson&#39;s film career took off in the 1970s with a definitive performance in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0065724/?ls">Five Easy Pieces (1970)</a>. Nicholson&#39;s other notable work during this period includes leading roles in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000591/?ls">Roman Polanski</a>&#39;s noir masterpiece <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0071315/?ls">Chinatown (1974)</a> and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0073486/?ls">One Flew Over the Cuckoo&#39;s Nest (1975)</a>, for which he won his first Best Actor Oscar.<br/><br/>The 1980s kicked off with another career-defining role for Nicholson as Jack Torrance in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000040/?ls">Stanley Kubrick</a>&#39;s adaptation of <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000175/?ls">Stephen King</a>&#39;s novel <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0081505/?ls">The Shining (1980)</a>. A string of well-received films followed, including <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0086425/?ls">Terms of Endearment (1983)</a>, which earned Nicholson his second Oscar; <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0089841/?ls">Prizzi&#39;s Honor (1985)</a>, and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0094332/?ls">The Witches of Eastwick (1987)</a>. He portrayed another renowned villain, The Joker, in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000318/?ls">Tim Burton</a>&#39;s <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0096895/?ls">Batman (1989)</a>. In the 1990s, he starred in such varied films as <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0104257/?ls">A Few Good Men (1992)</a>, for which he received another Oscar nomination, and a dual role in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0116996/?ls">Mars Attacks! (1996)</a>.<br/><br/>Although a glimpse at the darker side of Nicholson&#39;s acting range reappeared in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0407887/?ls">The Departed (2006)</a>, the actor&#39;s most recent roles highlight the physical and emotional complications one faces late in life. The most notable of these is the unapologetically misanthropic Melvin Udall in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0119822/?ls">As Good as It Gets (1997)</a>, for which he won his third Oscar. Shades of this persona are apparent in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0257360/?ls">About Schmidt (2002)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0337741/?ls">Something&#39;s Gotta Give (2003)</a>, and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0825232/?ls">The Bucket List (2007)</a>. In addition to his Academy Awards and Oscar nominations, Nicholson has seven Golden Globe Awards, and received a Kennedy Center Honor in 2001. He also became one of the youngest actors to receive the American Film Institute&#39;s Life Achievement award in 1994.<br/><br/>Nicholson has six children by five different women: <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0629846/?ls">Jennifer Nicholson</a> (b. 1963) from his only marriage to <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0461070/?ls">Sandra Knight</a>, which ended in 1966; <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm3693077/?ls">Caleb Goddard</a> (b. 1970) with <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0065724/?ls">Five Easy Pieces (1970)</a> co-star <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000769/?ls">Susan Anspach</a>, who was automatically adopted by Anspach&#39;s then-husband <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0323813/?ls">Mark Goddard</a>; <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm2162328/?ls">Honey Hollman</a> (b. 1982) with Danish supermodel <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0391248/?ls">Winnie Hollman</a>; <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm1574234/?ls">Lorraine Nicholson</a> (b. 1990) and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm2200658/?ls">Ray Nicholson</a> (b. 1992) with minor actress <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0112779/?ls">Rebecca Broussard</a>; and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm11853291/?ls">Tessa Gourin</a> (b. 1994) with real estate agent <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0332684/?ls">Jennine Marie Gourin</a>. Nicholson&#39;s longest relationship was the 17 nonmonogamous years he spent with <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001378/?ls">Anjelica Huston</a>; this ended when Broussard announced she was pregnant with his child.</div></div></div></div></div></div></li><li class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item"><div class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__c"><div class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__tc"><span class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__t" aria-disabled="false"></span><div class="sc-77f37b3d-0 jCbCZO dli-parent"><div class="sc-77f37b3d-1 gJmTWZ"><div class="sc-7c95f518-0 cDAKkN"><div data-testid="nlib-img-container" class="sc-7c95f518-1 iorieb"><div class="ipc-avatar ipc-avatar--base" role="group"><div class="ipc-media https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMTg3MDYyMDE5OF5BMl5BanBnXkFtZTcwNjgyNTEzNA@@._V1_QL75_UY120_CR18,0,120,120_.jpg 120w" sizes="50vw, (min-width: 480px) 34vw, (min-width: 600px) 26vw, (min-width: class="ipc-lockup-overlay__screen"></div></a></div></div><div class="sc-7c95f518-3 krmPLY"><div data-testid="nlib-meter-const-container"></div><div class="ipc-title ipc-title--base ipc-title--title ipc-title-link-no-icon ipc-title--on-textPrimary sc-7c95f518-2 ghWujX" data-testid="nlib-title"><a href="/name/nm0000008/?ref_=ls_t_3" class="ipc-title-link-wrapper" tabindex="0"><h3 class="ipc-title__text">3. Marlon Brando</h3></a></div><div class="sc-7c95f518-6 iDkHPP"><ul class="ipc-inline-list ipc-inline-list--show-dividers sc-7c95f518-4 lolxqE base" role="presentation" data-testid="nlib-professions"><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Actor</li><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Director</li><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Writer</li></ul><a class="ipc-link ipc-link--base sc-ab9eb9db-0 iRQWod" tabindex="0" aria-disabled="false" data-testid="nlib-known-for-title" href="/title/tt0078788/?ref_=ls_knf_3">Apocalypse Now (1979)</a></div></div></div><div><button data-testid="dli-add-to-list-button" class="ipc-icon-button ipc-icon-button--base ipc-icon-button--onAccent2" title="Add to list" tabindex="0" aria-label="Add to list" aria-disabled="false"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="24" height="24" class="ipc-icon ipc-icon--add" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="currentColor" role="presentation"><path d="M18 13h-5v5c0 .55-.45 1-1 1s-1-.45-1-1v-5H6c-.55 0-1-.45-1-1s.45-1 1-1h5V6c0-.55.45-1 1-1s1 .45 1 1v5h5c.55 0 1 .45 1 1s-.45 1-1 1z"></path></svg></button></div></div><div data-testid="dli-bio" class="sc-77f37b3d-2 dpXpaE"><div class="ipc-html-content ipc-html-content--base sc-77f37b3d-3 huKIYr" role="presentation"><div class="ipc-html-content-inner-div" role="presentation">Marlon Brando is widely considered the greatest movie actor of all
time, rivaled only by the more theatrically oriented
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000059/?ls">Laurence Olivier</a> in terms of esteem.
Unlike Olivier, who preferred the stage to the screen, Brando
concentrated his talents on movies after bidding the Broadway stage
adieu in 1949, a decision for which he was severely criticized when his
star began to dim in the 1960s and he was excoriated for squandering
his talents. No actor ever exerted such a profound influence on
succeeding generations of actors as did Brando. More than 50 years
after he first scorched the screen as Stanley Kowalski in the movie
version of <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0931783/?ls">Tennessee Williams</a>&#39;
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0044081/?ls">A Streetcar Named Desire (1951)</a>
and a quarter-century after his last great performance as Col. Kurtz in
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000338/?ls">Francis Ford Coppola</a>&#39;s
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0078788/?ls">Apocalypse Now (1979)</a>, all
American actors are still being measured by the yardstick that was
Brando. It was if the shadow of
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000858/?ls">John Barrymore</a>, the great
American actor closest to Brando in terms of talent and stardom,
dominated the acting field up until the 1970s. He did not, nor did any
other actor so dominate the public&#39;s consciousness of what WAS an actor
before or since Brando&#39;s 1951 on-screen portrayal of Stanley made him a
cultural icon. Brando eclipsed the reputation of other great actors
circa 1950, such as <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0612847/?ls">Paul Muni</a> and
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0545298/?ls">Fredric March</a>. Only the luster of
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000075/?ls">Spencer Tracy</a>&#39;s reputation hasn&#39;t
dimmed when seen in the starlight thrown off by Brando. However,
neither Tracy nor Olivier created an entire school of acting just by
the force of his personality. Brando did.<br/><br/>Marlon Brando, Jr. was born on April 3, 1924, in Omaha, Nebraska, to
Marlon Brando, Sr., a calcium carbonate salesman, and his artistically
inclined wife, the former Dorothy Julia Pennebaker. &quot;Bud&quot; Brando was
one of three children. His ancestry included English, Irish, German, Dutch, French Huguenot, Welsh, and Scottish;
his surname originated with a distant German immigrant ancestor named
&quot;Brandau.&quot; His oldest sister
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0104720/?ls">Jocelyn Brando</a> was also an actress,
taking after their mother, who engaged in amateur theatricals and
mentored a then-unknown <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000020/?ls">Henry Fonda</a>, another
Nebraska native, in her role as director of the Omaha Community
Playhouse. Frannie, Brando&#39;s other sibling, was a visual artist. Both
Brando sisters contrived to leave the Midwest for New York City,
Jocelyn to study acting and Frannie to study art. Marlon managed to
escape the vocational doldrums forecast for him by his cold, distant
father and his disapproving schoolteachers by striking out for The Big
Apple in 1943, following Jocelyn into the acting profession. Acting was
the only thing he was good at, for which he received praise, so he was
determined to make it his career - a high-school dropout, he had
nothing else to fall back on, having been rejected by the military due
to a knee injury he incurred playing football at Shattuck Military
Academy, Brando Sr.&#39;s alma mater. The school booted Marlon out as
incorrigible before graduation.<br/><br/>Acting was a skill he honed as a child, the lonely son of alcoholic
parents. With his father away on the road, and his mother frequently
intoxicated to the point of stupefaction, the young Bud would play-act
for her to draw her out of her stupor and to attract her attention and
love. His mother was exceedingly neglectful, but he loved her,
particularly for instilling in him a love of nature, a feeling which
informed his character Paul in
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0070849/?ls">Ultimo Tango a Parigi (1972)</a>
(&quot;Last Tango in Paris&quot;) when he is recalling his childhood for his
young lover Jeanne. &quot;I don&#39;t have many good memories,&quot; Paul confesses,
and neither did Brando of his childhood. Sometimes he had to go down to
the town jail to pick up his mother after she had spent the night in
the drunk tank and bring her home, events that traumatized the young
boy but may have been the grain that irritated the oyster of his
talent, producing the pearls of his performances.
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000063/?ls">Anthony Quinn</a>, his Oscar-winning
co-star in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0045296/?ls">Viva Zapata! (1952)</a> told
Brando&#39;s first wife <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0440542/?ls">Anna Kashfi</a>, &quot;I admire
Marlon&#39;s talent, but I don&#39;t envy the pain that created it.&quot;<br/><br/>Brando enrolled in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0685442/?ls">Erwin Piscator</a>&#39;s
Dramatic Workshop at New York&#39;s New School, and was mentored by
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0012245/?ls">Stella Adler</a>, a member of a famous Yiddish
Theatre acting family. Adler helped introduce to the New York stage the
&quot;emotional memory&quot; technique of Russian theatrical actor, director and
impresario
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm2507427/?ls">Konstantin Stanislavski</a>, whose
motto was &quot;Think of your own experiences and use them truthfully.&quot; The
results of this meeting between an actor and the teacher preparing him
for a life in the theater would mark a watershed in American acting and
culture.<br/><br/>Brando made his debut on the boards of Broadway on October 19, 1944, in
&quot;I Remember Mama,&quot; a great success. As a young Broadway actor, Brando
was invited by talent scouts from several different studios to
screen-test for them, but he turned them down because he would not let
himself be bound by the then-standard seven-year contract. Brando would
make his film debut quite some time later in
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0003593/?ls">Fred Zinnemann</a>&#39;s
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0042727/?ls">The Men (1950)</a> for producer
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0006452/?ls">Stanley Kramer</a>. Playing a paraplegic
soldier, Brando brought new levels of realism to the screen, expanding
on the verisimilitude brought to movies by Group Theatre alumni
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0002092/?ls">John Garfield</a>, the predecessor
closest to him in the raw power he projected on-screen. Ironically, it
was Garfield whom producer
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm1245243/?ls">Irene Mayer Selznick</a> had chosen to
play the lead in a new
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0931783/?ls">Tennessee Williams</a> play she was about
to produce, but negotiations broke down when Garfield demanded an
ownership stake in &quot;A Streetcar Named Desire.&quot;
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000044/?ls">Burt Lancaster</a> was next approached, but
couldn&#39;t get out of a prior film commitment. Then director
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001415/?ls">Elia Kazan</a> suggested Brando, whom he had
directed to great effect in
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0027173/?ls">Maxwell Anderson</a>&#39;s play
&quot;Truckline Café,&quot; in which Brando co-starred with
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001500/?ls">Karl Malden</a>, who was to remain a close
friend for the next 60 years.<br/><br/>During the production of &quot;Truckline Café,&quot; Kazan had found that
Brando&#39;s presence was so magnetic, he had to re-block the play to keep
Marlon near other major characters&#39; stage business, as the audience
could not take its eyes off of him. For the scene where Brando&#39;s
character re-enters the stage after killing his wife, Kazan placed him
upstage-center, partially obscured by scenery, but where the audience
could still see him as <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001500/?ls">Karl Malden</a> and
others played out their scene within the café set. When he eventually
entered the scene, crying, the effect was electric. A young
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0434461/?ls">Pauline Kael</a>, arriving late to the play,
had to avert her eyes when Brando made this entrance as she believed
the young actor on stage was having a real-life conniption. She did not
look back until her escort commented that the young man was a great
actor.<br/><br/>The problem with casting Brando as Stanley was that he was much younger
than the character as written by Williams. However, after a meeting
between Brando and Williams, the playwright eagerly agreed that Brando
would make an ideal Stanley. Williams believed that by casting a
younger actor, the Neanderthalish Kowalski would evolve from being a
vicious older man to someone whose unintentional cruelty can be
attributed to his youthful ignorance. Brando ultimately was
dissatisfied with his performance, though, saying he never was able to
bring out the humor of the character, which was ironic as his
characterization often drew laughs from the audience at the expense of
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001788/?ls">Jessica Tandy</a>&#39;s Blanche Dubois. During the
out-of-town tryouts, Kazan realized that Brando&#39;s magnetism was
attracting attention and audience sympathy away from Blanche to
Stanley, which was not what the playwright intended. The audience&#39;s
sympathy should be solely with Blanche, but many spectators were
identifying with Stanley. Kazan queried Williams on the matter,
broaching the idea of a slight rewrite to tip the scales back to more
of a balance between Stanley and Blanche, but Williams demurred,
smitten as he was by Brando, just like the preview audiences.<br/><br/>For his part, Brando believed that the audience sided with his Stanley
because <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001788/?ls">Jessica Tandy</a> was too shrill. He
thought <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000046/?ls">Vivien Leigh</a>, who played the part
in the movie, was ideal, as she was not only a great beauty but she WAS
Blanche Dubois, troubled as she was in her real life by mental illness
and nymphomania. Brando&#39;s appearance as Stanley on stage and on screen
revolutionized American acting by introducing &quot;The Method&quot; into
American consciousness and culture. Method acting, rooted in Adler&#39;s
study at the Moscow Art Theatre of Stanislavsky&#39;s theories that she
subsequently introduced to the Group Theatre, was a more naturalistic
style of performing, as it engendered a close identification of the
actor with the character&#39;s emotions. Adler took first place among
Brando&#39;s acting teachers, and socially she helped turn him from an
unsophisticated Midwestern farm boy into a knowledgeable and
cosmopolitan artist who one day would socialize with presidents.<br/><br/>Brando didn&#39;t like the term &quot;The Method,&quot; which quickly became the
prominent paradigm taught by such acting gurus as
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0833448/?ls">Lee Strasberg</a> at the Actors Studio. Brando
denounced Strasberg in his autobiography &quot;Songs My Mother Taught Me&quot;
(1994), saying that he was a talentless exploiter who claimed he had
been Brando&#39;s mentor. The Actors Studio had been founded by Strasberg
along with Kazan and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0012245/?ls">Stella Adler</a>&#39;s
husband, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0167353/?ls">Harold Clurman</a>, all Group
Theatre alumni, all political progressives deeply committed to the
didactic function of the stage. Brando credits his knowledge of the
craft to Adler and Kazan, while Kazan in his autobiography &quot;A Life&quot;
claimed that Brando&#39;s genius thrived due to the thorough training Adler
had given him. Adler&#39;s method emphasized that authenticity in acting is
achieved by drawing on inner reality to expose deep emotional
experience<br/><br/>Interestingly, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001415/?ls">Elia Kazan</a> believed that
Brando had ruined two generations of actors, his contemporaries and
those who came after him, all wanting to emulate the great Brando by
employing The Method. Kazan felt that Brando was never a Method actor,
that he had been highly trained by Adler and did not rely on gut
instincts for his performances, as was commonly believed. Many a young
actor, mistaken about the true roots of Brando&#39;s genius, thought that
all it took was to find a character&#39;s motivation, empathize with the
character through sense and memory association, and regurgitate it all
on stage to become the character. That&#39;s not how the superbly trained
Brando did it; he could, for example, play accents, whereas your
average American Method actor could not. There was a method to Brando&#39;s
art, Kazan felt, but it was not The Method.<br/><br/>After
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0044081/?ls">A Streetcar Named Desire (1951)</a>,
for which he received the first of his eight Academy Award nominations,
Brando appeared in a string of Academy Award-nominated performances -
in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0045296/?ls">Viva Zapata! (1952)</a>,
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0045943/?ls">Julius Caesar (1953)</a> and the summit
of his early career, Kazan&#39;s
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0047296/?ls">On the Waterfront (1954)</a>. For
his &quot;Waterfront&quot; portrayal of meat-headed longshoreman Terry Malloy,
the washed-up pug who &quot;coulda been a contender,&quot; Brando won his first
Oscar. Along with his iconic performance as the rebel-without-a-cause
Johnny in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0047677/?ls">The Wild One (1953)</a> (&quot;What
are you rebelling against?&quot; Johnny is asked. &quot;What have ya got?&quot; is his
reply), the first wave of his career was, according to
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000685/?ls">Jon Voight</a>, unprecedented in its audacious
presentation of such a wide range of great acting. Director
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001379/?ls">John Huston</a> said his performance of
Marc Antony was like seeing the door of a furnace opened in a dark
room, and co-star <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000024/?ls">John Gielgud</a>, the premier
Shakespearean actor of the 20th century, invited Brando to join his
repertory company.<br/><br/>It was this period of 1951-54 that revolutionized American acting,
spawning such imitators as <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000015/?ls">James Dean</a> - who modeled his acting and even his lifestyle on his hero Brando - the young <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000056/?ls">Paul Newman</a> and
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000537/?ls">Steve McQueen</a>. After Brando, every up-and-coming star with true acting talent and a brooding, alienated quality would be hailed as the &quot;New Brando,&quot; such as
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000886/?ls">Warren Beatty</a> in Kazan&#39;s
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0055471/?ls">Splendor in the Grass (1961)</a>.
&quot;We are all Brando&#39;s children,&quot;
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000197/?ls">Jack Nicholson</a> pointed out in
1972. &quot;He gave us our freedom.&quot; He was truly &quot;The Godfather&quot; of
American acting - and he was just 30 years old. Though he had a couple of failures, like <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0046903/?ls">Désirée (1954)</a> and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0049830/?ls">The Teahouse of the August Moon (1956)</a>, he was clearly miscast in them and hadn&#39;t sought out the parts so largely escaped blame.<br/><br/>In the second period of his career, 1955-62, Brando managed to uniquely
establish himself as a great actor who also was a Top 10 movie star,
although that star began to dim after the box-office high point of his
early career, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0050933/?ls">Sayonara (1957)</a> (for which
he received his fifth Best Actor Oscar nomination). Brando tried his
hand at directing a film, the well-reviewed
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0055257/?ls">One-Eyed Jacks (1961)</a> that he made
for his own production company, Pennebaker Productions (after his
mother&#39;s maiden name). <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000040/?ls">Stanley Kubrick</a>
had been hired to direct the film, but after months of script rewrites
in which Brando participated, Kubrick and Brando had a falling out and
Kubrick was sacked. According to his widow
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0473583/?ls">Christiane Kubrick</a>, Stanley believed
that Brando had wanted to direct the film himself all along.<br/><br/>Tales proliferated about the profligacy of Brando the director, burning
up a million and a half feet of expensive VistaVision film at 50 cents
a foot, fully ten times the normal amount of raw stock expended during
production of an equivalent motion picture. Brando took so long editing
the film that he was never able to present the studio with a cut.
Paramount took it away from him and tacked on a re-shot ending that
Brando was dissatisfied with, as it made the Oedipal figure of Dad
Longworth into a villain. In any normal film Dad would have been the
heavy, but Brando believed that no one was innately evil, that it was a
matter of an individual responding to, and being molded by, one&#39;s
environment. It was not a black-and-white world, Brando felt, but a
gray world in which once-decent people could do horrible things. This
attitude explains his sympathetic portrayal of Nazi officer Christian
Diestl in the film he made before shooting
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0055257/?ls">One-Eyed Jacks (1961)</a>,
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0229424/?ls">Edward Dmytryk</a>&#39;s filming of
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0789758/?ls">Irwin Shaw</a>&#39;s novel
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0052415/?ls">The Young Lions (1958)</a>. Shaw
denounced Brando&#39;s performance, but audiences obviously disagreed, as
the film was a major hit. It would be the last hit movie Brando would
have for more than a decade.<br/><br/><a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0055257/?ls">One-Eyed Jacks (1961)</a> generated
respectable numbers at the box office, but the production costs were
exorbitant - a then-staggering $6 million - which made it run a
deficit. A film essentially is &quot;made&quot; in the editing room, and Brando
found cutting to be a terribly boring process, which was why the studio
eventually took the film away from him. Despite his proved talent in
handling actors and a large production, Brando never again directed
another film, though he would claim that all actors essentially direct
themselves during the shooting of a picture.<br/><br/>Between the production and release of
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0055257/?ls">One-Eyed Jacks (1961)</a>, Brando
appeared in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001486/?ls">Sidney Lumet</a>&#39;s film version of
Tennessee Williams&#39; play &quot;Orpheus Descending,&quot;
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0052832/?ls">The Fugitive Kind (1960)</a> which
teamed him with fellow Oscar winners
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0536167/?ls">Anna Magnani</a> and
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0940946/?ls">Joanne Woodward</a>. Following in
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000072/?ls">Elizabeth Taylor</a>&#39;s trailblazing
footsteps, Brando became the second performer to receive a $1-million
salary for a motion picture, so high were the expectations for this
re-teaming of Kowalski and his creator (in 1961 critic
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm1094899/?ls">Hollis Alpert</a> had published a book &quot;Brando
and the Shadow of Stanley Kowalski&quot;). Critics and audiences waiting for
another incendiary display from Brando in a Williams work were
disappointed when the renamed
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0052832/?ls">The Fugitive Kind (1960)</a>
finally released. Though Tennessee was hot, with movie versions of
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0051459/?ls">Cat on a Hot Tin Roof (1958)</a>
and
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0053318/?ls">Suddenly, Last Summer (1959)</a>
burning up the box office and receiving kudos from the Academy of
Motion Picture Arts &amp; Sciences,
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0052832/?ls">The Fugitive Kind (1960)</a> was a
failure. This was followed by the so-so box-office reception of
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0055257/?ls">One-Eyed Jacks (1961)</a> in 1961 and
then by a failure of a more monumental kind:
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0056264/?ls">Mutiny on the Bounty (1962)</a>,
a remake of the famed 1935 film.<br/><br/>Brando signed on to
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0056264/?ls">Mutiny on the Bounty (1962)</a>
after turning down the lead in the
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000180/?ls">David Lean</a> classic
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0056172/?ls">Lawrence of Arabia (1962)</a>
because he didn&#39;t want to spend a year in the desert riding around on a
camel. He received another $1-million salary, plus $200,000 in overages
as the shoot went overtime and over budget. During principal
photography, highly respected director
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0715346/?ls">Carol Reed</a> (an eventual Academy Award
winner) was fired, and his replacement, two-time Oscar winner
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0587277/?ls">Lewis Milestone</a>, was shunted aside by
Brando as Marlon basically took over the direction of the film himself.
The long shoot became so notorious that President
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0448123/?ls">John F. Kennedy</a> asked director
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000697/?ls">Billy Wilder</a> at a cocktail party not &quot;when&quot;
but &quot;if&quot; the &quot;Bounty&quot; shoot would ever be over. The MGM remake of one
of its classic Golden Age films garnered a Best Picture Oscar
nomination and was one of the top grossing films of 1962, yet failed to
go into the black due to its Brobdingnagian budget estimated at $20
million, which is equivalent to $120 million when adjusted for
inflation.<br/><br/>Brando and Taylor, whose
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0056937/?ls">Cleopatra (1963)</a> nearly bankrupted 20th
Century-Fox due to its huge cost overruns (its final budget was more
than twice that of Brando&#39;s
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0056264/?ls">Mutiny on the Bounty (1962)</a>),
were pilloried by the show business press for being the epitome of the
pampered, self-indulgent stars who were ruining the industry. Seeking
scapegoats, the Hollywood press conveniently ignored the financial
pressures on the studios. The studios had been hurt by television and
by the antitrust-mandated divestiture of their movie theater chains,
causing a large outflow of production to Italy and other countries in
the 1950s and 1960s in order to lower costs. The studio bosses, seeking
to replicate such blockbuster hits as the remakes of
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0049833/?ls">The Ten Commandments (1956)</a>
and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0052618/?ls">Ben-Hur (1959)</a>, were the real
culprits behind the losses generated by large-budgeted films that found
it impossible to recoup their costs despite long lines at the box
office.<br/><br/>While Elizabeth Taylor, receiving the unwanted gift of reams of
publicity from her adulterous romance with
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0056937/?ls">Cleopatra (1963)</a> co-star
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000009/?ls">Richard Burton</a>, remained hot
until the tanking of her own Tennessee Williams-renamed debacle
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0062751/?ls">Boom (1968)</a>, Brando from 1963 until the end
of the decade appeared in one box-office failure after another as he
worked out a contract he had signed with Universal Pictures. The
industry had grown tired of Brando and his idiosyncrasies, though he
continued to be offered prestige projects up through 1968.<br/><br/>Some of the films Brando made in the 1960s were noble failures, such as
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0056632/?ls">The Ugly American (1963)</a>,
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0060120/?ls">The Appaloosa (1966)</a> and
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0062185/?ls">Reflections in a Golden Eye (1967)</a>.
For every &quot;Reflections,&quot; though, there seemed to be two or three
outright debacles, such as
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0057878/?ls">Bedtime Story (1964)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0059470/?ls">Morituri (1965)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0060232/?ls">The Chase (1966)</a>,
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0061523/?ls">A Countess from Hong Kong (1967)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0062776/?ls">Candy (1968)</a>,
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0064728/?ls">The Night of the Following Day (1969)</a>.
By the time Brando began making the anti-colonialist picture
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0064866/?ls">Burn! (1969)</a> in Colombia with
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0690597/?ls">Gillo Pontecorvo</a> in the director&#39;s
chair, he was box-office poison, despite having worked in the previous
five years with such top directors as
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0671957/?ls">Arthur Penn</a>,
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001379/?ls">John Huston</a> and the legendary
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000122/?ls">Charles Chaplin</a>, and with such
top-drawer co-stars as <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000057/?ls">David Niven</a>,
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000989/?ls">Yul Brynner</a>,
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000047/?ls">Sophia Loren</a> and Taylor.<br/><br/>The rap on Brando in the 1960s was that a great talent had ruined his
potential to be America&#39;s answer to
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000059/?ls">Laurence Olivier</a>, as his friend
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0714835/?ls">William Redfield</a> limned the dilemma in
his book &quot;Letters from an Actor&quot; (1967), a memoir about Redfield&#39;s
appearance in Burton&#39;s 1964 theatrical production of &quot;Hamlet.&quot; By
failing to go back on stage and recharge his artistic batteries,
something British actors such as Burton were not afraid to do, Brando
had stifled his great talent, by refusing to tackle the classical
repertoire and contemporary drama. Actors and critics had yearned for
an American response to the high-acting style of the Brits, and while
Method actors such as <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001768/?ls">Rod Steiger</a> tried to
create an American style, they were hampered in their quest, as their
king was lost in a wasteland of Hollywood movies that were beneath his
talent. Many of his early supporters now turned on him, claiming he was
a crass sellout.<br/><br/>Despite evidence in such films as
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0060120/?ls">The Appaloosa (1966)</a> and
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0062185/?ls">Reflections in a Golden Eye (1967)</a>
that Brando was in fact doing some of the best acting of his life,
critics, perhaps with an eye on the box office, slammed him for failing
to live up to, and nurture, his great gift. Brando&#39;s political
activism, starting in the early 1960s with his championing of Native
Americans&#39; rights, followed by his participation in the Southern
Christian Leadership Conference&#39;s March on Washington in 1963, and
followed by his appearance at a Black Panther rally in 1968, did not
win him many admirers in the establishment. In fact, there was a de
facto embargo on Brando films in the recently segregated (officially,
at least) southeastern US in the 1960s. Southern exhibitors simply
would not book his films, and producers took notice. After 1968, Brando
would not work for three years.<br/><br/><a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0434461/?ls">Pauline Kael</a> wrote of Brando that he was
Fortune&#39;s fool. She drew a parallel with the latter career of
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000858/?ls">John Barrymore</a>, a similarly
gifted thespian with talents as prodigious, who seemingly threw them
away. Brando, like the late-career Barrymore, had become a great ham,
evidenced by his turn as the faux Indian guru in the egregious
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0062776/?ls">Candy (1968)</a>, seemingly because the
material was so beneath his talent. Most observers of Brando in the
1960s believed that he needed to be reunited with his old mentor
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001415/?ls">Elia Kazan</a>, a relationship that had soured
due to Kazan&#39;s friendly testimony naming names before the notorious
House un-American Activities Committee. Perhaps Brando believed this,
too, as he originally accepted an offer to appear as the star of
Kazan&#39;s film adaptation of his own novel,
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0064041/?ls">The Arrangement (1969)</a>. However,
after the assassination of
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0455052/?ls">Martin Luther King</a>, Brando backed out
of the film, telling Kazan that he could not appear in a Hollywood film
after this tragedy. Also reportedly turning down a role opposite
box-office king <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000056/?ls">Paul Newman</a> in a
surefire script,
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0064115/?ls">Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid (1969)</a>,
Brando decided to make <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0064866/?ls">Burn! (1969)</a>
with Pontecorvo. The film, a searing indictment of racism and
colonialism, flopped at the box office but won the esteem of
progressive critics and cultural arbiters such as
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0957016/?ls">Howard Zinn</a>. He subsequently appeared in the British film <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0069007/?ls">The Nightcomers (1971)</a>, a prequel to &quot;Turn of the Screw&quot; and another critical and box office failure.<br/><br/>Kazan, after a life in film and the theater, said that, aside from
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000080/?ls">Orson Welles</a>, whose greatness lay in
film making, he only met one actor who was a genius: Brando. Richard
Burton, an intellectual with a keen eye for observation if not for his
own film projects, said that he found Brando to be very bright, unlike
the public perception of him as a Terry Malloy-type character that he
himself inadvertently promoted through his boorish behavior. Brando&#39;s
problem, Burton felt, was that he was unique, and that he had gotten
too much fame too soon at too early an age. Cut off from being nurtured
by normal contact with society, fame had distorted Brando&#39;s personality
and his ability to cope with the world, as he had not had time to grow
up outside the limelight.<br/><br/><a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001986/?ls">Truman Capote</a>, who eviscerated Brando in
print in the mid-&#39;50s and had as much to do with the public perception
of the dyslexic Brando as a dumbbell, always said that the best actors
were ignorant, and that an intelligent person could not be a good
actor. However, Brando was highly intelligent, and possessed of a rare
genius in a then-deprecated art, acting. The problem that an
intelligent performer has in movies is that it is the director, and not
the actor, who has the power in his chosen field. Greatness in the
other arts is defined by how much control the artist is able to exert
over his chosen medium, but in movie acting, the medium is controlled
by a person outside the individual artist. It is an axiom of the cinema
that a performance, as is a film, is &quot;created&quot; in the cutting room,
thus further removing the actor from control over his art. Brando had
tried his hand at directing, in controlling the whole artistic
enterprise, but he could not abide the cutting room, where a film and
the film&#39;s performances are made. This lack of control over his art was
the root of Brando&#39;s discontent with acting, with movies, and,
eventually, with the whole wide world that invested so much cachet in
movie actors, as long as &quot;they&quot; were at the top of the box-office
charts. Hollywood was a matter of &quot;they&quot; and not the work, and Brando
became disgusted.<br/><br/><a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000032/?ls">Charlton Heston</a>, who participated in
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0455052/?ls">Martin Luther King</a>&#39;s 1963 March on
Washington with Brando, believes that Marlon was the great actor of his
generation. However, noting a story that Brando had once refused a role
in the early 1960s with the excuse &quot;How can I act when people are
starving in India?,&quot; Heston believes that it was this attitude, the
inability to separate one&#39;s idealism from one&#39;s work, that prevented
Brando from reaching his potential. As
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001768/?ls">Rod Steiger</a> once said, Brando had it all,
great stardom and a great talent. He could have taken his audience on a
trip to the stars, but he simply would not. Steiger, one of Brando&#39;s
children even though a contemporary, could not understand it. When
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000051/?ls">James Mason</a>&#39; was asked in 1971 who
was the best American actor, he had replied that since Brando had let
his career go belly-up, it had to be
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001715/?ls">George C. Scott</a>, by default.<br/><br/>Paramount thought that only
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000059/?ls">Laurence Olivier</a> would suffice, but
Lord Olivier was ill. The young director believed there was only one
actor who could play godfather to the group of Young Turk actors he had
assembled for his film, The Godfather of method acting himself - Marlon
Brando. <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000338/?ls">Francis Ford Coppola</a> won
the fight for Brando, Brando won - and refused - his second Oscar, and
Paramount won a pot of gold by producing the then top-grossing film of
all-time, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0068646/?ls">The Godfather (1972)</a>, a
gangster movie most critics now judge one of the greatest American
films of all time. Brando followed his iconic portrayal of Don Corleone
with his Oscar-nominated turn in the high-grossing and highly
scandalous
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0070849/?ls">Ultimo Tango a Parigi (1972)</a>
(&quot;Last Tango in Paris&quot;), the first film dealing explicitly with
sexuality in which an actor of Brando&#39;s stature had participated. He
was now again a top ten box office star and once again heralded as the
greatest actor of his generation, an unprecedented comeback that put
him on the cover of &quot;Time&quot; magazine and would make him the highest-paid
actor in the history of motion pictures by the end of the decade.
Little did the world know that Brando, who had struggled through many
projects in good faith during the 1960s, delivering some of his best
acting, only to be excoriated and ignored as the films did not do well
at the box office, essentially was through with the movies.<br/><br/>After reaching the summit of his career, a rarefied atmosphere never
reached before or since by any actor, Brando essentially walked away.
He would give no more of himself after giving everything as he had done
in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0070849/?ls">Ultimo Tango a Parigi (1972)</a>,&quot; a performance that embarrassed him, according
to his autobiography. Brando had come as close to any actor to being
the &quot;auteur,&quot; or author, of a film, as the English-language scenes of
&quot;Tango&quot; were created by encouraging Brando to improvise. The
improvisations were written down and turned into a shooting script, and
the scripted improvisations were shot the next day.
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0434461/?ls">Pauline Kael</a>, the Brando of movie critics
in that she was the most influential arbiter of cinematic quality of
her generation and spawned a whole legion of Kael wannabes, said
Brando&#39;s performance in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0070849/?ls">Ultimo Tango a Parigi (1972)</a> had revolutionized the art of
film. Brando, who had to act to gain his mother&#39;s attention; Brando,
who believed acting at best was nothing special as everyone in the
world engaged in it every day of their lives to get what they wanted
from other people; Brando, who believed acting at its worst was a
childish charade and that movie stardom was a whorish fraud, would have
agreed with <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001603/?ls">Sam Peckinpah</a>&#39;s summation of
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0434461/?ls">Pauline Kael</a>: &quot;Pauline&#39;s a brilliant critic
but sometimes she&#39;s just cracking walnuts with her ass.&quot; He probably would have done so in a
simulacrum of those words, too.<br/><br/>After another three-year hiatus, Brando took on just one more major
role for the next 20 years, as the bounty hunter after
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000197/?ls">Jack Nicholson</a> in
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0671957/?ls">Arthur Penn</a>&#39;s
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0074906/?ls">The Missouri Breaks (1976)</a>, a
western that succeeded neither with the critics or at the box office. Following The Godfather and Tango, Brando&#39;s performance was disappointing for some reviewers, who accused him of giving an erratic and inconsistent performance. In 1977, Brando made a rare appearance on television in the miniseries <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0078678/?ls">Roots: The Next Generations (1979)</a>, portraying <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0734339/?ls">George Lincoln Rockwell</a>; he won a Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Supporting Actor in a Miniseries or a Movie for his performance. In 1978, he narrated the English version of <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0078140/?ls">Raoni (1978)</a>, a French-Belgian documentary film directed by Jean-Pierre Dutilleux and Luiz Carlos Saldanha that focused on the life of Raoni Metuktire and issues surrounding the survival of the indigenous Indian tribes of north central Brazil.<br/><br/>Later in his career, Brando concentrated on extracting the maximum amount of
capital for the least amount of work from producers, as when he got the
Salkind brothers to pony up a then-record $3.7 million against 10% of
the gross for 13 days work on
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0078346/?ls">Superman (1978)</a>. Factoring in inflation,
the straight salary for &quot;Superman&quot; equals or exceeds the new record of
$1 million a day <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000148/?ls">Harrison Ford</a> set
with
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0267626/?ls">K-19: The Widowmaker (2002)</a>. He agreed to the role only on assurance that he would be paid a large sum for what amounted to a small part, that he would not have to read the script beforehand, and his lines would be displayed somewhere off-camera. Brando also filmed scenes for the movie&#39;s sequel, Superman II, but after producers refused to pay him the same percentage he received for the first movie, he denied them permission to use the footage.<br/><br/>Before cashing his first paycheck for
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0078346/?ls">Superman (1978)</a>, Brando had picked up $2
million for his extended cameo in
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000338/?ls">Francis Ford Coppola</a>&#39;s
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0078788/?ls">Apocalypse Now (1979)</a> in a role,
that of Col. Kurtz, that he authored on-camera through improvisation
while Coppola shot take after take. It was Brando&#39;s last bravura star
performance. He co-starred with <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001715/?ls">George C. Scott</a> and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000024/?ls">John Gielgud</a> in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0080754/?ls">The Formula (1980)</a>, but the film was another critical and financial failure. Years later though, he did receive an eighth and final Oscar nomination
for his supporting role in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0097243/?ls">A Dry White Season (1989)</a>
after coming out of a near-decade-long retirement. Contrary to those
who claimed he now only was in it for the money, Brando donated his
entire seven-figure salary to an anti-apartheid charity. He then did an amusing performance in the comedy <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0099615/?ls">The Freshman (1990)</a>, winning rave reviews. He portrayed Tomas de Torquemada in the historical drama <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0103594/?ls">1492: Conquest of Paradise (1992)</a>, but his performance was denounced and the film was another box office failure. He made another comeback in the <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000136/?ls">Johnny Depp</a> romantic drama <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0112883/?ls">Don Juan DeMarco (1994)</a>, which co-starred <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001159/?ls">Faye Dunaway</a> as his wife. He then appeared in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0116654/?ls">The Island of Dr. Moreau (1996)</a>, co-starring <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000174/?ls">Val Kilmer</a>, who he didn&#39;t get along with. The filming was an unpleasant experience for Brando, as well as another critical and box office failure.<br/><br/>Brando had first attracted media attention at the age of 24, when
&quot;Life&quot; magazine ran a photo of himself and his sister Jocelyn, who were
both then appearing on Broadway. The curiosity continued, and
snowballed. Playing the paraplegic soldier of
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0042727/?ls">The Men (1950)</a>, Brando had gone to live
at a Veterans Administration hospital with actual disabled veterans,
and confined himself to a wheelchair for weeks. It was an acting
method, research, that no one in Hollywood had ever heard of before,
and that willingness to experience life.</div></div></div></div></div></div></li><li class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item"><div class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__c"><div class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__tc"><span class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__t" aria-disabled="false"></span><div class="sc-77f37b3d-0 jCbCZO dli-parent"><div class="sc-77f37b3d-1 gJmTWZ"><div class="sc-7c95f518-0 cDAKkN"><div data-testid="nlib-img-container" class="sc-7c95f518-1 iorieb"><div class="ipc-avatar ipc-avatar--base" role="group"><div class="ipc-media ipc-media--avatar ipc-image-media-ratio--avatar ipc-media--circle-radius ipc-media--base ipc-media--custom ipc-avatar__avatar-image ipc-media__img" style="width:60px"><img alt="Denzel Washington" class="ipc-image" loading="lazy" src="https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMjE5NDU2Mzc3MV5BMl5BanBnXkFtZTcwNjAwNTE5OQ@@._V1_QL75_UX60_CR0,0,60,60_.jpg" srcSet="https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMjE5NDU2Mzc3MV5BMl5BanBnXkFtZTcwNjAwNTE5OQ@@._V1_QL75_UX60_CR0,0,60,60_.jpg 60w, https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMjE5NDU2Mzc3MV5BMl5BanBnXkFtZTcwNjAwNTE5OQ@@._V1_QL75_UX90_CR0,0,90,90_.jpg 90w, https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMjE5NDU2Mzc3MV5BMl5BanBnXkFtZTcwNjAwNTE5OQ@@._V1_QL75_UX120_CR0,0,120,120_.jpg 120w" sizes="50vw, (min-width: 480px) 34vw, (min-width: 600px) 26vw, (min-width: 1024px) 16vw, (min-width: 1280px) 16vw" width="60"/></div><a class="ipc-lockup-overlay ipc-focusable" href="/name/nm0000243/?ref_=ls_i_4" aria-label="Denzel Washington"><div class="ipc-lockup-overlay__screen"></div></a></div></div><div class="sc-7c95f518-3 krmPLY"><div data-testid="nlib-meter-const-container"></div><div class="ipc-title ipc-title--base ipc-title--title ipc-title-link-no-icon ipc-title--on-textPrimary sc-7c95f518-2 ghWujX" data-testid="nlib-title"><a href="/name/nm0000243/?ref_=ls_t_4" class="ipc-title-link-wrapper" tabindex="0"><h3 class="ipc-title__text">4. Denzel Washington</h3></a></div><div class="sc-7c95f518-6 iDkHPP"><ul class="ipc-inline-list ipc-inline-list--show-dividers sc-7c95f518-4 lolxqE base" role="presentation" data-testid="nlib-professions"><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Actor</li><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Producer</li><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Director</li></ul><a class="ipc-link ipc-link--base sc-ab9eb9db-0 iRQWod" tabindex="0" aria-disabled="false" data-testid="nlib-known-for-title" href="/title/tt2671706/?ref_=ls_knf_4">Fences (2016)</a></div></div></div><div><button data-testid="dli-add-to-list-button" class="ipc-icon-button ipc-icon-button--base ipc-icon-button--onAccent2" title="Add to list" tabindex="0" aria-label="Add to list" aria-disabled="false"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="24" height="24" class="ipc-icon ipc-icon--add" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="currentColor" role="presentation"><path d="M18 13h-5v5c0 .55-.45 1-1 1s-1-.45-1-1v-5H6c-.55 0-1-.45-1-1s.45-1 1-1h5V6c0-.55.45-1 1-1s1 .45 1 1v5h5c.55 0 1 .45 1 1s-.45 1-1 1z"></path></svg></button></div></div><div data-testid="dli-bio" class="sc-77f37b3d-2 dpXpaE"><div class="ipc-html-content ipc-html-content--base sc-77f37b3d-3 huKIYr" role="presentation"><div class="ipc-html-content-inner-div" role="presentation">Denzel Hayes Washington, Jr. was born on December 28, 1954 in Mount Vernon, New York. He is the middle of three children of a beautician mother, Lennis, from Georgia, and a Pentecostal minister father, Denzel Washington, Sr., from Virginia. After graduating from high school, Denzel enrolled at Fordham University, intent on a career in journalism. However, he caught the acting bug while appearing in student drama productions and, upon graduation, he moved to San Francisco and enrolled at the American Conservatory Theater. He left A.C.T. after only one year to seek work as an actor. His first paid acting role was in a summer stock theater stage production in St. Mary&#39;s City, Maryland. The play was &quot;Wings of the Morning&quot;, which is about the founding of the colony of Maryland (now the state of Maryland) and the early days of the Maryland colonial assembly (a legislative body). He played the part of a real historical character, Mathias Da Sousa, although much of the dialogue was created. Afterwards he began to pursue screen roles in earnest. With his acting versatility and powerful presence, he had no difficulty finding work in numerous television productions.<br/><br/>He made his first big screen appearance in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0082138/?ls">Carbon Copy (1981)</a> with <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001719/?ls">George Segal</a>. Through the 1980s, he worked in both movies and television and was chosen for the plum role of Dr. Philip Chandler in NBC&#39;s hit medical series <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0083483/?ls">St. Elsewhere (1982)</a>, a role that he would play for six years. In 1989, his film career began to take precedence when he won the Oscar for Best Supporting Actor for his portrayal of Tripp, the runaway slave in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001880/?ls">Edward Zwick</a>&#39;s powerful historical masterpiece <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0097441/?ls">Glory (1989)</a>.<br/><br/>Washington has received much critical acclaim for his film work since the 1990s, including his portrayals of real-life figures such as South African anti-apartheid activist Steve Biko in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0092804/?ls">Cry Freedom (1987)</a>, Muslim minister and human rights activist Malcolm X in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0104797/?ls">Malcolm X (1992)</a>, boxer Rubin &quot;Hurricane&quot; Carter in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0174856/?ls">The Hurricane (1999)</a>, football coach Herman Boone in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0210945/?ls">Remember the Titans (2000)</a>, poet and educator Melvin B. Tolson in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0427309/?ls">The Great Debaters (2007)</a>, and drug kingpin Frank Lucas in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0765429/?ls">American Gangster (2007)</a>. Malcolm X and The Hurricane garnered him Oscar nominations for Best Actor, before he finally won that statuette in 2002 for his lead role in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0139654/?ls">Training Day (2001)</a>.<br/><br/>Through the 1990s, Denzel also co-starred in such big budget productions as <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0107798/?ls">The Pelican Brief (1993)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0107818/?ls">Philadelphia (1993)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0112740/?ls">Crimson Tide (1995)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0117372/?ls">The Preacher&#39;s Wife (1996)</a>, and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0115956/?ls">Courage Under Fire (1996)</a>, a role for which he was paid $10 million. He continued to define his onscreen persona as the tough, no-nonsense hero through the 2000s in films like <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0313443/?ls">Out of Time (2003)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0328107/?ls">Man on Fire (2004)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0454848/?ls">Inside Man (2006)</a>, and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt1111422/?ls">The Taking of Pelham 1 2 3 (2009)</a>. Cerebral and meticulous in his film work, he made his debut as a director with <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0168786/?ls">Antwone Fisher (2002)</a>; he also directed <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0427309/?ls">The Great Debaters (2007)</a> and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt2671706/?ls">Fences (2016)</a>.<br/><br/>In 2010, Washington headlined <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt1037705/?ls">The Book of Eli (2010)</a>, a post-Apocalyptic drama. Later that year, he starred as a veteran railroad engineer in the action film <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0477080/?ls">Unstoppable (2010)</a>, about an unmanned, half-mile-long runaway freight train carrying dangerous cargo. The film was his fifth and final collaboration with director <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001716/?ls">Tony Scott</a>, following <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0112740/?ls">Crimson Tide (1995)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0328107/?ls">Man on Fire (2004)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt5649074/?ls">Déjà Vu (2006)</a> and The Taking of Pelham 1 2 3. He has also been a featured actor in the films produced by <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000988/?ls">Jerry Bruckheimer</a> and has been a frequent collaborator of director <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000490/?ls">Spike Lee</a>.<br/><br/>In 2012, Washington starred in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt1907668/?ls">Flight (2012)</a>, for which he was nominated for an Academy Award for Best Actor. He co-starred with <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0005351/?ls">Ryan Reynolds</a> in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt1599348/?ls">Safe House (2012)</a>, and prepared for his role by subjecting himself to a torture session that included waterboarding. In 2013, Washington starred in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt1272878/?ls">2 Guns (2013)</a>, alongside <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000242/?ls">Mark Wahlberg</a>. In 2014, he starred in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0455944/?ls">The Equalizer (2014)</a>, an action thriller film directed by <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0298807/?ls">Antoine Fuqua</a> and written by <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0921013/?ls">Richard Wenk</a>, based on the television series of same name starring <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0940919/?ls">Edward Woodward</a>. During this time period, he also took on the role of producer for some of his films, including The Book of Eli and Safe House.<br/><br/>In 2016, he was selected as the recipient for the Cecil B. DeMille Lifetime Achievement Award at the 73rd Golden Globe Awards.<br/><br/>He lives in Los Angeles, California with his wife, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0669353/?ls">Pauletta Washington</a>, and their four children.</div></div></div></div></div></div></li><li class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item"><div class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__c"><div class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__tc"><span class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__t" aria-disabled="false"></span><div class="sc-77f37b3d-0 jCbCZO Meryl Streep</h3></a></div><div class="sc-7c95f518-6 iDkHPP"><ul class="ipc-inline-list ipc-inline-list--show-dividers sc-7c95f518-4 lolxqE base" role="presentation" data-testid="nlib-professions"><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Actress</li><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Writer</li><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Producer</li></ul><a class="ipc-link ipc-link--base sc-ab9eb9db-0 iRQWod" tabindex="0" aria-disabled="false" data-testid="nlib-known-for-title" href="/title/tt0089755/?ref_=ls_knf_5">Out of Africa (1985)</a></div></div></div><div><button data-testid="dli-add-to-list-button" class="ipc-icon-button ipc-icon-button--base ipc-icon-button--onAccent2" title="Add to list" tabindex="0" aria-label="Add to list" aria-disabled="false"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="24" height="24" class="ipc-icon ipc-icon--add" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="currentColor" role="presentation"><path d="M18 13h-5v5c0 .55-.45 1-1 1s-1-.45-1-1v-5H6c-.55 0-1-.45-1-1s.45-1 1-1h5V6c0-.55.45-1 1-1s1 .45 1 1v5h5c.55 0 1 .45 1 1s-.45 1-1 1z"></path></svg></button></div></div><div data-testid="dli-bio" class="sc-77f37b3d-2 dpXpaE"><div class="ipc-html-content ipc-html-content--base sc-77f37b3d-3 huKIYr" role="presentation"><div class="ipc-html-content-inner-div" role="presentation">Considered by many critics to be the greatest living actress, Meryl
Streep has been nominated for the Academy Award an astonishing 21
times, and has won it three times. Meryl was born Mary Louise Streep in
1949 in Summit, New Jersey, to Mary Wolf (Wilkinson), a commercial
artist, and Harry William Streep, Jr., a pharmaceutical executive. Her
father was of German and Swiss-German descent, and her mother had English, Irish, and German ancestry.<br/><br/>Meryl&#39;s early performing ambitions leaned toward the opera. She became
interested in acting while a student at Vassar and upon graduation she
enrolled in the Yale School of Drama. She gave an outstanding
performance in her first film role,
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0076245/?ls">Julia (1977)</a>, and the next year she was
nominated for her first Oscar for her role in
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0077416/?ls">The Deer Hunter (1978)</a>. She went
on to win the Academy Award for her performances in
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0079417/?ls">Kramer vs. Kramer (1979)</a> and
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0084707/?ls">Sophie&#39;s Choice (1982)</a>, in which
she gave a heart-wrenching portrayal of an inmate mother in a Nazi
death camp.<br/><br/>A perfectionist in her craft and meticulous and painstaking in her
preparation for her roles, Meryl turned out a string of highly
acclaimed performances over the next decade in great films like
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0086312/?ls">Silkwood (1983)</a>;
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0089755/?ls">Out of Africa (1985)</a>;
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0093277/?ls">Ironweed (1987)</a>; and
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0094924/?ls">Evil Angels (1988)</a>. Her career
declined slightly in the early 1990s as a result of her inability to
find suitable parts, but she shot back to the top in 1995 with her
performance as <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000142/?ls">Clint Eastwood</a>&#39;s
married lover in
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0112579/?ls">Sacrifice (1995)</a>
and as the prodigal daughter in
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0116999/?ls">Marvin&#39;s Room (1996)</a>. In 1998 she
made her first venture into the area of producing, and was the
executive producer for the moving
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0118526/?ls">...First Do No Harm (1997)</a>.
A realist when she talks about her future years in film, she remarked
that &quot;...no matter what happens, my work will stand...&quot;</div></div></div></div></div></div></li><li class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item"><div class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__c"><div class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__tc"><span class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__t" aria-disabled="false"></span><div class="sc-77f37b3d-0 jCbCZO dli-parent"><div class="sc-77f37b3d-1 gJmTWZ"><div class="sc-7c95f518-0 cDAKkN"><div data-testid="nlib-img-container" class="sc-7c95f518-1 iorieb"><div class="ipc-avatar ipc-avatar--base" role="group"><div class="ipc-media https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BNDc5YThiZjAtMjYwZi00YjllLTlkYjEtNjQyYTFiZTU3ZTM5XkEyXkFqcGc@._V1_QL75_UX90_CR0,0,90,90_.jpg 90w,
