class="ipc-lockup-overlay__screen"></div></a></div></div><div class="sc-7c95f518-3 krmPLY"><div data-testid="nlib-meter-const-container"></div><div class="ipc-title ipc-title--base ipc-title--title ipc-title-link-no-icon ipc-title--on-textPrimary sc-7c95f518-2 ghWujX" data-testid="nlib-title"><a href="/name/nm0000072/?ref_=ls_t_14" class="ipc-title-link-wrapper" tabindex="0"><h3 class="ipc-title__text">14. Elizabeth Taylor</h3></a></div><div class="sc-7c95f518-6 iDkHPP"><ul class="ipc-inline-list ipc-inline-list--show-dividers sc-7c95f518-4 lolxqE base" role="presentation" data-testid="nlib-professions"><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Actress</li><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Producer</li><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Soundtrack</li></ul><a class="ipc-link ipc-link--base sc-ab9eb9db-0 iRQWod" tabindex="0" aria-disabled="false" data-testid="nlib-known-for-title" href="/title/tt0061184/?ref_=ls_knf_14">Who&#x27;s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? (1966)</a></div></div></div><div><button data-testid="dli-add-to-list-button" class="ipc-icon-button ipc-icon-button--base ipc-icon-button--onAccent2" title="Add to list" tabindex="0" aria-label="Add to list" aria-disabled="false"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="24" height="24" class="ipc-icon ipc-icon--add" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="currentColor" role="presentation"><path d="M18 13h-5v5c0 .55-.45 1-1 1s-1-.45-1-1v-5H6c-.55 0-1-.45-1-1s.45-1 1-1h5V6c0-.55.45-1 1-1s1 .45 1 1v5h5c.55 0 1 .45 1 1s-.45 1-1 1z"></path></svg></button></div></div><div data-testid="dli-bio" class="sc-77f37b3d-2 dpXpaE"><div class="ipc-html-content ipc-html-content--base sc-77f37b3d-3 huKIYr" role="presentation"><div class="ipc-html-content-inner-div" role="presentation">Elizabeth Rosemond Taylor was considered one of the last, if not the last, major star to have come out of the old Hollywood studio system. She was known internationally for her beauty, especially for her violet eyes, with which she captured audiences early in her youth and kept the world hooked with ever after.<br/><br/>Taylor was born on February 27, 1932 in London, England. Although she was born an English subject, her parents, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm1192416/?ls">Sara Taylor</a> (née Sara Viola Warmbrodt) and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm1259816/?ls">Francis Taylor</a>, were Americans, art dealers from St. Louis, Missouri. Her father had moved to London to set up a gallery prior to Elizabeth&#39;s birth. Her mother had been an actress on the stage, but gave up that vocation when she married. Elizabeth lived in London until the age of seven, when the family left for the US when the clouds of war began brewing in Europe in 1939. They sailed without her father, who stayed behind to wrap up the loose ends of the art business.<br/><br/>The family relocated to Los Angeles, where Mrs. Taylor&#39;s own family had moved. Mr. Taylor followed not long afterward. A family friend noticed the strikingly beautiful little Elizabeth and suggested that she be taken for a screen test. Her test impressed executives at Universal Pictures enough to sign her to a contract. Her first foray onto the screen was in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0035427/?ls">There&#39;s One Born Every Minute (1942)</a>, released when she was ten. Universal dropped her contract after that one film, but Elizabeth was soon picked up by MGM.<br/><br/>The first production she made with that studio was <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0036098/?ls">Lassie Come Home (1943)</a>, and on the strength of that one film, MGM signed her for a full year. She had minuscule parts in her next two films, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0037462/?ls">The White Cliffs of Dover (1944)</a> and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0036969/?ls">Jane Eyre (1943)</a> (the former made while she was on loan to 20th Century-Fox). Then came the picture that made Elizabeth a star: MGM&#39;s <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0037120/?ls">National Velvet (1944)</a>. She played Velvet Brown opposite <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001682/?ls">Mickey Rooney</a>. The film was a smash hit, grossing over $4 million. Elizabeth now had a long-term contract with MGM and was its top child star. She made no films in 1945, but returned in 1946 in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0038427/?ls">Courage of Lassie (1946)</a>, another success. In 1947, when she was 15, she starred in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0039566/?ls">Papa Gutta (1947)</a> with such heavyweights as <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001635/?ls">William Powell</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0002050/?ls">Irene Dunne</a> and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0686032/?ls">Zasu Pitts</a>, which was one of the biggest box office hits of the year. She also co-starred in the ensemble film <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0041594/?ls">Little Women (1949)</a>, which was also a box office huge success.<br/><br/>Throughout the 1950s, Elizabeth appeared in film after film with mostly good results, starting with her role in the <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0828419/?ls">George Stevens</a> film <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0043924/?ls">A Place in the Sun (1951)</a>, co-starring her good friend <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001050/?ls">Montgomery Clift</a>. The following year, she co-starred in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0044760/?ls">Ivanhoe (1952)</a>, one of the biggest box office hits of the year. Her busiest year was 1954. She had a supporting role in the box office flop <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0046759/?ls">Beau Brummell (1954)</a>, but later that year starred in the hits <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0047162/?ls">The Last Time I Saw Paris (1954)</a> and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0046951/?ls">Elephant Walk (1954)</a>. She was 22 now, and even at that young age was considered one of the world&#39;s great beauties. In 1955 she appeared in the hit <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0049261/?ls">Giant (1956)</a> with <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000015/?ls">James Dean</a>.<br/><br/>Sadly, Dean never saw the release of the film, as he died in a car accident in 1955. The next year saw Elizabeth co-star with <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001050/?ls">Montgomery Clift</a> in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0050882/?ls">Raintree County (1957)</a>, an overblown epic made, partially, in Kentucky. Critics called it dry as dust. In addition, Clift was seriously injured during the film, with Taylor helping save his life. Despite the film&#39;s shortcomings and off-camera tragedy, Elizabeth was nominated for an Academy Award for her portrayal of Southern belle Susanna Drake. However, on Oscar night the honor went to <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0940946/?ls">Joanne Woodward</a> for <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0051077/?ls">The Three Faces of Eve (1957)</a>.<br/><br/>In 1958 Elizabeth starred as Maggie Pollitt in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0051459/?ls">Cat on a Hot Tin Roof (1958)</a>. The film received rave reviews from the critics and Elizabeth was nominated again for an Academy Award for best actress, but this time she lost to <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001333/?ls">Susan Hayward</a> in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0051758/?ls">I Want to Live! (1958)</a>. She was still a hot commodity in the film world, though. In 1959 she appeared in another mega-hit and received yet another Oscar nomination for <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0053318/?ls">Suddenly, Last Summer (1959)</a>. Once again, however, she lost out, this time to <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0797531/?ls">Simone Signoret</a> for <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0053226/?ls">Room at the Top (1958)</a>. Her Oscar drought ended in 1960 when she brought home the coveted statue for her performance in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0053622/?ls">BUtterfield 8 (1960)</a> as Gloria Wandrous, a call girl who is involved with a married man. Some critics blasted the movie but they couldn&#39;t ignore her performance. There were no more films for Elizabeth for three years. She left MGM after her contract ran out, but would do projects for the studio later down the road. In 1963 she starred in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0056937/?ls">Cleopatra (1963)</a>, which was one of the most expensive productions up to that time--as was her salary, a whopping $1,000,000. The film took years to complete, due in part to a serious illness during which she nearly died.<br/><br/>This was the film where she met her future and fifth husband, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000009/?ls">Richard Burton</a> (the previous four were Conrad Hilton, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0928697/?ls">Michael Wilding</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0865239/?ls">Mike Todd</a>--who died in a plane crash--and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0279472/?ls">Eddie Fisher</a>). Her next films, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0057634/?ls">The V.I.P.s (1963)</a> and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0059674/?ls">The Sandpiper (1965)</a>, were lackluster at best. Elizabeth was to return to fine form, however, with the role of Martha in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0061184/?ls">Who&#39;s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? (1966)</a>. Her performance as the loudmouthed, shrewish, unkempt, yet still alluring Martha was easily her finest to date. For this she would win her second Oscar and one that was more than well-deserved. The following year, she and Burton co-starred in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0061407/?ls">The Taming of the Shrew (1967)</a>, again giving winning performances. However, her films afterward were box office failures, including <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0062185/?ls">Reflections in a Golden Eye (1967)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0061502/?ls">The Comedians (1967)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0062751/?ls">Boom (1968)</a> (again co-starring with Burton), <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0063571/?ls">Secret Ceremony (1968)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0066184/?ls">The Only Game in Town (1970)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0069516/?ls">Zee and Co (1972)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0068674/?ls">Hammersmith Is Out (1972)</a> (with Burton again), <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0069736/?ls">Ash Wednesday (1973)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0070444/?ls">Night Watch (1973)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0071442/?ls">The Driver&#39;s Seat (1974)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0074225/?ls">The Blue Bird (1976)</a> (considered by many to be her worst), <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0076319/?ls">A Little Night Music (1977)</a>, and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0080139/?ls">Winter Kills (1979)</a> (a controversial film which was never given a full release and in which she only had a small role). She later appeared in some movies, both theatrical and made-for-television, and a number of television programs. In February 1997, Elizabeth entered the hospital for the removal of a brain tumor. The operation was successful. As for her private life, she divorced Burton in 1974, only to remarry him in 1975 and divorce him, permanently, in 1976. She had two more husbands, U.S. Senator <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0992825/?ls">John Warner</a> and construction worker <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm1654794/?ls">Larry Fortensky</a>, whom she met in rehab.<br/><br/>In 1959, Taylor converted to Judaism, and continued to identify herself as Jewish throughout her life, being active in Jewish causes. Upon the death of her friend, actor <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001369/?ls">Rock Hudson</a>, in 1985, she began her crusade on behalf of AIDS sufferers. In the 1990s, she also developed a successful series of scents. In her later years, her acting career was relegated to the occasional TV-movie or TV guest appearance.<br/><br/>Elizabeth Taylor died on March 23, 2011 in Los Angeles, from congestive heart failure. Her final resting place is Forest Lawn Memorial Park, in Glendale, California.</div></div></div></div></div></div></li><li class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item"><div class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__c"><div class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__tc"><span class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__t" aria-disabled="false"></span><div class="sc-77f37b3d-0 jCbCZO dli-parent"><div class="sc-77f37b3d-1 gJmTWZ"><div class="sc-7c95f518-0 cDAKkN"><div data-testid="nlib-img-container" class="sc-7c95f518-1 iorieb"><div class="ipc-avatar ipc-avatar--base" role="group"><div class="ipc-media ipc-media--avatar ipc-image-media-ratio--avatar ipc-media--circle-radius ipc-media--base ipc-media--custom ipc-avatar__avatar-image ipc-media__img" 26vw, (min-width: 1024px) 16vw, (min-width: 1280px) 16vw" width="60"/></div><a class="ipc-lockup-overlay ipc-focusable" href="/name/nm0000012/?ref_=ls_i_15" aria-label="Bette Davis"><div class="ipc-lockup-overlay__screen"></div></a></div></div><div class="sc-7c95f518-3 krmPLY"><div data-testid="nlib-meter-const-container"></div><div class="ipc-title ipc-title--base ipc-title--title ipc-title-link-no-icon ipc-title--on-textPrimary sc-7c95f518-2 ghWujX" data-testid="nlib-title"><a href="/name/nm0000012/?ref_=ls_t_15" class="ipc-title-link-wrapper" tabindex="0"><h3 class="ipc-title__text">15. Bette Davis</h3></a></div><div class="sc-7c95f518-6 iDkHPP"><ul class="ipc-inline-list ipc-inline-list--show-dividers sc-7c95f518-4 lolxqE base" role="presentation" data-testid="nlib-professions"><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Actress</li><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Make-Up Department</li><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Producer</li></ul><a class="ipc-link ipc-link--base sc-ab9eb9db-0 iRQWod" tabindex="0" aria-disabled="false" data-testid="nlib-known-for-title" href="/title/tt0042192/?ref_=ls_knf_15">All About Eve (1950)</a></div></div></div><div><button data-testid="dli-add-to-list-button" class="ipc-icon-button ipc-icon-button--base ipc-icon-button--onAccent2" title="Add to list" tabindex="0" aria-label="Add to list" aria-disabled="false"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="24" height="24" class="ipc-icon ipc-icon--add" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="currentColor" role="presentation"><path d="M18 13h-5v5c0 .55-.45 1-1 1s-1-.45-1-1v-5H6c-.55 0-1-.45-1-1s.45-1 1-1h5V6c0-.55.45-1 1-1s1 .45 1 1v5h5c.55 0 1 .45 1 1s-.45 1-1 1z"></path></svg></button></div></div><div data-testid="dli-bio" class="sc-77f37b3d-2 dpXpaE"><div class="ipc-html-content ipc-html-content--base sc-77f37b3d-3 huKIYr" role="presentation"><div class="ipc-html-content-inner-div" role="presentation">Ruth Elizabeth Davis was born April 5, 1908, in Lowell, Massachusetts, to Ruth Augusta (Favor) and Harlow Morrell Davis, a patent attorney. Her parents divorced when she was 10. She and her sister were raised by their mother. Her early interest was dance. To Bette, dancers led a glamorous life, but then she discovered the stage, and gave up dancing for acting. To her, it presented much more of a challenge.<br/><br/>After graduation from Cushing Academy, she was refused admittance to <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0499170/?ls">Eva Le Gallienne</a>&#39;s Manhattan Civic Repertory. She enrolled in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0026960/?ls">John Murray Anderson</a>&#39;s Dramatic School and was the star pupil. She was in the off-Broadway play &quot;The Earth Between&quot; (1923), and her Broadway debut in 1929 was in &quot;Broken Dishes&quot;. She also appeared in &quot;Solid South&quot;. Late in 1930, she was hired by Universal, where she made her first film, called <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0021636/?ls">Bad Sister (1931)</a>. When she arrived in Hollywood, the studio representative who went to meet her train left without her because he could find no one who looked like a movie star. An official at Universal complained she had &quot;as much sex appeal as <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0838843/?ls">Slim Summerville</a>&quot; and her performance in &quot;Bad Sister&quot; didn&#39;t impress.<br/><br/>In 1932, she signed a seven-year deal with Warner Brothers Pictures. Her first film with them was <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0023181/?ls">The Man Who Played God (1932)</a>. She became a star after this appearance, known as the actress that could play a variety of very strong and complex roles. More fairly successful movies followed, but it was the role of Mildred Rogers in RKO&#39;s <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0025586/?ls">Of Human Bondage (1934)</a> that would give Bette major acclaim from the film critics. She had a significant number of write-in votes for the Best Actress Oscar, but didn&#39;t win. Warner Bros. felt their seven-year deal with Bette was more than justified. They had a genuine star on their hands. With this success under her belt, she began pushing for stronger and more meaningful roles. In 1935, she received her first Oscar for her role in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0026261/?ls">Dangerous (1935)</a> as Joyce Heath.<br/><br/>In 1936, she was suspended without pay for turning down a role that she deemed unworthy of her talent. She went to England, where she had planned to make movies, but was stopped by Warner Bros. because she was still under contract to them. They did not want her to work anywhere. Although she sued to get out of her contract, she lost. Still, they began to take her more seriously after that.<br/><br/>Returning after losing her lawsuit, her roles improved dramatically. In 1938, Bette received a second Academy Award win for her work in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0030287/?ls">Jezebel (1938)</a> opposite the soon-to-be-legendary <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000020/?ls">Henry Fonda</a>. The only role she didn&#39;t get that she wanted was Scarlett O&#39;Hara in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0031381/?ls">Gone with the Wind (1939)</a>. Warners wouldn&#39;t loan her to <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0006388/?ls">David O. Selznick</a> unless he hired <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001224/?ls">Errol Flynn</a> to play Rhett Butler,
which both Selznick and Davis thought was a terrible choice. It was rumored she had numerous affairs, among them <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0107575/?ls">George Brent</a> and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0943758/?ls">William Wyler</a>, and she was married four times, three of which ended in divorce. She admitted her career always came first.<br/><br/>She made many successful films in the 1940s, but each picture was weaker than the last and by the time her Warner Brothers contract had ended in 1949, she had been reduced to appearing in such films as the unintentionally hilarious <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0041172/?ls">Beyond the Forest (1949)</a>. She made a huge comeback in 1950 when she replaced an ill <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001055/?ls">Claudette Colbert</a> in, and
received an Oscar nomination for, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0042192/?ls">All About Eve (1950)</a>. She worked in films through the 1950s, but her career eventually came to a standstill, and in 1961 she placed a now famous Job Wanted ad in the trade papers.<br/><br/>She received an Oscar nomination for her role as a demented former child star in
<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0056687/?ls">What Ever Happened to Baby Jane? (1962)</a>. This brought about a new round of super-stardom for generations of fans who were not familiar with her work. Two years later, she starred in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0058213/?ls">Hush...Hush, Sweet Charlotte (1964)</a>. Bette was married four times.<br/><br/>In 1977 she received the AFI&#39;s Lifetime Achievement Award and in 1979 she won a Best Actress Emmy for <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0079956/?ls">Strangers: The Story of a Mother and Daughter (1979)</a>. In 1977-78 she moved from Connecticut to Los Angeles and filmed a pilot for the series <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0085032/?ls">Hotel (1983)</a>, which she called Brothel. She refused to do the TV series and suffered a stroke during this time.<br/><br/>Her last marriage, to actor <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0581282/?ls">Gary Merrill</a>, lasted ten years, longer than any of the previous three. In 1985, her daughter Barbara Davis (&quot;B.D.&quot;) Hyman published a scandalous book about Bette called &quot;My Mother&#39;s Keeper.&quot; Bette worked in the later 1980s in films and TV, even though a stroke had impaired her appearance and mobility. She wrote a book, &quot;This &#39;N That&quot;, during her recovery from the stroke. Her last book was &quot;Bette Davis, The Lonely Life&quot;, issued in paperback in 1990. It included an update from 1962 to 1989. She wrote the last chapter in San Sebastian, Spain.<br/><br/>Sadly, Bette Davis died on October 6, 1989, of metastasized breast cancer, in Neuilly-sur-Seine, Hauts-de-Seine, France. Many of her fans refused to believe she was gone.</div></div></div></div></div></div></li><li class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item"><div class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__c"><div class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__tc"><span class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__t" aria-disabled="false"></span><div class="sc-77f37b3d-0 jCbCZO dli-parent"><div class="sc-77f37b3d-1 gJmTWZ"><div class="sc-7c95f518-0 cDAKkN"><div data-testid="nlib-img-container" class="sc-7c95f518-1 iorieb"><div class="ipc-avatar ipc-avatar--base" role="group"><div class="ipc-media ipc-media--avatar ipc-image-media-ratio--avatar ipc-media--circle-radius ipc-media--base ipc-media--custom ipc-avatar__avatar-image ipc-media__img" style="width:60px"><img alt="James Stewart" class="ipc-image" loading="lazy" src="https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMjIwNzMzODY0NV5BMl5BanBnXkFtZTcwMDk3NDQyOA@@._V1_QL75_UX60_CR0,0,60,60_.jpg" srcSet="https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMjIwNzMzODY0NV5BMl5BanBnXkFtZTcwMDk3NDQyOA@@._V1_QL75_UX60_CR0,0,60,60_.jpg 60w, https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMjIwNzMzODY0NV5BMl5BanBnXkFtZTcwMDk3NDQyOA@@._V1_QL75_UX90_CR0,0,90,90_.jpg 90w, https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMjIwNzMzODY0NV5BMl5BanBnXkFtZTcwMDk3NDQyOA@@._V1_QL75_UX120_CR0,0,120,120_.jpg 120w" sizes="50vw, (min-width: 480px) 34vw, (min-width: 600px) 26vw, (min-width: 1024px) 16vw, (min-width: 1280px) 16vw" width="60"/></div><a class="ipc-lockup-overlay ipc-focusable" href="/name/nm0000071/?ref_=ls_i_16" aria-label="James Stewart"><div class="ipc-lockup-overlay__screen"></div></a></div></div><div class="sc-7c95f518-3 krmPLY"><div data-testid="nlib-meter-const-container"></div><div class="ipc-title ipc-title--base ipc-title--title ipc-title-link-no-icon ipc-title--on-textPrimary sc-7c95f518-2 ghWujX" data-testid="nlib-title"><a href="/name/nm0000071/?ref_=ls_t_16" class="ipc-title-link-wrapper" tabindex="0"><h3 class="ipc-title__text">16. James Stewart</h3></a></div><div class="sc-7c95f518-6 iDkHPP"><ul class="ipc-inline-list ipc-inline-list--show-dividers sc-7c95f518-4 lolxqE base" role="presentation" data-testid="nlib-professions"><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Actor</li><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Director</li><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Producer</li></ul><a class="ipc-link ipc-link--base sc-ab9eb9db-0 iRQWod" tabindex="0" aria-disabled="false" data-testid="nlib-known-for-title" href="/title/tt0052357/?ref_=ls_knf_16">Vertigo (1958)</a></div></div></div><div><button data-testid="dli-add-to-list-button" class="ipc-icon-button ipc-icon-button--base ipc-icon-button--onAccent2" title="Add to list" tabindex="0" aria-label="Add to list" aria-disabled="false"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="24" height="24" class="ipc-icon ipc-icon--add" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="currentColor" role="presentation"><path d="M18 13h-5v5c0 .55-.45 1-1 1s-1-.45-1-1v-5H6c-.55 0-1-.45-1-1s.45-1 1-1h5V6c0-.55.45-1 1-1s1 .45 1 1v5h5c.55 0 1 .45 1 1s-.45 1-1 1z"></path></svg></button></div></div><div data-testid="dli-bio" class="sc-77f37b3d-2 dpXpaE"><div class="ipc-html-content ipc-html-content--base sc-77f37b3d-3 huKIYr" role="presentation"><div class="ipc-html-content-inner-div" role="presentation">James Maitland Stewart was born on May 20, 1908, in Indiana, Pennsylvania, to Elizabeth Ruth (Johnson) and Alexander Maitland Stewart, who owned a hardware store. He was of Scottish, Ulster-Scots, and some English descent. Stewart was educated at a local prep school, Mercersburg Academy, where he was a keen athlete (football and track), musician (singing and accordion playing), and sometime actor.<br/><br/>In 1929, he won a place at Princeton University, where he studied architecture with some success and became further involved with the performing arts as a musician and actor with the University Players. After graduation, engagements with the University Players took him around the northeastern United States, including a run on Broadway in 1932. But work dried up as the Great Depression deepened, and it was not until 1934, when he followed his friend <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000020/?ls">Henry Fonda</a> to Hollywood, that things began to pick up.<br/><br/>After his first screen appearance in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0024838/?ls">Art Trouble (1934)</a>, Stewart worked for a time for MGM as a contract player and slowly began making a name for himself in increasingly high-profile roles throughout the rest of the 1930s. His famous collaborations with <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001008/?ls">Frank Capra</a>, in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0030993/?ls">You Can&#39;t Take It with You (1938)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0031679/?ls">Mr. Smith Goes to Washington (1939)</a>, and, after World War II, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0038650/?ls">It&#39;s a Wonderful Life (1946)</a> helped to launch his career as a star and to establish his screen persona as the likable every man.<br/><br/>Having learned to fly in 1935, he was drafted into the United States Army in 1940 as a private (after twice failing the medical for being underweight). During the course of World War II, he rose to the rank of colonel, first as an instructor at home in the United States, and later on combat missions in Europe. He remained involved with the United States Air Force Reserve after the war and officially retired in 1968. In 1959, he was promoted to brigadier general, becoming the highest-ranking actor in U.S. military history.<br/><br/>Stewart&#39;s acting career took off properly after the war. During the course of his long professional life, he had roles in some of Hollywood&#39;s best-remembered films, starring in a string of Westerns, bringing his every man qualities to movies like <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0056217/?ls">The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance (1962)</a>), biopics (<a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0041928/?ls">The Stratton Story (1949)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0047030/?ls">The Glenn Miller Story (1954)</a>, and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0051003/?ls">The Spirit of St. Louis (1957)</a>, for instance, thrillers (most notably his frequent collaborations with <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000033/?ls">Alfred Hitchcock</a>), and even some screwball comedies.<br/><br/>On June 25, 1997, a thrombosis formed in his right leg, leading to a pulmonary embolism, and a week later on July 2, 1997, surrounded by his children, James Stewart died at age 89 at his home in Beverly Hills, California. His last words to his family were, &quot;I&#39;m going to be with Gloria now.&quot;</div></div></div></div></div></div></li><li class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item"><div class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__c"><div class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__tc"><span class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__t" aria-disabled="false"></span><div class="sc-77f37b3d-0 jCbCZO dli-parent"><div class="sc-77f37b3d-1 gJmTWZ"><div class="sc-7c95f518-0 cDAKkN"><div data-testid="nlib-img-container" class="sc-7c95f518-1 iorieb"><div class="ipc-avatar ipc-avatar--base" role="group"><div class="ipc-media ipc-media--avatar ipc-image-media-ratio--avatar ipc-media--circle-radius ipc-media--base ipc-media--custom ipc-avatar__avatar-image ipc-media__img" style="width:60px"><img alt="Gregory Peck" class="ipc-image" loading="lazy" src="https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BYWU1YTkwOGEtZTdjOC00ZDEyLThkZWUtMzY4ZjYzYWQyM2FlXkEyXkFqcGc@._V1_QL75_UX60_CR0,0,60,60_.jpg" srcSet="https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BYWU1YTkwOGEtZTdjOC00ZDEyLThkZWUtMzY4ZjYzYWQyM2FlXkEyXkFqcGc@._V1_QL75_UX60_CR0,0,60,60_.jpg 60w, https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BYWU1YTkwOGEtZTdjOC00ZDEyLThkZWUtMzY4ZjYzYWQyM2FlXkEyXkFqcGc@._V1_QL75_UX90_CR0,0,90,90_.jpg 90w, https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BYWU1YTkwOGEtZTdjOC00ZDEyLThkZWUtMzY4ZjYzYWQyM2FlXkEyXkFqcGc@._V1_QL75_UX120_CR0,0,120,120_.jpg 120w" sizes="50vw, (min-width: 480px) 34vw, (min-width: 600px) 26vw, (min-width: 1024px) 16vw, (min-width: 1280px) 16vw" width="60"/></div><a class="ipc-lockup-overlay ipc-focusable" href="/name/nm0000060/?ref_=ls_i_17" aria-label="Gregory Peck"><div class="ipc-lockup-overlay__screen"></div></a></div></div><div class="sc-7c95f518-3 krmPLY"><div data-testid="nlib-meter-const-container"></div><div class="ipc-title ipc-title--base ipc-title--title ipc-title-link-no-icon ipc-title--on-textPrimary sc-7c95f518-2 ghWujX" data-testid="nlib-title"><a href="/name/nm0000060/?ref_=ls_t_17" class="ipc-title-link-wrapper" tabindex="0"><h3 class="ipc-title__text">17. Gregory Peck</h3></a></div><div class="sc-7c95f518-6 iDkHPP"><ul class="ipc-inline-list ipc-inline-list--show-dividers sc-7c95f518-4 lolxqE base" role="presentation" data-testid="nlib-professions"><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Actor</li><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Producer</li><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Additional Crew</li></ul><a class="ipc-link ipc-link--base sc-ab9eb9db-0 iRQWod" tabindex="0" aria-disabled="false" data-testid="nlib-known-for-title" href="/title/tt0056592/?ref_=ls_knf_17">To Kill a Mockingbird (1962)</a></div></div></div><div><button data-testid="dli-add-to-list-button" class="ipc-icon-button ipc-icon-button--base ipc-icon-button--onAccent2" title="Add to list" tabindex="0" aria-label="Add to list" aria-disabled="false"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="24" height="24" class="ipc-icon ipc-icon--add" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="currentColor" role="presentation"><path d="M18 13h-5v5c0 .55-.45 1-1 1s-1-.45-1-1v-5H6c-.55 0-1-.45-1-1s.45-1 1-1h5V6c0-.55.45-1 1-1s1 .45 1 1v5h5c.55 0 1 .45 1 1s-.45 1-1 1z"></path></svg></button></div></div><div data-testid="dli-bio" class="sc-77f37b3d-2 dpXpaE"><div class="ipc-html-content ipc-html-content--base sc-77f37b3d-3 huKIYr" role="presentation"><div class="ipc-html-content-inner-div" role="presentation">Eldred Gregory Peck was born on April 5, 1916 in La Jolla, California, to Bernice Mae (Ayres) and Gregory Pearl Peck, a chemist and druggist in San Diego. He had Irish (from his paternal grandmother), English, and some German, ancestry. His parents divorced when he was five years old. An only child, he was sent to live with his grandmother. He never felt he had a stable childhood. His fondest memories are of his grandmother taking him to the movies every week and of his dog, which followed him everywhere. He studied pre-med at UC-Berkeley and, while there, got bitten by the acting bug and decided to change the focus of his studies. He enrolled in the Neighborhood Playhouse in New York and debuted on Broadway after graduation. His debut was in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0930539/?ls">Emlyn Williams</a>&#39; play &quot;The Morning Star&quot; (1942). By 1943, he was in Hollywood, where he debuted in the RKO film <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0036748/?ls">Days of Glory (1944)</a>.<br/><br/>Stardom came with his next film, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0036983/?ls">The Keys of the Kingdom (1944)</a>, for which he was nominated for an Academy Award. Peck&#39;s screen presence displayed the qualities for which he became well known. He was tall, rugged and heroic, with a basic decency that transcended his roles. He appeared in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000033/?ls">Alfred Hitchcock</a>&#39;s <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0038109/?ls">Spellbound (1945)</a> as an amnesia victim accused of murder. In <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0039111/?ls">The Yearling (1946)</a>, he was again nominated for an Academy Award and won the Golden Globe. He was especially effective in westerns and appeared in such varied fare as <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0006388/?ls">David O. Selznick</a>&#39;s critically blasted <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0038499/?ls">Duel in the Sun (1946)</a>, the somewhat better received <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0040978/?ls">Yellow Sky (1948)</a> and the acclaimed <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0042531/?ls">The Gunfighter (1950)</a>. He was nominated again for the Academy Award for his roles in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0039416/?ls">Gentleman&#39;s Agreement (1947)</a>, which dealt with anti-Semitism, and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0041996/?ls">Twelve O&#39;Clock High (1949)</a>, a story of high-level stress in an Air Force bomber unit in World War II.<br/><br/>With a string of hits to his credit, Peck made the decision to only work in films that interested him. He continued to appear as the heroic, larger-than-life figures in such films as <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0043379/?ls">Captain Horatio Hornblower R.N. (1951)</a> and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0049513/?ls">Moby Dick (1956)</a>. He worked with <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000030/?ls">Audrey Hepburn</a> in her debut film, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0046250/?ls">Roman Holiday (1953)</a>. Peck finally won the Oscar, after four nominations, for his performance as lawyer Atticus Finch in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0056592/?ls">To Kill a Mockingbird (1962)</a>. In the early 1960s, he appeared in two darker films than he usually made, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0055824/?ls">Cape Fear (1962)</a> and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0056903/?ls">Captain Newman, M.D. (1963)</a>, which dealt with the way people live. He also gave a powerful performance as Captain Keith Mallory in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0054953/?ls">The Guns of Navarone (1961)</a>, one of the biggest box-office hits of that year.<br/><br/>In the early 1970s, he produced two films, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0069406/?ls">The Trial of the Catonsville Nine (1972)</a> and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0071438/?ls">The Dove (1974)</a>, when his film career stalled. He made a comeback playing, somewhat woodenly, Robert Thorn in the horror film <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0075005/?ls">The Omen (1976)</a>. After that, he returned to the bigger-than-life roles he was best known for, such as <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0076342/?ls">MacArthur (1977)</a> and the monstrous Nazi Dr. Josef Mengele in the huge hit <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0077269/?ls">The Boys from Brazil (1978)</a>. In the 1980s, he moved into television with the miniseries <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0083387/?ls">The Blue and the Gray (1982)</a> and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0086251/?ls">The Scarlet and the Black (1983)</a>. In 1991, he appeared in the remake of his 1962 film, playing a different role, in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000217/?ls">Martin Scorsese</a>&#39;s <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0101540/?ls">Cape Fear (1991)</a>. He was also cast as the progressive-thinking owner of a wire and cable business in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0102609/?ls">Other People&#39;s Money (1991)</a>.<br/><br/>In 1967, Peck received the Academy&#39;s <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0380965/?ls">Jean Hersholt</a> Humanitarian Award. He was also been awarded the US Presidential Medal of Freedom. Always politically progressive, he was active in such causes as anti-war protests, workers&#39; rights and civil rights. In 2003, his Peck&#39;s portrayal of Atticus Finch was named the greatest film hero of the past 100 years by the American Film Institute. Gregory Peck died at age 87 on June 12, 2003 in Los Angeles, California.</div></div></div></div></div></div></li><li class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item"><div class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__c"><div class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__tc"><span class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__t" aria-disabled="false"></span><div class="sc-77f37b3d-0 jCbCZO dli-parent"><div class="sc-77f37b3d-1 gJmTWZ"><div class="sc-7c95f518-0 cDAKkN"><div data-testid="nlib-img-container" class="sc-7c95f518-1 iorieb"><div class="ipc-avatar ipc-avatar--base" role="group"><div class="ipc-media ipc-media--avatar ipc-image-media-ratio--avatar ipc-media--circle-radius ipc-media--base ipc-media--custom ipc-avatar__avatar-image ipc-media__img" style="width:60px"><img alt="Al Pacino" class="ipc-image" loading="lazy" src="https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMTQzMzg1ODAyNl5BMl5BanBnXkFtZTYwMjAxODQ1._V1_QL75_UX60_CR0,0,60,60_.jpg" srcSet="https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMTQzMzg1ODAyNl5BMl5BanBnXkFtZTYwMjAxODQ1._V1_QL75_UX60_CR0,0,60,60_.jpg 60w, https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMTQzMzg1ODAyNl5BMl5BanBnXkFtZTYwMjAxODQ1._V1_QL75_UX90_CR0,0,90,90_.jpg 90w, https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMTQzMzg1ODAyNl5BMl5BanBnXkFtZTYwMjAxODQ1._V1_QL75_UX120_CR0,0,120,120_.jpg 120w" sizes="50vw, (min-width: 480px) 34vw, (min-width: 600px) 26vw, (min-width: 1024px) 16vw, (min-width: 1280px) 16vw" width="60"/></div><a class="ipc-lockup-overlay ipc-focusable" href="/name/nm0000199/?ref_=ls_i_18" aria-label="Al Pacino"><div class="ipc-lockup-overlay__screen"></div></a></div></div><div class="sc-7c95f518-3 krmPLY"><div data-testid="nlib-meter-const-container"></div><div class="ipc-title ipc-title--base ipc-title--title ipc-title-link-no-icon ipc-title--on-textPrimary sc-7c95f518-2 ghWujX" data-testid="nlib-title"><a href="/name/nm0000199/?ref_=ls_t_18" class="ipc-title-link-wrapper" tabindex="0"><h3 class="ipc-title__text">18. Al Pacino</h3></a></div><div class="sc-7c95f518-6 iDkHPP"><ul class="ipc-inline-list ipc-inline-list--show-dividers sc-7c95f518-4 lolxqE base" role="presentation" data-testid="nlib-professions"><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Actor</li><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Director</li><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Producer</li></ul><a class="ipc-link ipc-link--base sc-ab9eb9db-0 iRQWod" tabindex="0" aria-disabled="false" data-testid="nlib-known-for-title" href="/title/tt0070666/?ref_=ls_knf_18">Serpico (1973)</a></div></div></div><div><button data-testid="dli-add-to-list-button" class="ipc-icon-button ipc-icon-button--base ipc-icon-button--onAccent2" title="Add to list" tabindex="0" aria-label="Add to list" aria-disabled="false"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="24" height="24" class="ipc-icon ipc-icon--add" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="currentColor" role="presentation"><path d="M18 13h-5v5c0 .55-.45 1-1 1s-1-.45-1-1v-5H6c-.55 0-1-.45-1-1s.45-1 1-1h5V6c0-.55.45-1 1-1s1 .45 1 1v5h5c.55 0 1 .45 1 1s-.45 1-1 1z"></path></svg></button></div></div><div data-testid="dli-bio" class="sc-77f37b3d-2 dpXpaE"><div class="ipc-html-content ipc-html-content--base sc-77f37b3d-3 huKIYr" role="presentation"><div class="ipc-html-content-inner-div" role="presentation">Alfredo James &quot;Al&quot; &#39;Pacino established himself as a film actor during one of cinema&#39;s most vibrant decades, the 1970s, and has become an enduring and iconic figure in the world of American movies.<br/><br/>He was born April 25, 1940 in Manhattan, New York City, to Italian-American parents, Rose (nee Gerardi) and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0655416/?ls">Sal Pacino</a>. They divorced when he was young. His mother moved them into his grandparents&#39; home in the South Bronx. Pacino found himself often repeating the plots and voices of characters he had seen in the movies. Bored and unmotivated in school, he found a haven in school plays, and his interest soon blossomed into a full-time career. Starting onstage, he went through a period of depression and poverty, sometimes having to borrow bus fare to succeed to auditions. He made it into the prestigious Actors Studio in 1966, studying under <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0833448/?ls">Lee Strasberg</a>, creator of the Method Approach that would become the trademark of many 1970s-era actors.<br/><br/>After appearing in a string of plays in supporting roles, Pacino finally attained success off-Broadway with <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0395262/?ls">Israel Horovitz</a>&#39;s &quot;The Indian Wants the Bronx&quot;, winning an Obie Award for the 1966-67 season. That was followed by a Tony Award for &quot;Does the Tiger Wear a Necktie?&quot; His first feature films made little departure from the gritty realistic stage performances that earned him respect: he played a drug addict in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0067549/?ls">The Panic in Needle Park (1971)</a> after his film debut in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0064651/?ls">Me, Natalie (1969)</a>. The role of Michael Corleone in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0068646/?ls">The Godfather (1972)</a> was one of the most sought-after of the time: <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000602/?ls">Robert Redford</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000886/?ls">Warren Beatty</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000197/?ls">Jack Nicholson</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0641939/?ls">Ryan O&#39;Neal</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000134/?ls">Robert De Niro</a> and a host of other actors either wanted it or were mentioned, but director <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000338/?ls">Francis Ford Coppola</a> wanted Pacino for the role.<br/><br/>Coppola was successful but Pacino was reportedly in constant fear of being fired during the very difficult shoot. The film was a monster hit that earned Pacino his first Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actor. However, instead of taking on easier projects for the big money he could now command, Pacino threw his support behind what he considered tough but important films, such as the true-life crime drama <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0070666/?ls">Serpico (1973)</a> and the tragic real-life bank robbery film <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0072890/?ls">Dog Day Afternoon (1975)</a>. He was nominated three consecutive years for the &quot;Best Actor&quot; Academy Award. He faltered slightly with <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0075774/?ls">Bobby Deerfield (1977)</a>, but regained his stride with <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0078718/?ls">And Justice for All (1979)</a>, for which he received another Academy Award nomination for Best Actor. Unfortunately, this would signal the beginning of a decline in his career, which produced flops like <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0080569/?ls">Cruising (1980)</a> and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0083598/?ls">Author! Author! (1982)</a>.<br/><br/>Pacino took on another vicious gangster role and cemented his legendary status in the ultra-violent cult film <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0086250/?ls">Scarface (1983)</a>, but a monumental mistake was about to follow. <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0089913/?ls">Revolution (1985)</a> endured an endless and seemingly cursed shoot in which equipment was destroyed, weather was terrible, and Pacino fell ill with pneumonia. Constant changes in the script further derailed the project. The Revolutionary War-themed film, considered among the worst films ever made, resulted in awful reviews and kept him off the screen for the next four years. Returning to the stage, Pacino did much to give back and contribute to the theatre, which he considers his first love. He directed a film, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0097769/?ls">The Local Stigmatic (1990)</a>, but it remains unreleased. He lifted his self-imposed exile with the striking <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0098273/?ls">Sea of Love (1989)</a> as a hard-drinking policeman. This marked the second phase of Pacino&#39;s career, being the first to feature his now famous dark, owl eyes and hoarse, gravelly voice.<br/><br/>Returning to the Corleones, Pacino made <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0099674/?ls">The Godfather Part III (1990)</a> and earned raves for his first comedic role in the colorful adaptation <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0099422/?ls">Dick Tracy (1990)</a>. This earned him another Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actor, and two years later he was nominated for <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0104348/?ls">Glengarry Glen Ross (1992)</a>. He went into romantic mode for <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0101912/?ls">Frankie and Johnny (1991)</a>. In 1992, he finally won the Academy Award for Best Actor for his amazing performance in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0105323/?ls">Scent of a Woman (1992)</a>. A mixture of technical perfection (he plays a blind man) and charisma, the role was tailor-made for him, and remains a classic.<br/><br/>The next few years would see Pacino becoming more comfortable with acting and movies as a business, turning out great roles in great films with more frequency and less of the demanding personal involvement of his wilder days. <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0106519/?ls">Carlito&#39;s Way (1993)</a> proved another gangster classic, as did the epic crime drama <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0113277/?ls">Heat (1995)</a> directed by <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000520/?ls">Michael Mann</a> and co-starring <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000134/?ls">Robert De Niro</a>. He directed the film adaptation of Shakespeare&#39;s <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0116913/?ls">Looking for Richard (1996)</a>. During this period, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0115907/?ls">City Hall (1996)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0119008/?ls">Donnie Brasco (1997)</a> and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0118971/?ls">The Devil&#39;s Advocate (1997)</a> all came out. Reteaming with Mann and then <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000231/?ls">Oliver Stone</a>, he gave commanding performances in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0140352/?ls">The Insider (1999)</a> and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0146838/?ls">Any Given Sunday (1999)</a>.<br/><br/>In the 2000s, Pacino starred in a number of theatrical blockbusters, including <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0496806/?ls">Ocean&#39;s Thirteen (2007)</a>, but his choice in television roles (the vicious, closeted Roy Cohn in the HBO miniseries <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0318997/?ls">Angels in America (2003)</a> and his sensitive portrayal of Jack Kevorkian, in the television movie <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt1132623/?ls">You Don&#39;t Know Jack (2010)</a>) are reminiscent of the bolder choices of his early career. Each television project garnered him an Emmy Award for Outstanding Lead Actor in a Miniseries or a Movie.<br/><br/>Never wed, Pacino has a daughter, Julie Marie, with acting teacher Jan Tarrant, and a set of twins with former longtime girlfriend <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000350/?ls">Beverly D&#39;Angelo</a>. His romantic history includes <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001049/?ls">Jill Clayburgh</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0902610/?ls">Veruschka von Lehndorff</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0540098/?ls">Carole Mallory</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000700/?ls">Debra Winger</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001839/?ls">Tuesday Weld</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0445715/?ls">Marthe Keller</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0148947/?ls">Carmen Cervera</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000599/?ls">Kathleen Quinlan</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0387605/?ls">Lyndall Hobbs</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000542/?ls">Penelope Ann Miller</a>, and a two-decade intermittent relationship with &quot;Godfather&quot; co-star <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000473/?ls">Diane Keaton</a>. He currently lives with Argentinian actress <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm1376482/?ls">Lucila Solá</a>, who is 36 years his junior.<br/><br/>As of 2022, Pacino is 82-years-old. He has never retired from acting, and continues to appear regularly in film.</div></div></div></div></div></div></li><li class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item"><div class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__c"><div class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__tc"><span class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__t" aria-disabled="false"></span><div class="sc-77f37b3d-0 jCbCZO dli-parent"><div class="sc-77f37b3d-1 gJmTWZ"><div class="sc-7c95f518-0 cDAKkN"><div data-testid="nlib-img-container" class="sc-7c95f518-1 iorieb"><div class="ipc-avatar ipc-avatar--base" role="group"><div class="ipc-media ipc-media--avatar ipc-image-media-ratio--avatar ipc-media--circle-radius ipc-media--base ipc-media--custom ipc-avatar__avatar-image ipc-media__img" style="width:60px"><img alt="Tom Hanks at an event for Larry Crowne (2011)" class="ipc-image" loading="lazy" src="https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMTQ2MjMwNDA3Nl5BMl5BanBnXkFtZTcwMTA2NDY3NQ@@._V1_QL75_UX60_CR0,0,60,60_.jpg" srcSet="https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMTQ2MjMwNDA3Nl5BMl5BanBnXkFtZTcwMTA2NDY3NQ@@._V1_QL75_UX60_CR0,0,60,60_.jpg 60w, https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMTQ2MjMwNDA3Nl5BMl5BanBnXkFtZTcwMTA2NDY3NQ@@._V1_QL75_UX90_CR0,0,90,90_.jpg 90w, https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMTQ2MjMwNDA3Nl5BMl5BanBnXkFtZTcwMTA2NDY3NQ@@._V1_QL75_UX120_CR0,0,120,120_.jpg 120w" sizes="50vw, (min-width: 480px) 34vw, (min-width: 600px) 26vw, (min-width: 1024px) 16vw, (min-width: 1280px) 16vw" width="60"/></div><a class="ipc-lockup-overlay ipc-focusable" href="/name/nm0000158/?ref_=ls_i_19" aria-label="Tom Hanks"><div class="ipc-lockup-overlay__screen"></div></a></div></div><div class="sc-7c95f518-3 krmPLY"><div data-testid="nlib-meter-const-container"></div><div class="ipc-title ipc-title--base ipc-title--title ipc-title-link-no-icon ipc-title--on-textPrimary sc-7c95f518-2 ghWujX" data-testid="nlib-title"><a href="/name/nm0000158/?ref_=ls_t_19" class="ipc-title-link-wrapper" tabindex="0"><h3 class="ipc-title__text">19. Tom Hanks</h3></a></div><div class="sc-7c95f518-6 iDkHPP"><ul class="ipc-inline-list ipc-inline-list--show-dividers sc-7c95f518-4 lolxqE base" role="presentation" data-testid="nlib-professions"><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Producer</li><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Actor</li><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Writer</li></ul><a class="ipc-link ipc-link--base sc-ab9eb9db-0 iRQWod" tabindex="0" aria-disabled="false" data-testid="nlib-known-for-title" href="/title/tt0162222/?ref_=ls_knf_19">Cast Away (2000)</a></div></div></div><div><button data-testid="dli-add-to-list-button" class="ipc-icon-button ipc-icon-button--base ipc-icon-button--onAccent2" title="Add to list" tabindex="0" aria-label="Add to list" aria-disabled="false"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="24" height="24" class="ipc-icon ipc-icon--add" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="currentColor" role="presentation"><path d="M18 13h-5v5c0 .55-.45 1-1 1s-1-.45-1-1v-5H6c-.55 0-1-.45-1-1s.45-1 1-1h5V6c0-.55.45-1 1-1s1 .45 1 1v5h5c.55 0 1 .45 1 1s-.45 1-1 1z"></path></svg></button></div></div><div data-testid="dli-bio" class="sc-77f37b3d-2 dpXpaE"><div class="ipc-html-content ipc-html-content--base sc-77f37b3d-3 huKIYr" role="presentation"><div class="ipc-html-content-inner-div" role="presentation">Thomas Jeffrey Hanks was born in Concord, California, to Janet Marylyn (Frager), a hospital worker, and Amos Mefford Hanks, an itinerant cook. His mother&#39;s family, originally surnamed &quot;Fraga&quot;, was entirely Portuguese, while his father was of mostly English ancestry. Tom grew up in what he has called a &quot;fractured&quot; family. He moved around a great deal after his parents&#39; divorce, living with a succession of step-families. No problems, no alcoholism - just a confused childhood. He has no acting experience in college and credits the fact that he could not get cast in a college play with actually starting his career. He went downtown, and auditioned for a community theater play, was invited by the director of that play to go to Cleveland, and there his acting career started.<br/><br/><a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000165/?ls">Ron Howard</a> was working on <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0088161/?ls">Splash (1984)</a>, a fantasy-comedy about a mermaid who falls in love with a business executive. Howard considered Hanks for the role of the main character&#39;s wisecracking brother, which eventually went to <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001006/?ls">John Candy</a>. Instead, Hanks landed the lead role and the film went on to become a surprise box office success, grossing more than $69 million. After several flops and a moderate success with the comedy <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0092925/?ls">Dragnet (1987)</a>, Hanks&#39; stature in the film industry rose. The broad success with the fantasy-comedy <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0094737/?ls">Big (1988)</a> established him as a major Hollywood talent, both as a box office draw and within the film industry as an actor. For his performance in the film, Hanks earned his first Academy Award nomination as Best Actor.<br/><br/>Hanks climbed back to the top again with his portrayal of a washed-up baseball legend turned manager in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0104694/?ls">A League of Their Own (1992)</a>. Hanks has stated that his acting in earlier roles was not great, but that he subsequently improved. In an interview with Vanity Fair, Hanks noted his &quot;modern era of movie making ... because enough self-discovery has gone on ... My work has become less pretentiously fake and over the top&quot;. This &quot;modern era&quot; began for Hanks, first with <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0108160/?ls">Sleepless in Seattle (1993)</a> and then with <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0107818/?ls">Philadelphia (1993)</a>. The former was a blockbuster success about a widower who finds true love over the radio airwaves. Richard Schickel of Time magazine called his performance &quot;charming&quot;, and most critics agreed that Hanks&#39; portrayal ensured him a place among the premier romantic-comedy stars of his generation.<br/><br/>In Philadelphia, he played a gay lawyer with AIDS who sues his firm for discrimination. Hanks lost 35 pounds and thinned his hair in order to appear sickly for the role. In a review for People, Leah Rozen stated, &quot;Above all, credit for Philadelphia&#39;s success belongs to Hanks, who makes sure that he plays a character, not a saint. He is flat-out terrific, giving a deeply felt, carefully nuanced performance that deserves an Oscar.&quot; Hanks won the 1993 Academy Award for Best Actor for his role in Philadelphia. During his acceptance speech, he revealed that his high school drama teacher Rawley Farnsworth and former classmate John Gilkerson, two people with whom he was close, were gay.<br/><br/>Hanks followed Philadelphia with the blockbuster <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0109830/?ls">Forrest Gump (1994)</a> which grossed a worldwide total of over $600 million at the box office. Hanks remarked: &quot;When I read the script for Gump, I saw it as one of those kind of grand, hopeful movies that the audience can go to and feel ... some hope for their lot and their position in life ... I got that from the movies a hundred million times when I was a kid. I still do.&quot; Hanks won his second Best Actor Academy Award for his role in Forrest Gump, becoming only the second actor to have accomplished the feat of winning consecutive Best Actor Oscars.<br/><br/>Hanks&#39; next role - astronaut and commander Jim Lovell, in the docudrama <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0112384/?ls">Apollo 13 (1995)</a> - reunited him with Ron Howard. Critics generally applauded the film and the performances of the entire cast, which included actors Kevin Bacon, Bill Paxton, Gary Sinise, Ed Harris, and Kathleen Quinlan. The movie also earned nine Academy Award nominations, winning two. Later that year, Hanks starred in Disney/Pixar&#39;s computer-animated film <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0114709/?ls">Toy Story (1995)</a>, as the voice of Sheriff Woody. A year later, he made his directing debut with the musical comedy <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0117887/?ls">That thing you are (1996)</a> about the rise and fall of a 1960s pop group, also playing the role of a music producer.<br/><br/>As of 2022, Hanks is 66-years-old. He has never retired from acting, and has remained active in the film industry for more than four decades.</div></div></div></div></div></div></li><li class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item"><div class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__c"><div class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__tc"><span class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__t" aria-disabled="false"></span><div class="sc-77f37b3d-0 jCbCZO dli-parent"><div class="sc-77f37b3d-1 gJmTWZ"><div class="sc-7c95f518-0 cDAKkN"><div data-testid="nlib-img-container" class="sc-7c95f518-1 iorieb"><div class="ipc-avatar ipc-avatar--base" role="group"><div class="ipc-media ipc-media--avatar ipc-image-media-ratio--avatar ipc-media--circle-radius ipc-media--base ipc-media--custom ipc-avatar__avatar-image ipc-media__img" style="width:60px"><img alt="Cate Blanchett" class="ipc-image" loading="lazy" src="https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMTc1MDI0MDg1NV5BMl5BanBnXkFtZTgwMDM3OTAzMTE@._V1_QL75_UX60_CR0,0,60,60_.jpg" srcSet="https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMTc1MDI0MDg1NV5BMl5BanBnXkFtZTgwMDM3OTAzMTE@._V1_QL75_UX60_CR0,0,60,60_.jpg 60w, https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMTc1MDI0MDg1NV5BMl5BanBnXkFtZTgwMDM3OTAzMTE@._V1_QL75_UX90_CR0,0,90,90_.jpg 90w, https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMTc1MDI0MDg1NV5BMl5BanBnXkFtZTgwMDM3OTAzMTE@._V1_QL75_UX120_CR0,0,120,120_.jpg 120w" sizes="50vw, (min-width: 480px) 34vw, (min-width: 600px) 26vw, (min-width: 1024px) 16vw, (min-width: 1280px) 16vw" width="60"/></div><a class="ipc-lockup-overlay ipc-focusable" href="/name/nm0000949/?ref_=ls_i_20" aria-label="Cate Blanchett"><div class="ipc-lockup-overlay__screen"></div></a></div></div><div class="sc-7c95f518-3 krmPLY"><div data-testid="nlib-meter-const-container"></div><div class="ipc-title ipc-title--base ipc-title--title ipc-title-link-no-icon ipc-title--on-textPrimary sc-7c95f518-2 ghWujX" data-testid="nlib-title"><a href="/name/nm0000949/?ref_=ls_t_20" class="ipc-title-link-wrapper" tabindex="0"><h3 class="ipc-title__text">20. Cate Blanchett</h3></a></div><div class="sc-7c95f518-6 iDkHPP"><ul class="ipc-inline-list ipc-inline-list--show-dividers sc-7c95f518-4 lolxqE base" role="presentation" data-testid="nlib-professions"><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Actress</li><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Producer</li><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Writer</li></ul><a class="ipc-link ipc-link--base sc-ab9eb9db-0 iRQWod" tabindex="0" aria-disabled="false" data-testid="nlib-known-for-title" href="/title/tt2402927/?ref_=ls_knf_20">Carol (2015)</a></div></div></div><div><button data-testid="dli-add-to-list-button" class="ipc-icon-button ipc-icon-button--base ipc-icon-button--onAccent2" title="Add to list" tabindex="0" aria-label="Add to list" aria-disabled="false"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="24" height="24" class="ipc-icon ipc-icon--add" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="currentColor" role="presentation"><path d="M18 13h-5v5c0 .55-.45 1-1 1s-1-.45-1-1v-5H6c-.55 0-1-.45-1-1s.45-1 1-1h5V6c0-.55.45-1 1-1s1 .45 1 1v5h5c.55 0 1 .45 1 1s-.45 1-1 1z"></path></svg></button></div></div><div data-testid="dli-bio" class="sc-77f37b3d-2 dpXpaE"><div class="ipc-html-content ipc-html-content--base sc-77f37b3d-3 huKIYr" role="presentation"><div class="ipc-html-content-inner-div" role="presentation">Cate Blanchett was born on May 14, 1969 in Melbourne, Victoria, Australia, to June (Gamble), an Australian teacher and property developer, and Robert DeWitt Blanchett, Jr., an American advertising executive, originally from Texas. She has an older brother and a younger sister. When she was ten years old, her 40-year-old father died of a sudden heart attack. Her mother never remarried, and her grandmother moved in to help her mother.<br/><br/>Cate graduated from Australia&#39;s National Institute of Dramatic Art in 1992 and, in a little over a year, had won both critical and popular acclaim. On graduating from NIDA, she joined the Sydney Theatre Company&#39;s production of <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm1135663/?ls">Caryl Churchill</a>&#39;s &quot;Top Girls&quot;, then played Felice Bauer, the bride, in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0004857/?ls">Tim Daly</a>&#39;s &quot;Kafka Dances&quot;, winning the 1993 Newcomer Award from the Sydney Theatre Critics Circle for her performance. From there, Blanchett moved to the role of Carol in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000519/?ls">David Mamet</a>&#39;s searing polemic &quot;Oleanna&quot;, also for the Sydney Theatre Company, and won the Rosemont Best Actress Award, her second award that year. She then co-starred in the ABC Television&#39;s prime time drama <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0110004/?ls">Heartland (1994)</a>, again winning critical acclaim. In 1995, she was nominated for Best Female Performance for her role as Ophelia in the Belvoir Street Theatre Company&#39;s production of &quot;Hamlet&quot;. Other theatre credits include Helen in the Sydney Theatre Company&#39;s &quot;Sweet Phoebe&quot;, Miranda in &quot;The Tempest&quot; and Rose in &quot;The Blind Giant is Dancing&quot;, both for the Belvoir Street Theatre Company. In other television roles, Blanchett starred as Bianca in ABC&#39;s <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0122814/?ls">Bordertown (1995)</a>, as Janie Morris in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0096592/?ls">G.P. (1989)</a> and in ABC&#39;s popular series <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0110858/?ls">Police Rescue (1994)</a>. She made her feature film debut in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0119859/?ls">Paradise Road (1997)</a>.<br/><br/>Cate married writer <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0881490/?ls">Andrew Upton</a> in 1997. She had met him a year earlier on a movie set, and they didn&#39;t like each other at first. He thought she was aloof, and she thought he was arrogant, but then they connected over a poker game at a party, and she went home with him that night. Three weeks later he proposed marriage and they quickly married before she went off to England to play her breakthrough role in films: the title character in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0127536/?ls">Elizabeth (1998)</a> for which she won numerous awards for her performance, including the Golden Globe for Best Actress in a Drama. Cate was also nominated for an Academy Award for the role but lost out to <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000569/?ls">Gwyneth Paltrow</a>. 2001 was a particularly busy year, with starring roles in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0219965/?ls">Bandits (2001)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0120824/?ls">The Shipping News (2001)</a>, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0245046/?ls">Charlotte Gray (2001)</a> and playing Elf Queen Galadriel in the &quot;Lord Of The Rings&quot; trilogy. She also gave birth to her first child, son Dashiell, in 2001. In 2004, she gave birth to her second son Roman.<br/><br/>Also, in 2004, she played actress <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000031/?ls">Katharine Hepburn</a> in Martin Scorsese&#39;s film <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0338751/?ls">The Aviator (2004)</a>, for which she received an Academy Award as Best Supporting Actress. Two years later, she received an Academy Award nomination as Best Supporting Actress for playing a teacher having an affair with an underage student in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0465551/?ls">Notes on a Scandal (2006)</a>. In 2007, she returned to the role that made her a star in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0414055/?ls">Elizabeth: The Golden Age (2007)</a>. It earned her an Oscar nomination as Best Actress. She was nominated for another Oscar that same year as Best Supporting Actress for playing <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0001168/?ls">Bob Dylan</a> in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0368794/?ls">I&#39;m Not There (2007)</a>. In 2008, she gave birth to her third child, son Ignatius. She and her husband became artistic directors of the Sydney Theatre Company, choosing to spend more time in Australia raising their three sons. She also purchased a multi-million dollar home in Sydney, Australia and named it Bulwarra and made extensive renovations to it. Because of her life in Australia, her film work became sporadic, until <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0000095/?ls">Woody Allen</a> cast her in the title role in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt2334873/?ls">Blue Jasmine (2013)</a>, which won her the Academy Award as Best Actress. She ended her job as artistic director of the Sydney Theatre Company, while her husband continued there for two more years before he too resigned.<br/><br/>In 2015, she adopted her daughter Edith in her father&#39;s homeland of the United States. That same year, she and her husband sold their multi-million dollar home in Australia at a profit and moved to America. Reasons varied from her wanting to work more in America to wanting to familiarize herself with her late father&#39;s American heritage. She played the title role of <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt2402927/?ls">Carol (2015)</a>, a 1950s American housewife in a lesbian affair with a younger woman, for which she received an Oscar nomination as Best Actress. While most actresses might slow down in their forties, Blanchett did the opposite by stretching her boundaries even further, such as when she played 13 different characters in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt4511200/?ls">Manifesto (2015)</a> and then making her Broadway debut in 2017 in &quot;The Present&quot;, which is her husband&#39;s adaptation of Chekhov&#39;s play &quot;Platonov&quot; for which she earned a Tony nomination as Best Actress in a Play. Also in 2017, she was selected for the highest honor in her birth country: the Companion of the Order of Australia (AC).</div></div></div></div></div></div></li><li class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item"><div class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__c"><div class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__tc"><span class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__t" iorieb"><div class="ipc-avatar ipc-avatar--base" role="group"><div class="ipc-media ipc-media--avatar ipc-image-media-ratio--avatar ipc-media--circle-radius ipc-media--base ipc-media--custom Audrey Hepburn</h3></a></div><div class="sc-7c95f518-6 iDkHPP"><ul class="ipc-inline-list ipc-inline-list--show-dividers sc-7c95f518-4 lolxqE base" role="presentation" data-testid="nlib-professions"><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Actress</li><li role="presentation" class="ipc-inline-list__item sc-7c95f518-5 eXHlql">Soundtrack</li></ul><a class="ipc-link ipc-link--base sc-ab9eb9db-0 iRQWod" tabindex="0" aria-disabled="false" data-testid="nlib-known-for-title" href="/title/tt0054698/?ref_=ls_knf_21">Breakfast at Tiffany&#x27;s (1961)</a></div></div></div><div><button data-testid="dli-add-to-list-button" class="ipc-icon-button ipc-icon-button--base ipc-icon-button--onAccent2" title="Add to list" tabindex="0" aria-label="Add to list" aria-disabled="false"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="24" height="24" class="ipc-icon ipc-icon--add" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="currentColor" role="presentation"><path d="M18 13h-5v5c0 .55-.45 1-1 1s-1-.45-1-1v-5H6c-.55 0-1-.45-1-1s.45-1 1-1h5V6c0-.55.45-1 1-1s1 .45 1 1v5h5c.55 0 1 .45 1 1s-.45 1-1 1z"></path></svg></button></div></div><div data-testid="dli-bio" class="sc-77f37b3d-2 dpXpaE"><div class="ipc-html-content ipc-html-content--base sc-77f37b3d-3 huKIYr" role="presentation"><div class="ipc-html-content-inner-div" role="presentation">Audrey Hepburn was born as Audrey Kathleen Ruston on May 4, 1929 in Ixelles, Brussels, Belgium. Her mother, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0887054/?ls">Baroness Ella Van Heemstra</a>, was a Dutch noblewoman. Her father, Joseph Victor Anthony Ruston, was a businessman and Honorary British Consul in the Dutch East Indies; he was born in Úzice, Bohemia, of English, Austrian, and Czech-Jewish descent.<br/><br/>After her parents&#39; divorce, Audrey went to London with her mother where she went to a private girls school. Later, when her mother moved back to the Netherlands, she attended private schools as well. While she vacationed with her mother in Arnhem, Netherlands, Hitler&#39;s army took over the town. It was here that she fell on hard times during the Nazi occupation. Audrey suffered from depression and malnutrition.<br/><br/>After the liberation, she went to a ballet school in London on a scholarship and later began a modeling career. As a model, she was graceful and, it seemed, she had found her niche in life--until the film producers came calling. In 1948, after being spotted modeling by a producer, she was signed to a bit part in the European film <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0040639/?ls">Nederlands in zeven lessen (1948)</a>. Later, she had a speaking role in the 1951 film, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0044225/?ls">Young Wives&#39; Tale (1951)</a> as Eve Lester. The part still wasn&#39;t much, so she headed to America to try her luck there. Audrey gained immediate prominence in the US with her role in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0046250/?ls">Roman Holiday (1953)</a>. This film turned out to be a smashing success, and she won an Oscar as Best Actress.<br/><br/>On September 25, 1954, she married actor <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0002072/?ls">Mel Ferrer</a>. She also starred in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0047437/?ls">Sabrina (1954)</a>, for which she received another Academy Award nomination. She starred in the films <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0050419/?ls">Funny Face (1957)</a> and <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0050658/?ls">Love in the Afternoon (1957)</a>. She received yet another Academy Award nomination for her role in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0053131/?ls">The Nun&#39;s Story (1959)</a>. On July 17, 1960, she gave birth to her first son, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0274625/?ls">Sean Hepburn Ferrer</a>.<br/><br/>Audrey reached the pinnacle of her career when she played Holly Golightly in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0054698/?ls">Breakfast at Tiffany&#39;s (1961)</a>, for which she received another Oscar nomination. She scored commercial success again playing Regina Lampert in the espionage caper <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0056923/?ls">Charade (1963)</a>. One of Audrey&#39;s most radiant roles was in the fine production of <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0058385/?ls">My Fair Lady (1964)</a>. After a couple of other movies, most notably <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0062407/?ls">Two for the Road (1967)</a>, she hit pay dirt and another nomination in <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0062467/?ls">Wait Until Dark (1967)</a>.<br/><br/>In 1967, Audrey decided to retire from acting while she was on top. She divorced from <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm0002072/?ls">Mel Ferrer</a> in 1968. On January 19, 1969, she married Dr. Andrea Dotti. On February 8, 1970, she gave birth to her second son, <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/name/nm6114340/?ls">Luca Dotti</a> in Lausanne, Vaud, Switzerland. From time to time, she would appear on the silver screen.<br/><br/>In 1988, she became a special ambassador to the United Nations UNICEF fund helping children in Latin America and Africa, a position she retained until 1993. She was named to People&#39;s magazine as one of the 50 most beautiful people in the world. Her last film was <a class="ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity" href="/title/tt0096794/?ls">Always (1989)</a>.<br/><br/>Audrey Hepburn died, aged 63, on January 20, 1993 in Tolochnaz, Vaud, Switzerland, from appendicular cancer. She had made a total of 31 high quality movies. Her elegance and style will always be remembered in film history as evidenced by her being named in Empire magazine&#39;s &quot;The Top 100 Movie Stars of All Time&quot;.</div></div></div></div></div></div></li><li class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item"><div class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__c"><div class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__tc"><span class="ipc-metadata-list-summary-item__t" aria-disabled="false"></span><div class="sc-77f37b3d-0 jCbCZO dli-parent"><div class="sc-77f37b3d-1 gJmTWZ"><div class="sc-7c95f518-0 cDAKkN"><div
