Houghton Hepburn was born on May 12, 1907 in Hartford, Connecticut to a suffragist, Katharine Martha (Houghton), and a doctor, Thomas Norval Hepburn, who both always encouraged her to speak her mind, develop it fully, and exercise her body to its full potential. An athletic tomboy as a child, she was very close to her brother Tom; at 14 she was devastated to find him dead, the apparent result of accidentally hanging himself while practicing a hanging trick their father had taught them. For many years afterward, she used his November 8 birth date as her own. She became shy around girls her age and was largely schooled at home. She did attend Bryn Mawr College, where she decided to become an actress, appearing in many of their productions.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eAfter graduating, she began getting small roles in plays on Broadway and elsewhere. She always attracted attention, especially for her role in \u0026quot;Art and Mrs. Bottle\u0026quot; (1931). She finally broke into stardom when she took the starring role of the Amazon princess Antiope in \u0026quot;A Warrior\u0026#39;s Husband\u0026quot; (1932). The inevitable film offers followed; after making a few screen tests, she was cast in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0022685/?ls\"\u003eA Bill of Divorcement (1932)\u003c/a\u003e, opposite \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000858/?ls\"\u003eJohn Barrymore\u003c/a\u003e. The film was a hit, and after agreeing to her salary demands, RKO signed her to a contract. She made five films between 1932 and 1934. For her third, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0024353/?ls\"\u003eMorning Glory (1933)\u003c/a\u003e, she won her first Academy Award. Her fourth, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0024264/?ls\"\u003eLittle Women (1933)\u003c/a\u003e, was the most successful picture of its day.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eBut stories were beginning to leak out, of her haughty behavior off- screen and her refusal to play the Hollywood Game, always wearing slacks and no makeup, never posing for pictures or giving interviews. Audiences were shocked at her unconventional behavior instead of applauding it, and so when she returned to Broadway in 1934 to star in \u0026quot;The Lake\u0026quot;, the critics panned her, and the audiences, who at first bought up tickets, soon deserted her. When she returned to Hollywood, things didn\u0026#39;t get much better. From 1935-1938, she had only two hits: \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0026056/?ls\"\u003eAlice Adams (1935)\u003c/a\u003e, which brought her her second Oscar nomination, and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0029604/?ls\"\u003eStage Door (1937)\u003c/a\u003e; the many flops included \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0026134/?ls\"\u003eBreak of Hearts (1935)\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0027067/?ls\"\u003eSylvia Scarlett (1935)\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0027948/?ls\"\u003eMary of Scotland (1936)\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0029454/?ls\"\u003eQuality Street (1937)\u003c/a\u003e, and the now-classic \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0029947/?ls\"\u003eBaby You Have This (1938)\u003c/a\u003e.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eWith so many flops, she came to be labeled \u0026quot;box-office poison\u0026quot;. Sidney had little formal education and at the age of 15 was sent to Miami to live with his brother, in order to forestall a growing tendency toward delinquency. In the U.S., he experienced the racial chasm that divides the country, a great shock to a boy coming from a society with a majority of African descent.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eAt 18, he went to New York, did menial jobs and slept in a bus terminal toilet. An impulsive audition at the American Negro Theatre was rejected so forcefully that Poitier dedicated the next six months to overcoming his accent and improving his performing skills. On his second try, he was accepted. Spotted in rehearsal by a casting agent, he won a bit part in the Broadway production of \u0026quot;Lysistrata\u0026quot;, for which he earned good reviews. The Newmans were well-to-do and Paul Newman grew up in affluent Shaker Heights. Before he became an actor, Newman ran the family sporting goods store in Cleveland, Ohio.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eBy 1950, the 25-year-old Newman had been kicked out of Ohio University, where he belonged to the Phi Kappa Tau fraternity, for unruly behavior (denting the college president\u0026#39;s car with a beer keg), served three years in the United States Navy during World War II as a radio operator, graduated from Ohio\u0026#39;s Kenyon College, married his first wife, Jacqueline \u0026quot;Jackie\u0026quot; Witte (born 1929), and had his first child, Scott. Gregory Peck was born on April 5, 1916 in La Jolla, California, to Bernice Mae (Ayres) and Gregory Pearl Peck, a chemist and druggist in San Diego. He had Irish (from his paternal grandmother), English, and some German, ancestry. His parents divorced when he was five years old. An only child, he was sent to live with his grandmother. He never felt he had a stable childhood. His fondest memories are of his grandmother taking him to the movies every week and of his dog, which followed him everywhere. He studied pre-med at UC-Berkeley and, while there, got bitten by the acting bug and decided to change the focus of his studies. He enrolled in the Neighborhood Playhouse in New York and debuted on Broadway after graduation. His debut was in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0930539/?ls\"\u003eEmlyn Williams\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39; play \u0026quot;The Morning Star\u0026quot; (1942). Jeffrey Hanks was born in Concord, California, to Janet Marylyn (Frager), a hospital worker, and Amos Mefford Hanks, an itinerant cook. His mother\u0026#39;s family, originally surnamed \u0026quot;Fraga\u0026quot;, was entirely Portuguese, while his father was of mostly English ancestry. Tom grew up in what he has called a \u0026quot;fractured\u0026quot; family. He moved around a great deal after his parents\u0026#39; divorce, living with a succession of step-families. No problems, no alcoholism - just a confused childhood. He has no acting experience in college and credits the fact that he could not get cast in a college play with actually starting his career. was the ultra-cool male film star of the 1960s, and rose from a troubled youth spent in reform schools to being the world\u0026#39;s most popular actor. Over 40 years after his untimely death from mesothelioma in 1980, Steve McQueen is still considered hip and cool, and he endures as an icon of popular culture.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eMcQueen was born in Beech Grove, Indiana, to mother Julian (Crawford) and father William Terence McQueen, a stunt pilot. The young McQueen appeared as Vin, alongside \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000989/?ls\"\u003eYul Brynner\u003c/a\u003e, in the star-laden \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0054047/?ls\"\u003eThe Magnificent Seven (1960)\u003c/a\u003e and effectively hijacked the lead from the bigger star by ensuring he was nearly always doing something in every shot he and Brynner were in together, such as adjusting his hat or gun belt. He next scored with audiences with two interesting performances, first in the World War II drama \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0056062/?ls\"\u003eHell Is for Heroes (1962)\u003c/a\u003e and then in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0056676/?ls\"\u003eThe War Lover (1962)\u003c/a\u003e. Riding a wave of popularity, McQueen delivered another crowd pleaser as Hilts, the Cooler King, in the knockout World War II P.O.W. film \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0057115/?ls\"\u003eThe Great Escape (1963)\u003c/a\u003e, featuring his famous leap over the barbed wire on a motorcycle while being pursued by Nazi troops (in fact, however, the stunt was actually performed by his good friend, stunt rider \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0252379/?ls\"\u003eBud Ekins\u003c/a\u003e).\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eMcQueen next appeared in several films of mixed quality, including \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0057517/?ls\"\u003eSoldier in the Rain (1963)\u003c/a\u003e; \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0057263/?ls\"\u003eLove with the Proper Stranger (1963)\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0058930/?ls\"\u003eBaby the Rain Must Fall (1965)\u003c/a\u003e. McQueen was genuine hot property and next appeared with \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0001159/?ls\"\u003eFaye Dunaway\u003c/a\u003e in the provocative crime drama \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0063688/?ls\"\u003eThe Thomas Crown Affair (1968)\u003c/a\u003e, next in what many consider his signature role, that of a maverick, taciturn detective in the mega-hit \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0062765/?ls\"\u003eBullitt (1968)\u003c/a\u003e, renowned for its famous chase sequence through San Francisco between McQueen\u0026#39;s Ford Mustang GT and the killer\u0026#39;s black Dodge Charger.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eInterestingly, McQueen\u0026#39;s next role was a total departure from the action genre, as he played Southerner Boon Hogganbeck in the family-oriented \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0064886/?ls\"\u003eThe Reivers (1969)\u003c/a\u003e, based on the popular \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0001203/?ls\"\u003eWilliam Faulkner\u003c/a\u003e novel. The film was a monster hit and set the benchmark for other disaster movies that followed. However, it was McQueen\u0026#39;s last film role for several years. After a four-year hiatus he surprised fans, and was almost unrecognizable under long hair and a beard, as a rabble-rousing early environmentalist in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0075993/?ls\"\u003eAn Enemy of the People (1978)\u003c/a\u003e, based on the \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0406585/?ls\"\u003eHenrik Ibsen\u003c/a\u003e play.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eMcQueen\u0026#39;s last two film performances were in the unusual Western \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0080031/?ls\"\u003eTom Horn (1980)\u003c/a\u003e, then he portrayed real-life bounty hunter Ralph \u0026quot;Papa\u0026#39; Thorson (\u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0861774/?ls\"\u003eRalph Thorson\u003c/a\u003e) in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0080907/?ls\"\u003eThe Hunter (1980)\u003c/a\u003e. In 1978, McQueen developed a persistent cough that would not go away. He quit smoking cigarettes and underwent antibiotic treatments without improvement. Shortness of breath grew more pronounced and on December 22, 1979, after he completed work on \u0026#39;The Hunter\u0026#39;, a biopsy revealed pleural mesothelioma, a rare lung cancer associated with asbestos exposure for which there is no known cure. The asbestos was thought to have been in the protective suits worn in his race car driving days, but in fact the auto racing suits McQueen wore were made of Nomex, a DuPont fire-resistant aramid fiber that contains no asbestos. McQueen later gave a medical interview in which he believed that asbestos used in movie sound stage insulation and race-drivers\u0026#39; protective suits and helmets could have been involved, but he thought it more likely that his illness was a direct result of massive exposure while removing asbestos lagging from pipes aboard a troop ship while in the US Marines.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eBy February 1980, there was evidence of widespread metastasis. While he tried to keep the condition a secret, the National Enquirer disclosed that he had \u0026quot;terminal cancer\u0026quot; on March 11, 1980. In July, McQueen traveled to Rosarito Beach, Mexico for an unconventional treatment after American doctors told him they could do nothing to prolong his life. Controversy arose over McQueen\u0026#39;s Mexican trip, because McQueen sought a non-traditional cancer treatment called the Gerson Therapy that used coffee enemas, frequent washing with shampoos, daily injections of fluid containing live cells from cows and sheep, massage and laetrile, a supposedly \u0026quot;natural\u0026quot; anti-cancer drug available in Mexico, but not approved by the US Food and Drug Administration. McQueen paid for these unconventional medical treatments by himself in cash payments which was said to have cost an upwards of $40,000 per month during his three-month stay in Mexico. McQueen was treated by William Donald Kelley, whose only medical license had been (until revoked in 1976) for orthodontics.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eMcQueen returned to the United States in early October 1980. Despite metastasis of the cancer through McQueen\u0026#39;s body, Kelley publicly announced that McQueen would be completely cured and return to normal life. McQueen\u0026#39;s condition soon worsened and \u0026quot;huge\u0026quot; tumors developed in his abdomen. In late October, McQueen flew to Ciudad Juarez, Chihuahua, Mexico to have an abdominal tumor on his liver (weighing around five pounds) removed, despite warnings from his American doctors that the tumor was inoperable and his heart could not withstand the surgery. McQueen checked into a Juarez clinic under the alias \u0026quot;Sam Shepard\u0026quot; where the local Mexican doctors and staff at the small, low-income clinic were unaware of his actual identity.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eSteve McQueen passed away on November 7, 1980, at age 50 after the cancer surgery which was said to be successful. He was cremated and his ashes were scattered at sea. He married three times and had a lifelong love of motor racing, once remarking, \u0026quot;Racing is life. Judy\u0026#39;s divorce from \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0741328/?ls\"\u003eDavid Rose\u003c/a\u003e had been finalized on June 8, 1944 after almost three years of marriage, and despite her brief fling with \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000080/?ls\"\u003eOrson Welles\u003c/a\u003e, who at the time was married to screen sex goddess \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000028/?ls\"\u003eRita Hayworth\u003c/a\u003e, on June 15, 1945 Judy made Vincente her second husband, tying the knot with him that afternoon at her mother\u0026#39;s home with her boss \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0562454/?ls\"\u003eLouis B. Mayer\u003c/a\u003e giving her away and her best friend Betty Asher serving as bridesmaid. They spent three months on honeymoon in New York and afterwards Judy discovered that she was pregnant.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eOn March 12, 1946 in Los Angeles, California, Judy gave birth to their daughter, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0591485/?ls\"\u003eLiza Minnelli\u003c/a\u003e, via cesarean section. It was a joyous time for the couple, but Judy was out of commission for weeks due to the cesarean and her postnatal depression, so she spent much of her time recuperating in bed. She soon returned to work, but married life was never the same for Vincente and Judy after they filmed \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0040694/?ls\"\u003eThe Pirate (1948)\u003c/a\u003e together in 1947. Judy\u0026#39;s mental health was fast deteriorating and she began hallucinating things and making false accusations toward people, especially her husband, making the filming a nightmare. She also began an affair with aspiring Russian actor \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000989/?ls\"\u003eYul Brynner\u003c/a\u003e, but after the affair ended, Judy soon regained health and tried to salvage her failing marriage. She then teamed up with dancing legend \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000001/?ls\"\u003eFred Astaire\u003c/a\u003e for the delightful musical \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0040308/?ls\"\u003eHappy Easter (1948)\u003c/a\u003e, which resulted in a successful comeback despite having Vincente fired from directing the musical. Afterwards, Judy\u0026#39;s health deteriorated and she began the first of several suicide attempts. In May 1949, she was checked into a rehabilitation center, which caused her much distress.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eShe soon regained strength and was visited frequently by her lover \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000069/?ls\"\u003eFrank Sinatra\u003c/a\u003e, but never saw much of Vincente or Liza. At 28, Judy received her third suspension and was fired by MGM, and her second marriage was soon dissolved.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eHaving taken up with \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0525184/?ls\"\u003eSidney Luft\u003c/a\u003e, Judy traveled to London to star at the legendary Palladium. With her newfound fame on stage, Judy was stopped in her tracks in February 1952 when she became pregnant by her new lover, Sid. At the age of 30, she made him her third husband on June 8, 1952; the wedding was held at a friend\u0026#39;s ranch in Pasadena. Her relationship with her mother had long since been dissolved by this point, and after the birth of her second daughter, Lorna Luft, on November 21, 1952, she refused to allow her mother to see her granddaughter. Ethel then died in January 1953 of a heart attack, leaving Judy devastated and feeling guilty about not reconciling with her mother before her untimely demise.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eAfter the funeral, Judy signed a film contract with Warner Bros. to star in the musical remake of \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0029606/?ls\"\u003eA Star Is Born (1937)\u003c/a\u003e, which had starred \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0310980/?ls\"\u003eJanet Gaynor\u003c/a\u003e, who had won the first-ever Academy Award for Best Actress in 1929. She won a Golden Globe for her brilliant and truly outstanding performance as Esther Blodgett, nightclub singer turned movie star, but when it came to the Academy Awards, a distraught Judy lost out on the Best Actress Oscar to \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000038/?ls\"\u003eGrace Kelly\u003c/a\u003e for her portrayal of the wife of an alcoholic star in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0046874/?ls\"\u003eThe Country Girl (1954)\u003c/a\u003e. Continuing her work on stage, Judy gave birth to her beloved son, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0525180/?ls\"\u003eJoey Luft\u003c/a\u003e, on March 29, 1955. Her battles with alcoholism and drugs led to Judy\u0026#39;s making numerous headlines in newspapers, but she soldiered on, forming a close friendship with President John F. Kennedy. In 1963, Judy and Sid finally separated permanently, and on May 19, 1965 their divorce was finalized after almost 13 years of marriage. remarkable, soft-spoken American began in films as a diffident juvenile. With passing years, he matured into a star character actor who exemplified not only integrity and strength, but an ideal of the common man fighting against social injustice and oppression. He was born in Grand Island, Hall, Nebraska, the son of Herberta Elma (Jaynes) and William Brace Fonda, who was a commercial printer, and proprietor of the W. B. Fonda Printing Company in Omaha, Nebraska. His distant ancestors were Italians who had fled their country and moved to Holland, presumably because of political or religious persecution. In the mid-1600s, they crossed the Atlantic and settled in upstate New York where they founded a community with the Fonda name.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eGrowing up, Henry developed an early interest in journalism after having a story published in a local newspaper. At the age of twelve, he helped in his father\u0026#39;s printing business for $2 a week. Following graduation from high school in 1923, he got a part-time job in Minneapolis with the Northwestern Bell Telephone Company which allowed him at first to pursue journalistic studies at the University of Minnesota. As it became difficult to juggle his working hours with his academic roster, he obtained another position as a physical education instructor at $30 a week, including room and board. By this time, he had grown to a height of six foot one and was a natural for basketball.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eIn 1925, having returned to Omaha, Henry reevaluated his options and came to the conclusion that journalism was not his forte, after all. For a while, he tried his hand at several temporary jobs, including as a mechanic and a window dresser. Then, despite opposition from his parents, Henry accepted an offer from Gregory Foley, director of the Omaha Playhouse, to play the title role in \u0026#39;Merton of the Movies\u0026#39;. His father would not speak to him for a month. The play and its star received fairly good notices in the local press. It ran for a week, after which Henry observed \u0026quot;the idea of being Merton and not myself taught me that I could hide behind a mask\u0026quot;. For the rest of the repertory season, Henry advanced to assistant director which enabled him to design and paint sets as well as act. A casual trip to New York, however, had already made him set his sights on Broadway.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eIn 1928, he headed east and briefly played in summer stock before joining the University Players, a group of talented Princeton and Harvard graduates among whose number were such future luminaries as \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000071/?ls\"\u003eJames Stewart\u003c/a\u003e (who would remain his closest lifelong friend), \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0517597/?ls\"\u003eJoshua Logan\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0808949/?ls\"\u003eKent Smith\u003c/a\u003e. After all, he had just completed a successful run on Broadway in the stage version. The cheesy publicity tag line for the picture was \u0026quot;you\u0026#39;ll be fonder of Fonda\u0026quot;, but the film was an undeniable hit. Wanger, realizing he had a good thing going, next cast Henry in a succession of A-grade pictures which capitalized on his image as the sincere, unaffected country boy. Pick of the bunch were the Technicolor outdoor western \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0028401/?ls\"\u003eThe Trail of the Lonesome Pine (1936)\u003c/a\u003e, the gritty Depression-era drama \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0029808/?ls\"\u003eYou Only Live Once (1937)\u003c/a\u003e (with Henry as a back-to-the-wall good guy forced into becoming a fugitive from the law by circumstance), the screwball comedy \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0027979/?ls\"\u003eThe Moon\u0026#39;s Our Home (1936)\u003c/a\u003e (with ex-wife Sullavan), the excellent pre-civil war-era romantic drama \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0030287/?ls\"\u003eJezebel (1938)\u003c/a\u003e and the equally superb \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0032155/?ls\"\u003eYoung Mr. Lincoln (1939)\u003c/a\u003e, in which Henry gave his best screen performance to date as the \u0026#39;jackleg lawyer from Springfield\u0026#39;. The studio responded by placing her on a six-month suspension, all of the studios at the time operating under the policy that players were nothing more than property to do with as they saw fit. As if that weren\u0026#39;t bad enough, when her contract with Warners was up, she was told that she needed to make up the time lost because of the suspension. Irate, she sued the studio, and for the length of the court battle she didn\u0026#39;t appear in a single film. The result, however, was worth it. In a landmark decision, the court said that not only would Olivia not need to make up the time, but also that all performers would be limited to a seven-year contract that would include any suspensions handed down. This became known as the \u0026quot;de Havilland decision\u0026quot;: no longer could studios treat their performers as chattel. to be one of the most pivotal stars of the early days of Hollywood, Charlie Chaplin lived an interesting life both in his films and behind the camera. He is most recognized as an icon of the silent film era, often associated with his popular character, the Little Tramp; the man with the toothbrush mustache, bowler hat, bamboo cane, and a funny walk.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eCharles Spencer Chaplin was born in Walworth, London, England on April 16, 1889, to Hannah Harriet Pedlingham (Hill) and Charles Chaplin, both music hall performers, who were married on June 22, 1885. After Charles Sr. separated from Hannah to perform in New York City, Hannah then tried to resurrect her stage career. Unfortunately, her singing voice had a tendency to break at unexpected moments. When this happened, the stage manager spotted young Charlie standing in the wings and led him on stage, where five-year-old Charlie began to sing a popular tune. Charlie and his half-brother, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0152260/?ls\"\u003eSyd Chaplin\u003c/a\u003e spent their lives in and out of charity homes and workhouses between their mother\u0026#39;s bouts of insanity. Hannah was committed to Cane Hill Asylum in May 1903 and lived there until 1921, when Chaplin moved her to California.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eChaplin began his official acting career at the age of eight, touring with the Eight Lancashire Lads. At age 18, he began touring with \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0439833/?ls\"\u003eFred Karno\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s vaudeville troupe, joining them on the troupe\u0026#39;s 1910 United States tour. He traveled west to California in December 1913 and signed on with Keystone Studios\u0026#39; popular comedy director \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0784407/?ls\"\u003eMack Sennett\u003c/a\u003e, who had seen Chaplin perform on stage in New York. Charlie soon wrote his brother Syd, asking him to become his manager. While at Keystone, Chaplin appeared in and directed 35 films, starring as the Little Tramp in nearly all.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eIn November 1914, he left Keystone and signed on at Essanay, where he made 15 films. In 1916, he signed on at Mutual and made 12 films. In June 1917, Chaplin signed up with First National Studios, after which he built Chaplin Studios. In 1919, he and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0001196/?ls\"\u003eDouglas Fairbanks\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0681933/?ls\"\u003eMary Pickford\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000428/?ls\"\u003eD.W. Griffith\u003c/a\u003e formed United Artists (UA).\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eChaplin\u0026#39;s life and career was full of scandal and controversy. His first big scandal was during World War I, at which time his loyalty to England, his home country, was questioned. He had never applied for American citizenship, but claimed that he was a \u0026quot;paying visitor\u0026quot; to the United States. Many British citizens called Chaplin a coward and a slacker. This and other career eccentricities sparked suspicion with FBI chief \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0393890/?ls\"\u003eJ. Edgar Hoover\u003c/a\u003e and the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC), who believed that he was injecting Communist propaganda into his films. In May 1943, Barry returned to inform Chaplin that she was pregnant and filed a paternity suit, claiming that the unborn child was his. During the 1944 trial, blood tests proved that Chaplin was not the father, but at the time, blood tests were inadmissible evidence, and he was ordered to pay $75 a week until the child turned 21.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eChaplin also was scrutinized for his support in aiding the Russian struggle against the invading Nazis during World War II, and the United States government questioned his moral and political views, suspecting him of having Communist ties. Conversely, when Chaplin and his family traveled to London for the premier of \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0044837/?ls\"\u003eLimelight (1952)\u003c/a\u003e, he was denied re-entry to the United States. Hayworth was born Margarita Carmen Cansino on October 17, 1918, in Brooklyn, New York, into a family of dancers. Her father, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0134444/?ls\"\u003eEduardo Cansino\u003c/a\u003e Reina, was a dancer as was his father before him. He emigrated from Spain in 1913. Rita\u0026#39;s American mother, Volga Margaret (Hayworth), who was of mostly Irish descent, met Eduardo in 1916 and were married the following year. Rita, herself, studied as a dancer in order to follow in her family\u0026#39;s footsteps. She joined her family on stage when she was eight years old when her family was filmed in a movie called \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0124553/?ls\"\u003eLa Fiesta (1926)\u003c/a\u003e. It was her first film appearance, albeit an uncredited one. Sotted by Fox studio head \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0790638/?ls\"\u003eWinfield R. Sheehan\u003c/a\u003e, she signed her first studio contract, and make her film debut at age sixteen, in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0026262/?ls\"\u003eDante\u0026#39;s Inferno (1935)\u003c/a\u003e, followed by \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0025017/?ls\"\u003eCruz Diablo (1934)\u003c/a\u003e. She continued to play small bit parts in several films under the name of \u0026quot;Rita Cansino\u0026quot;. Fox dropped her after five small roles, but expert, exploitative promotion by her first husband Edward Judson soon brought Rita a new contract at Columbia Pictures, where studio head \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0169902/?ls\"\u003eHarry Cohn\u003c/a\u003e changed her surname to Hayworth and approved raising her hairline by electrolysis. This was the film that exuded the warmth and seductive vitality that was to make her famous. Her natural, raw beauty was showcased later that year in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0033405/?ls\"\u003eBlood and Sand (1941)\u003c/a\u003e, filmed in Technicolor.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eRita was probably the second most popular actress after \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0002107/?ls\"\u003eBetty Grable\u003c/a\u003e. Her dancing, for which she had studied all her life, was astounding. After the hit \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0038559/?ls\"\u003eGilida (1946)\u003c/a\u003e (her dancing had made the film and it had made her), her career was on the skids. The drought began between \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0040525/?ls\"\u003eThe Lady from Shanghai (1947)\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0044493/?ls\"\u003eChampagne Safari (1954)\u003c/a\u003e. Wood was an American actress of Russian and Ukrainian descent. She started her career as a child actress and eventually transitioned into teenage roles, young adult roles, and middle-aged roles. She drowned off Catalina Island on November 29, 1981 at age 43.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eWood was born July 20, 1938 in San Francisco to Russian immigrant parents: housewife \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm11602318/?ls\"\u003eMaria Gurdin\u003c/a\u003e (née Zoudilova; transliterated as Zoodiloff on legal records), known by multiple aliases including Mary, Marie and Musia, and second husband \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm11602317/?ls\"\u003eNick Gurdin\u003c/a\u003e (née Zacharenko), a janitor and prop builder. Nicholas was born in Primorsky Krai, son of a chocolate-factory worker. Maria was born in Barnaul, southern Siberia to a wealthy industrialist. Natalie\u0026#39;s maternal grandfather owned soap and candle factories.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eWood\u0026#39;s parents had to migrate due to the Russian Civil War. Her paternal grandfather joined the anti-Bolshevik civilian forces early in the war and was killed in a street fight between Red and White Russian soldiers. This convinced the Zacharenkos to migrate to Shanghai, China, where they had relatives. Wood\u0026#39;s paternal grandmother remarried in 1927 and moved the family to Vancouver, British Columbia. In 1933 they resettled along the U.S. West Coast. Nicholas met Wood\u0026#39;s mother, four years his senior, while she was still married to Alexander Tatuloff, an Armenian mechanic she divorced in 1936.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eMary Tatuloff, Wood\u0026#39;s mother, had unfulfilled ambitions of becoming a ballet dancer. She grew up in the Chinese city of Harbin and had married Alexander there in 1925. The Tatuloffs had one daughter, Ovsanna, before coming to America in 1930. After marrying Nicholas Zacharenko in 1938, five months before Wood\u0026#39;s birth, Mary (now calling herself Marie) transferred her dream of stardom onto her second child. Marie frequently took a young Wood with her to the cinema, where she could study the films of Hollywood child stars.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eWood\u0026#39;s parents changed the family name to Gurdin upon obtaining U.S. citizenship, and her pseudonymous mother finally settled on a permanent first name: Maria. In 1942 they bought a house in Santa Rosa, where young Natalie was noticed by members of a crew during a film shoot. She got to audition for roles as an actress, and the family moved to Los Angeles to help seek out roles for her. RKO Radio Pictures\u0026#39; executives \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0324544/?ls\"\u003eWilliam Goetz\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0507079/?ls\"\u003eDavid Lewis\u003c/a\u003e chose the stage name Wood for her, in reference to director \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0939992/?ls\"\u003eSam Wood\u003c/a\u003e. Natalie\u0026#39;s younger sister Svetlana Gurdin would eventually follow an acting career as well, under the stage name \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0939836/?ls\"\u003eLana Wood\u003c/a\u003e.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eWood made her film debut in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0035970/?ls\"\u003eHappy Land (1943)\u003c/a\u003e. She was only five years old, and her scene as the \u0026quot;Little Girl Who Drops Ice Cream Cone\u0026quot; lasted 15 seconds. Wood somehow attracted the interest of film director \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0681635/?ls\"\u003eIrving Pichel\u003c/a\u003e who remained in contact with her family. She had few job offers over the following two years, but Pichel helped her get a screen test for a more substantial role in the romance film \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0039041/?ls\"\u003eTomorrow Is Forever (1946)\u003c/a\u003e. Wood passed through an audition and won the role of Margaret Ludwig, a post-World War II German orphan. At the time, Wood was unable to \u0026quot;cry on cue\u0026quot; for a key scene, so her mother tore a butterfly to pieces in front of her, giving her a reason to cry for the scene.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eWood started appearing regularly in films following this role and soon received a contract with 20th Century Fox. Her first major role was that of Susan Walker in the Christmas film \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0039628/?ls\"\u003eMiracle on 34th Street (1947)\u003c/a\u003e, which was a commercial and critical hit. Wood got her first taste of fame, and afterwards Macy\u0026#39;s invited her to appear in the store\u0026#39;s annual Thanksgiving Day parade. Following her early success, Wood receive many more film offers. She typically appeared in family films, cast as the daughter of such stars as \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0534045/?ls\"\u003eFred MacMurray\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm4008790/?ls\"\u003eMargaret Sullivan\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000071/?ls\"\u003eJames Stewart\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000951/?ls\"\u003eJoan Blondell\u003c/a\u003e, and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000012/?ls\"\u003eBette Davis\u003c/a\u003e. Wood found herself in high demand and appeared in over twenty films as a child actress.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eThe California laws of the era required that until reaching adulthood, child actors had to spend at least three hours per day in the classroom. Wood received her primary education on the studio lots, receiving three hours of school lessons whenever she was working on a film. She was reportedly a \u0026quot;straight A student.\u0026quot; Director \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000581/?ls\"\u003eJoseph L. Mankiewicz\u003c/a\u003e was quite impressed by Wood\u0026#39;s intellect. After school hours ended, Wood would hurry to the set to film her scenes.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eWhile Wood acquired the services of agents, her early career was micromanaged by her mother. An older Wood gained her first major television role in the short-lived sitcom \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0045434/?ls\"\u003eThe Pride of the Family (1953)\u003c/a\u003e. At the age of 16, she found more success with the role of Judy in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0048545/?ls\"\u003eRebel Without a Cause (1955)\u003c/a\u003e. She played the role of a teenage girl who wears makeup and dresses up in racy clothes to attract the attention of a father who typically ignores her. The film\u0026#39;s success helped Wood make the transition from child actress to an ingenue. She was nominated for an Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eHer next significant film was \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0049730/?ls\"\u003eThe Searchers (1956)\u003c/a\u003e, a western in which she played the role of abduction victim Debbie Edwards, niece of \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000078/?ls\"\u003eJohn Wayne\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s character. The film was a commercial and critical hit, and has since become regarded as a masterpiece. Also in 1956, Wood graduated from Van Nuys High School. She signed a contract with Warner Brothers, where she was kept busy with several new films. To her disappointment, she was typically cast as the girlfriend of the protagonist and received roles of little depth. For a while, WB had her paired with teen heartthrob \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0002147/?ls\"\u003eTab Hunter\u003c/a\u003e. The studio was hoping that the pairing would serve as a box-office draw, but this did not work out. One of Wood\u0026#39;s only serious roles from this period was the title character in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0051911/?ls\"\u003eMarjorie Morningstar (1958)\u003c/a\u003e, as a young Jewish girl whose efforts to create her own identity and career path clash with the expectations of her family. The film was a critical success, and fit well with other films exploring the restlessness of youth in the \u0026#39;50s.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eWood\u0026#39;s first major box office flop was the biographical film \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0053582/?ls\"\u003eAll the Fine Young Cannibals (1960)\u003c/a\u003e, examining the rags to riches story of jazz musician \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0048329/?ls\"\u003eChet Baker\u003c/a\u003e without actually using his name. The film\u0026#39;s box office earnings barely covered the production costs, and MGM recorded a loss of $1,108,000. For the first time. Wood\u0026#39;s appeal to the audience was in doubt. With her career in decline following this failure, Wood was seen as \u0026quot;washed up\u0026quot; by many in the film community. But director \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0001415/?ls\"\u003eElia Kazan\u003c/a\u003e gave her the chance to audition for the role of the sexually-repressed Wilma Dean Loomis in his upcoming film \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0055471/?ls\"\u003eSplendor in the Grass (1961)\u003c/a\u003e. Kazan cast Wood as the female lead, because he found in her (in his words): a \u0026quot;true-blue quality with a wanton side that is held down by social pressure.\u0026quot; Kazan is credited for producing Wood\u0026#39;s most powerful moment as an actress. The film was a critical success, with Wood nominated for an Academy Award for Best Actress.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eWood\u0026#39;s next important film was \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0055614/?ls\"\u003eWest Side Story (1961)\u003c/a\u003e, where she played Maria, a restless Puerto Rican girl. Wood was once again called to represent the restlessness of youth, this time in a story involving youth gangs and juvenile delinquents. The film was a great commercial success with about $44 million gross, the highest-grossing film of 1961. It was also critically acclaimed, and is still regarded as one of the best films of Wood\u0026#39;s career. Her next film was \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0056048/?ls\"\u003eGypsy (1962)\u003c/a\u003e, playing the role of burlesque entertainer and stripper \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0497346/?ls\"\u003eGypsy Rose Lee\u003c/a\u003e. Film historians credit the film as an even better role for Wood than that of Maria, with witty dialogue, a greater emotional range, and complex characterization. The film was the eighth highest-grossing release of 1962, and was well-received critically.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eWood\u0026#39;s next significant role was that of Macy\u0026#39;s salesclerk Angie Rossini in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0057263/?ls\"\u003eLove with the Proper Stranger (1963)\u003c/a\u003e. In the film, Angie has a one-night-stand with musician Rocky Papasano, played by \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000537/?ls\"\u003eSteve McQueen\u003c/a\u003e, finds herself pregnant and desperately seeks an abortion. The film under-performed at the box office but was critically well-received. Wood received her third (and last) nomination for an Academy Award. At age 25, Wood was tied with \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0942863/?ls\"\u003eTeresa Wright\u003c/a\u003e as the youngest person to score three Oscar nominations. Wood held that designation until 2013, when \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm2225369/?ls\"\u003eJennifer Lawrence\u003c/a\u003e achieved her third nomination at age 23.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eWood continued her successful film career until 1966, but her health status was not as successful. She was suffering emotionally and had sought professional therapy. She paid Warner Bros. $175,000 to cancel her contract and was able to retire for a while. She also fired her entire support team: agents, managers, publicist, accountant, and attorneys. She took a three-year hiatus from acting.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eWood made her comeback in the comedy \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0064100/?ls\"\u003eBob \u0026amp; Carol \u0026amp; Ted \u0026amp; Alice (1969)\u003c/a\u003e with the themes of sexual liberation and wife swapping. It was a box office hit. Wood decided to gamble her $750,000 fee on a percentage of the gross, earning a million dollars in profits. She chose not to capitalize on the film\u0026#39;s success, however, and did not take another acting job for five years.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eIn 1970, Wood was married to the screenwriter \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0339995/?ls\"\u003eRichard Gregson\u003c/a\u003e and was expecting her first child, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0906031/?ls\"\u003eNatasha Gregson Wagner\u003c/a\u003e. She went into semi-retirement to be a stay-at-home mom, appearing in only four more theatrical films before her death. These films were the mystery comedy \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0073526/?ls\"\u003ePeeper (1975)\u003c/a\u003e, the science fiction film \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0079550/?ls\"\u003eMeteor (1979)\u003c/a\u003e, the comedy \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0081032/?ls\"\u003eThe Last Married Couple in America (1980)\u003c/a\u003e, and the posthumously-released science fiction film \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0085271/?ls\"\u003eBrainstorm (1983)\u003c/a\u003e.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eIn the late \u0026#39;70s, Wood found success in television roles, appearing in several made-for-TV movies and the mini-series \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0078616/?ls\"\u003eFrom Here to Eternity (1979)\u003c/a\u003e. Her project received high ratings, and she had plans to make her theatrical debut in a 1982 production of Anastasia.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eOn November 28, 1981, Wood joined her last husband \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0001822/?ls\"\u003eRobert Wagner\u003c/a\u003e, their married friend \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000686/?ls\"\u003eChristopher Walken\u003c/a\u003e, and captain \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm9673610/?ls\"\u003eDennis Davern\u003c/a\u003e on a weekend boat trip to Catalina Island. Conspicuously absent from the group was Christopher\u0026#39;s wife, casting director \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0907467/?ls\"\u003eGeorgianne Walken\u003c/a\u003e. The four of them were on board the Wagners\u0026#39; yacht \u0026quot;Splendour.\u0026quot; Earwitness \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm2088867/?ls\"\u003eMarilyn Wayne\u003c/a\u003e heard cries for help around 11:05 P.M. and a \u0026quot;man\u0026#39;s voice slurred, and in aggravated tone, say something to the effect of, \u0026#39;Oh, hold on, we\u0026#39;re coming to get you,\u0026#39; and not long after, the cries for help subsided.\u0026quot; On the morning of November 29, Wood\u0026#39;s corpse was recovered 1 mile (1.6 kilometers) away from the boat, near small Valiant-brand inflatable dinghy beached nearby. The toxicology report revealed her blood alcohol level was at .14, over the legal limit of .10. Wood was buried on December 2 at Westwood Village Memorial Park Cemetery in Los Angeles. Monroe is of English, Irish, Scottish and Welsh descent. She became one of the world\u0026#39;s most enduring iconic figures and is remembered both for her winsome embodiment of the Hollywood sex symbol and her tragic personal and professional struggles within the film industry. Her life and death are still the subjects of much controversy and speculation.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eShe was born Norma Jeane Mortenson at the Los Angeles County Hospital on June 1, 1926. Her mother, Gladys Pearl (Monroe), was born in Piedras Negras, Coahuila, Mexico, to American parents from Indiana and Missouri, and was a film-cutter at Consolidated Film Industries. Marilyn\u0026#39;s biological father has been established through DNA testing as Charles Stanley Gifford, who had been born in Newport, Rhode Island, to a family with deep roots in the state. Because Gladys was mentally and financially unable to care for young Marilyn, Gladys placed her in the care of a foster family, The Bolenders. Although the Bolender family wanted to adopt Marilyn, Gladys was eventually able to stabilize her lifestyle and took Marilyn back in her care when Marilyn was 7 years old. However, shortly after regaining custody of Marilyn, Gladys had a complete mental breakdown and was diagnosed as a paranoid schizophrenic and was committed to a state mental hospital. Gladys spent the rest of her life going in and out of hospitals and rarely had contact with young Marilyn. Once Marilyn became an adult and celebrated as a film star, she paid a woman by the name of Inez Melson to look in on the institutionalized Gladys and give detailed reports of her progress. Gladys outlived her daughter, dying in 1984.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eMarilyn was then taken in by Gladys\u0026#39; best friend Grace Goddard, who, after a series of foster homes, placed Marilyn into the Los Angeles Orphan\u0026#39;s Home in 1935. Marilyn was traumatized by her experience there despite the Orphan\u0026#39;s Home being an adequate living facility. Grace Goddard eventually took Marilyn back to live with her in 1937 although this stay did not last long as Grace\u0026#39;s husband began molesting Marilyn. Marilyn went to live with Grace\u0026#39;s Aunt Ana after this incident, although due to Aunt Ana\u0026#39;s advanced age she could not care properly for Marilyn. Marilyn once again for the third time had to return to live with the Goddards. The Goddards planned to relocated and according to law, could not take Marilyn with them. She only had two choices: return to the orphanage or get married. Marilyn was only 16 years old.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eShe decided to marry a neighborhood friend named James Dougherty; he went into the military, she modeled, they divorced in 1946. She owned 400 books (including Tolstoy, Whitman, Milton), listened to Beethoven records, studied acting at the Actors\u0026#39; lab in Hollywood, and took literature courses at UCLA downtown. 20th Century Fox gave her a contract but let it lapse a year later. In 1948, Columbia gave her a six-month contract, turned her over to coach Natasha Lytess and featured her in the B movie Ladies of the Chorus (1948) in which she sang three numbers : \u0026quot;Every Baby Needs a Da Da Daddy\u0026quot;, \u0026quot;Anyone Can Tell I Love You\u0026quot; and \u0026quot;The Ladies of the Chorus\u0026quot; with Adele Jergens (dubbed by Virginia Rees) and others. Joseph L. Mankiewicz saw her in a small part in The Asphalt Jungle (1950) and put her in All About Eve (1950) , resulting in 20th Century re-signing her to a seven-year contract. Niagara (1953) and Gentlemen Prefer Blondes (1953) launched her as a sex symbol superstar.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eWhen she went to a supper honoring her in the The Seven Year Itch (1955) , she arrived in a red chiffon gown borrowed from the studio (she had never owned a gown). That same year, she married and divorced baseball great Joe DiMaggio (their wedding night was spent in Paso Robles, California). After The Seven Year Itch (1955) , she wanted serious acting to replace the sexpot image and went to New York\u0026#39;s Actors Studio. She worked with director Lee Strasberg and also underwent psychoanalysis to learn more about herself. Critics praised her transformation in Bus Stop (1956) and the press was stunned by her marriage to playwright Arthur Miller . True to form, she had no veil to match her beige wedding dress so she dyed one in coffee; he wore one of the two suits he owned. They went to England that fall where she made The Prince and the Showgirl (1957) with Laurence Olivier , fighting with him and falling further prey to alcohol and pills. Two miscarriages and gynecological surgery followed. So had an affair with Yves Montand . Work on her last picture The Misfits (1961) , written for her by departing husband Miller, was interrupted by exhaustion. Her turn as the naïve but trigger-happy and sexually aggressive Parker earned her Academy Award and Golden Globe nominations, and provided a direct route to the front of the line for Hollywood leading ladies in an unbelievably short amount of time.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eDunaway followed this success with another hit, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0063688/?ls\"\u003eThe Thomas Crown Affair (1968)\u003c/a\u003e, in which her coolly sensual insurance investigator generated considerable sparks with playboy and jewel thief \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000537/?ls\"\u003eSteve McQueen\u003c/a\u003e. She then bounced between arthouse efforts like \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0066262/?ls\"\u003ePuzzle of a Downfall Child (1970)\u003c/a\u003e, directed by her ex-boyfriend, photographer \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0770234/?ls\"\u003eJerry Schatzberg\u003c/a\u003e, and the revisionist Western \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0067003/?ls\"\u003eDoc (1971)\u003c/a\u003e, as well as big-budget efforts like \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0065988/?ls\"\u003eLittle Big Man (1970)\u003c/a\u003e, which cast her as a predatory preacher\u0026#39;s wife with designs on \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000163/?ls\"\u003eDustin Hoffman\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s reluctant Native American hero. Dunaway also balanced these projects with several well-regarded theatrical productions, including a 1972-73 stint as Blanche Du Bois in \u0026quot;A Streetcar Named Desire,\u0026quot; and notable TV movies like \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0069511/?ls\"\u003eThe Woman I Love (1972)\u003c/a\u003e, which cast her as the Duchess of Windsor, and TV broadcasts of \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0067207/?ls\"\u003eHogan\u0026#39;s Goat (1971)\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0071109/?ls\"\u003eAfter the Fall (1974)\u003c/a\u003e. But her turn as the duplicitous Lady De Winter in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0504513/?ls\"\u003eRichard Lester\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s splashy, slapstick take on \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0072281/?ls\"\u003eThe Three Musketeers (1973)\u003c/a\u003e and its sequel \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0073012/?ls\"\u003eThe Four Musketeers (1974)\u003c/a\u003e preceded a long period of critical and box office hits, starting with her masterful performance in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0071315/?ls\"\u003eChinatown (1974)\u003c/a\u003e.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eDunaway\u0026#39;s turn as Evelyn Mulwray, the mysterious woman who draws detective Jake Gittes (\u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000197/?ls\"\u003eJack Nicholson\u003c/a\u003e) into a dark and complicated web of murder, incest, and catastrophic business deals, seemed the epitome of every femme fatale to ever stride across a chiaroscuro-lit scene in classic noir. But Dunaway also found the horribly wounded core of her character as well, and turned Evelyn from a pastiche to a full-blown and emotionally resonant human being. Critics and award groups rushed to nominate Dunaway for the role, and she netted her second Academy Award nod, as well as Golden Globe and BAFTA nominations. Dunaway had fought hard for her performance - her battles with director \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000591/?ls\"\u003eRoman Polanski\u003c/a\u003e were no secret - but sadly, she lost the Oscar to \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000995/?ls\"\u003eEllen Burstyn\u003c/a\u003e for \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0071115/?ls\"\u003eAlice Doesn\u0026#39;t Live Here Anymore (1974)\u003c/a\u003e. However, it would be Dunaway\u0026#39;s performance which stood the test of time.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eHigh-gloss turns in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0072308/?ls\"\u003eThe Towering Inferno (1974)\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0001628/?ls\"\u003eSydney Pollack\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s political thriller \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0073802/?ls\"\u003eThree Days of the Condor (1975)\u003c/a\u003e preceded one of her best television performances; that of Depression-era radio preacher Aimee Semple MacPherson in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0074411/?ls\"\u003eThe Disappearance of Aimee (1976)\u003c/a\u003e. Even more startling was her sterling role in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0074958/?ls\"\u003eNetwork (1976)\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0154665/?ls\"\u003ePaddy Chayefsky\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s blistering take on the television industry. Dunaway pulled out all the stops as an executive on the rise who stops at nothing to advance her career - even bedding veteran producer \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000034/?ls\"\u003eWilliam Holden\u003c/a\u003e. Critics again rose in unison to praise Dunaway, and she finally netted an Oscar for the role, as well as a Golden Globe.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eSurprisingly, Dunaway\u0026#39;s career began to falter after her Oscar win. She was effective as a fashion photographer who experiences disturbing visions in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0077530/?ls\"\u003eEyes of Laura Mars (1978)\u003c/a\u003e, but was wasted in thankless roles as the dissatisfied ex of washed-up boxer \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000685/?ls\"\u003eJon Voight\u003c/a\u003e in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0078950/?ls\"\u003eThe Champ (1979)\u003c/a\u003e and wife to \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000069/?ls\"\u003eFrank Sinatra\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s detective in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0080738/?ls\"\u003eThe First Deadly Sin (1980)\u003c/a\u003e. And then came \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0082766/?ls\"\u003eMommie Dearest (1981)\u003c/a\u003e, director \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0675068/?ls\"\u003eFrank Perry\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s biopic of actress \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0001076/?ls\"\u003eJoan Crawford\u003c/a\u003e based on the tell-all book by her daughter \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0186726/?ls\"\u003eChristina Crawford\u003c/a\u003e. Crawford herself had praised Dunaway in the early stages of her career, and while some critics gave positive reviews to her performance - in particular, the extent to which she physically transformed herself into Crawford - most fixated on the hysterical dialogue and garish scenes of child abuse. Clips of Dunaway as Crawford bellowing \u0026quot;No wire hangers!\u0026quot; became immediate laugh-getters on late-night television, and a substantial gay following rose up in response to the film\u0026#39;s high camp value. Dunaway, however, found none of the response amusing, and later admitted her regret in taking the role. Whether laughable or pure genius, no one could deny that Dunaway threw her everything into the role. The film\u0026#39;s continued cult success proved she had succeeded in becoming Crawford.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eThe fallout from \u0026quot;Mommie Dearest\u0026quot; obscured Dunaway\u0026#39;s follow-up projects, which included the title role in the TV movie \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0082347/?ls\"\u003eEvita Peron (1981)\u003c/a\u003e and a return to Broadway in 1982\u0026#39;s \u0026quot;The Curse of an Aching Heart\u0026quot;. Discouraged, she moved to London with her second husband, photographer \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0974241/?ls\"\u003eTerry O\u0026#39;Neill\u003c/a\u003e, who had also served as a producer on \u0026quot;Mommie Dearest.\u0026quot; For the next few years, Dunaway appeared sporadically in films, most of which underscored her newly minted status as a camp icon. \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0086582/?ls\"\u003eThe Wicked Lady (1983)\u003c/a\u003e was an absurd, near-softcore period drama by \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0935382/?ls\"\u003eMichael Winner\u003c/a\u003e, with Dunaway as an 18th-century highway robber. Fans of her early dramatic work were similarly aghast by her turn as a shrieking witch battling \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000644/?ls\"\u003eHelen Slater\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s Girl of Steel in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0088206/?ls\"\u003eSupergirl (1984)\u003c/a\u003e. Only a Golden Globe-winning appearance in the cumbersome miniseries \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0086705/?ls\"\u003eEllis Island (1984)\u003c/a\u003e offered any respite from the negative press which now continued to follow her.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eDunaway returned to the United States in 1987 following her divorce from O\u0026#39;Neill, and attempted to rebuild her career and reputation by appearing in several independent dramas. She was widely praised for her performance as a once-glamorous woman felled by alcohol in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0775447/?ls\"\u003eBarbet Schroeder\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0092618/?ls\"\u003eBarfly (1987)\u003c/a\u003e, and served as executive producer and star of \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0097080/?ls\"\u003eCold Sassy Tree (1989)\u003c/a\u003e, a TV adaptation of the popular novel by \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0122824/?ls\"\u003eOlive Ann Burns\u003c/a\u003e about an independent-minded woman who romances a recently widowed store owner (\u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0001847/?ls\"\u003eRichard Widmark\u003c/a\u003e). Dunaway was exceptionally busy for the remainder of the decade in both major Hollywood features and independent fare, though her strong women now occasionally sported an unfortunate shrill side. She was \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000380/?ls\"\u003eRobert Duvall\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s frosty wife in the dystopian thriller \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0099731/?ls\"\u003eThe Handmaid\u0026#39;s Tale (1990)\u003c/a\u003e and contributed a vocal cameo as Evelyn Mulwray in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0100828/?ls\"\u003eThe Two Jakes (1990)\u003c/a\u003e, the ill-fated sequel to \u0026quot;Chinatown\u0026quot;. Other notable performances came as the unhappy wife of psychiatrist \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000008/?ls\"\u003eMarlon Brando\u003c/a\u003e in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0112883/?ls\"\u003eDon Juan DeMarco (1994)\u003c/a\u003e, as the daughter of imprisoned Klansman \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000432/?ls\"\u003eGene Hackman\u003c/a\u003e in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0115862/?ls\"\u003eThe Chamber (1996)\u003c/a\u003e, and as a bartender caught in the middle of a hostage standoff in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000228/?ls\"\u003eKevin Spacey\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0115495/?ls\"\u003eAlbino Alligator (1996)\u003c/a\u003e. She later received Screen Actors Guild and Golden Globe nominations as the matron of a wealthy Jewish family in turmoil in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0120392/?ls\"\u003eThe Twilight of the Golds (1996)\u003c/a\u003e. Perhaps her best turn of the decade was as a seductive murderess who attempts to sway the unflappable Lt. Columbo (\u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000393/?ls\"\u003ePeter Falk\u003c/a\u003e) in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0106589/?ls\"\u003eColumbo: It\u0026#39;s All in the Game (1993)\u003c/a\u003e, which earned her a 1994 Emmy. She won her third Golden Globe as modeling agency head \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm7316814/?ls\"\u003eWilhelmina Cooper\u003c/a\u003e in the biopic \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0123865/?ls\"\u003eGia (1998)\u003c/a\u003e, starring \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0001401/?ls\"\u003eAngelina Jolie\u003c/a\u003e as doomed model \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm1817020/?ls\"\u003eGia Carangi\u003c/a\u003e.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eThe 1990s were also not without incident for Dunaway. She was embroiled in an ugly lawsuit against \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0515908/?ls\"\u003eAndrew Lloyd Webber\u003c/a\u003e after he closed a Los Angeles production of his musical version of \u0026quot;Sunset Blvd.\u0026quot; with claims that she was unable to sing to his standards. The suit was later settled out of court for an undisclosed sum. A national tour of \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0573645/?ls\"\u003eTerrence McNally\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s \u0026quot;Master Class\u0026quot;, about the legendary opera diva \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0006568/?ls\"\u003eMaria Callas\u003c/a\u003e, ended with her involvement in a suit over legal rights to the play. The project was expected to become her next great film role but remained uncompleted more than a decade after the 1996 tour. Her attempt at sitcom stardom in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0106034/?ls\"\u003eIt Had to Be You (1993)\u003c/a\u003e, co-starring \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0001810/?ls\"\u003eRobert Urich\u003c/a\u003e, was met with universal disinterest, and the project was announced as being retooled without Dunaway prior to its cancellation.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eDunaway\u0026#39;s schedule remained busy from 2000 onward, mostly in television and small independent features. She co-starred with \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000242/?ls\"\u003eMark Wahlberg\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0001618/?ls\"\u003eJoaquin Phoenix\u003c/a\u003e as the wife of career criminal \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0001001/?ls\"\u003eJames Caan\u003c/a\u003e in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0138946/?ls\"\u003eThe Yards (2000)\u003c/a\u003e, then made her directorial debut with the short \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0288325/?ls\"\u003eThe Yellow Bird (2001)\u003c/a\u003e, based on the play by \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0931783/?ls\"\u003eTennessee Williams\u003c/a\u003e. Younger audiences had their first taste of Dunaway\u0026#39;s particular star power as \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0813812/?ls\"\u003eIan Somerhalder\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s mother in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0292644/?ls\"\u003eThe Rules of Attraction (2002)\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000812/?ls\"\u003eRoger Avary\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s amped-up adaptation of the \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0254735/?ls\"\u003eBret Easton Ellis\u003c/a\u003e novel, before Dunaway turned up the heat as a merciless celebrity judge on the reality series \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0449462/?ls\"\u003eThe Starlet (2005)\u003c/a\u003e.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eDunaway penned her memoirs, Looking For Gatsby, in 1995, one year before receiving her star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. Attached throughout her professional career to intriguing men ranging from \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0115533/?ls\"\u003eLenny Bruce\u003c/a\u003e to \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000052/?ls\"\u003eMarcello Mastroianni\u003c/a\u003e, she was twice married; her first husband was singer \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0937900/?ls\"\u003ePeter Wolf\u003c/a\u003e of the popular seventies rock group, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm9051592/?ls\"\u003eThe J. Geils Band\u003c/a\u003e. \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm1141255/?ls\"\u003eLiam O\u0026#39;Neill\u003c/a\u003e, her son by second husband Terry, followed in her footsteps with minor acting roles beginning in 2004. His father later dropped a bombshell in 2003 by revealing that Liam was not their biological son, but was adopted - a claim that Dunaway had previously denied.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eA series of occasional roles in little-seen films followed, but Dunaway was unexpectedly thrust back into the public eye at the 2017 Academy Awards. Reunited with \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000886/?ls\"\u003eWarren Beatty\u003c/a\u003e on the occasion of the 50th anniversary of \u0026quot;Bonnie and Clyde,\u0026quot; the pair were tapped to present the Best Picture award to close the night. Before proceeding onstage, Beatty was mistakenly handed a backup envelope for Best Actress in a Leading Role, which had already been won by \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm1297015/?ls\"\u003eEmma Stone\u003c/a\u003e for \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt3783958/?ls\"\u003eLa La Land (2016)\u003c/a\u003e. Unsure what to do when he opened the envelope and discovered the error, Beatty stalled for time and showed the card to Dunaway; misunderstanding his intent, the actress announced that the Best Picture Oscar went to \u0026quot;La La Land.\u0026quot; During producer \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm3527897/?ls\"\u003eJordan Horowitz\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s acceptance speech, he was informed that the actual Best Picture winner was \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt4975722/?ls\"\u003eMoonlight (2016)\u003c/a\u003e. During the onstage chaos that ensued, Beatty delivered a heartfelt explanation and apology for the snafu while undergoing good-natured ribbing from host \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0453994/?ls\"\u003eJimmy Kimmel\u003c/a\u003e.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eAfter a break from her career and the memorable Oscars moment, Dunaway got back in the saddle as an actress working more frequently. Over the next year, she appeared in three films, starring in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt4030600/?ls\"\u003eThe Bye Bye Man (2017)\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt6113488/?ls\"\u003eThe Case for Christ (2017)\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt3481634/?ls\"\u003eInconceivable (2017)\u003c/a\u003e. She also fronted Gucci\u0026#39;s summer 2018 ad campaign for their Sylvie handbag. Dunaway looked like she was going to return to Broadway with 2019\u0026#39;s \u0026quot;Tea at Five,\u0026quot; a one-woman show in which she portrayed \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000031/?ls\"\u003eKatharine Hepburn\u003c/a\u003e, but she was fired from the play due to backstage fights with production staff during its Boston run. What followed was a lawsuit brought by her former assistant and a wave of articles alleging decades of bad behavior, with many declaring the 78-year-old screen legend \u0026quot;canceled.\u0026quot;\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eDunaway laid low for the next few years, save for a role alongside fellow cancel culture victim Kevin Spacey in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0626259/?ls\"\u003eFranco Nero\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt9383986/?ls\"\u003eL\u0026#39;umo de d\u0026#39;esigno Dio (2022)\u003c/a\u003e, for which she replaced Nero\u0026#39;s wife \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000603/?ls\"\u003eVanessa Redgrave\u003c/a\u003e. Louise McDormand was born on June 23, 1957, in Gibson City, Illinois. She was adopted by Canadian-born parents Noreen Eloise (Nickleson), a nurse from Ontario, and Rev. Vernon Weir McDormand, a Disciples of Christ minister from Nova Scotia, who raised her in the suburbs of Pittsburgh. She earned a BA in theater from Bethany College in 1979 and an MFA from Yale University in 1982. Her career after graduation began onstage, and she has retained her association with the theater throughout her career. She soon obtained prominent roles in movies as well, first starring in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0086979/?ls\"\u003eBlood Simple (1984)\u003c/a\u003e, in which she worked with filmmaker \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0001054/?ls\"\u003eJoel Coen\u003c/a\u003e, whom she married that year. She frequently collaborated with Coen and his brother, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0001053/?ls\"\u003eEthan Coen\u003c/a\u003e, in their films.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eMcDormand\u0026#39;s skilled and versatile acting has been recognized by both the critics and the Academy, and in addition to many critics\u0026#39; awards, she has been nominated for an Academy Award six times - Supporting in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0095647/?ls\"\u003eMississippi Burning (1988)\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0181875/?ls\"\u003eAlmost Famous (2000)\u003c/a\u003e, and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0395972/?ls\"\u003eNorth Country (2005)\u003c/a\u003e, and Lead in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0116282/?ls\"\u003eFargo (1996)\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt5027774/?ls\"\u003eThree Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri (2017)\u003c/a\u003e, and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt9770150/?ls\"\u003eNomadland (2020)\u003c/a\u003e, winning the Oscar for the latter three. In 2010, Plummer finally got an Oscar nod for his portrayal of another legend, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0866243/?ls\"\u003eLev Tolstoy\u003c/a\u003e in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0824758/?ls\"\u003eThe Last Station (2009)\u003c/a\u003e.
