Eastwood Jr. was born May 31, 1930 in San Francisco, to Clinton Eastwood Sr., a bond salesman and later manufacturing executive for Georgia-Pacific Corporation, and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm2503495/?ls\"\u003eRuth Wood\u003c/a\u003e (née Margret Ruth Runner), a housewife turned IBM clerk. He grew up in nearby Piedmont. At school Clint took interest in music and mechanics, but was an otherwise bored student; this resulted in being held back a grade. In 1949, the year he graduated from high school, his parents and younger sister Jeanne moved to Seattle. Clint spent a couple years in the Pacific Northwest himself, operating log broncs in Springfield, Oregon, with summer gigs life-guarding in Renton, Washington. Returning to California in 1951, he did a two-year stint at Fort Ord Military Reservation and later enrolled at L.A. City College, but dropped out to pursue acting.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eDuring the mid-1950s he landed uncredited bit parts in such B-films as \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0048554/?ls\"\u003eRevenge of the Creature (1955)\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0048696/?ls\"\u003eTarantula (1955)\u003c/a\u003e while digging swimming pools and driving a garbage truck to supplement his income. In 1958, he landed his first consequential acting role in the long-running TV show \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0052504/?ls\"\u003eRawhide (1959)\u003c/a\u003e with \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0281661/?ls\"\u003eEric Fleming\u003c/a\u003e. Although only a secondary player the first seven seasons, he was promoted to series star when Fleming departed--both literally and figuratively--in its final year, along the way becoming a recognizable face to television viewers around the country.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eEastwood\u0026#39;s big-screen breakthrough came as The Man with No Name in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0001466/?ls\"\u003eSergio Leone\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s trilogy of excellent spaghetti westerns: \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0058461/?ls\"\u003eA Fistful of Dollars (1964)\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0059578/?ls\"\u003ePer qualche dollaro in più (1965)\u003c/a\u003e, and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0060196/?ls\"\u003eIl Buono, Il Brutto, Il Cattivo (1966)\u003c/a\u003e. The movies were shown exclusively in Italy during their respective copyright years with \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0758066/?ls\"\u003eEnrico Maria Salerno\u003c/a\u003e providing the voice of Eastwood\u0026#39;s character, finally getting American distribution in 1967-68. As the last film racked up respectable grosses, Eastwood, 37, rose from a barely registering actor to sought-after commodity in just a matter of months. Again a success was the late-blooming star\u0026#39;s first U.S.-made western, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0061747/?ls\"\u003eHang \u0026#39;Em High (1968)\u003c/a\u003e. He followed that up with the lead role in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0062824/?ls\"\u003eCoogan\u0026#39;s Bluff (1968)\u003c/a\u003e (the loose inspiration for the TV series \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0065317/?ls\"\u003eSam McCloud (1970)\u003c/a\u003e), before playing second fiddle to \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000009/?ls\"\u003eRichard Burton\u003c/a\u003e in the World War II epic \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0065207/?ls\"\u003eWhere Eagles Dare (1968)\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0001511/?ls\"\u003eLee Marvin\u003c/a\u003e in the bizarre musical \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0064782/?ls\"\u003ePaint Your Wagon (1969)\u003c/a\u003e. In \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0065134/?ls\"\u003eTwo Mules for Sister Sara (1970)\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0065938/?ls\"\u003eKelly\u0026#39;s Heroes (1970)\u003c/a\u003e, Eastwood leaned in an experimental direction by combining tough-guy action with offbeat humor.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e1971 proved to be his busiest year in film. He starred as a sleazy Union soldier in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0066819/?ls\"\u003eThe Beguiled (1971)\u003c/a\u003e to critical acclaim, and made his directorial debut with the classic erotic thriller \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0067588/?ls\"\u003ePlay Misty for Me (1971)\u003c/a\u003e. His role as the hard edge police inspector in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0066999/?ls\"\u003eDirty Harry (1971)\u003c/a\u003e, meanwhile, boosted him to cultural icon status and helped popularize the loose-cannon cop genre. Eastwood put out a steady stream of entertaining movies thereafter: the westerns \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0068768/?ls\"\u003eJoe Kidd (1972)\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0068699/?ls\"\u003eHigh Plains Drifter (1973)\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0075029/?ls\"\u003eThe Outlaw: Josey Wales (1976)\u003c/a\u003e (his first of six onscreen collaborations with then live-in love \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0516800/?ls\"\u003eSondra Locke\u003c/a\u003e), the Dirty Harry sequels \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0070355/?ls\"\u003eMagnum Force (1973)\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0074483/?ls\"\u003eThe Enforcer (1976)\u003c/a\u003e, the action-packed road adventures \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0072288/?ls\"\u003eThunderbolt and Lightfoot (1974)\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0076070/?ls\"\u003eThe Gauntlet (1977)\u003c/a\u003e, and the prison film \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0079116/?ls\"\u003eEscape from Alcatraz (1979)\u003c/a\u003e. He branched out into the comedy genre in 1978 with \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0077523/?ls\"\u003eEvery Which Way But Loose (1978)\u003c/a\u003e, which became the biggest hit of his career up to that time; taking inflation into account, it still is. In short, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0072926/?ls\"\u003eThe Eiger Sanction (1975)\u003c/a\u003e notwithstanding, the 1970s were nonstop success for Eastwood.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eEastwood kicked off the 1980s with \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0080377/?ls\"\u003eAny Way You Can (1980)\u003c/a\u003e, the blockbuster sequel to Every Which Way but Loose. The fourth Dirty Harry film, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0086383/?ls\"\u003eSudden Impact (1983)\u003c/a\u003e, was the highest-grossing film of the franchise and spawned his trademark catchphrase: \u0026quot;Make my day.\u0026quot; He also starred in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0080472/?ls\"\u003eBronco Billy (1980)\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0083943/?ls\"\u003eFirefox (1982)\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0088272/?ls\"\u003eTightrope (1984)\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0087062/?ls\"\u003eCity Heat (1984)\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0089767/?ls\"\u003ePale Rider (1985)\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0091187/?ls\"\u003eHeartbreak Ridge (1986)\u003c/a\u003e, all of which were solid hits, with \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0084088/?ls\"\u003eHonkytonk Man (1982)\u003c/a\u003e being his only commercial failure of the period. In 1988, he did his fifth and final Dirty Harry movie, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0094963/?ls\"\u003eThe Dead Pool (1988)\u003c/a\u003e. Although it was a success overall, it did not have the box office punch the previous films had. About this time, with outright bombs like \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0098097/?ls\"\u003ePink Cadillac (1989)\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0100514/?ls\"\u003eThe Rookie (1990)\u003c/a\u003e, it seemed Eastwood\u0026#39;s star was declining as it never had before. He then started taking on low-key projects, directing \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0094747/?ls\"\u003eBird (1988)\u003c/a\u003e, a biopic of \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0662127/?ls\"\u003eCharlie Parker\u003c/a\u003e that earned him a Golden Globe, and starring in and directing \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0100928/?ls\"\u003eWhite Hunter Black Heart (1990)\u003c/a\u003e, an uneven, loose biopic of \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0001379/?ls\"\u003eJohn Huston\u003c/a\u003e (both films had a limited release).\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eEastwood bounced back big time with his dark western \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0105695/?ls\"\u003eUnforgiven (1992)\u003c/a\u003e, which garnered the then 62-year-old his first ever Academy Award nomination (Best Actor), and an Oscar win for Best Director. Churning out a quick follow-up hit, he took on the secret service in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0107206/?ls\"\u003eIn the Line of Fire (1993)\u003c/a\u003e, then accepted second billing for the first time since 1970 in the interesting but poorly received \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0107808/?ls\"\u003eA Perfect World (1993)\u003c/a\u003e with \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000126/?ls\"\u003eKevin Costner\u003c/a\u003e. Next was a love story, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0112579/?ls\"\u003eSacrifice (1995)\u003c/a\u003e, where Eastwood surprised audiences with a sensitive performance alongside none other than \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000658/?ls\"\u003eMeryl Streep\u003c/a\u003e. But it soon became apparent he was going backwards after his brief revival. Subsequent films were credible, but nothing really stuck out. \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0118548/?ls\"\u003eAbsolute Power (1997)\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0186566/?ls\"\u003eSpace Cowboys (2000)\u003c/a\u003e did well enough, while \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0139668/?ls\"\u003eTrue Crime (1999)\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0309377/?ls\"\u003eBlood Work (2002)\u003c/a\u003e were received badly, as was \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0119668/?ls\"\u003eMidnight in the Garden of Good and Evil (1997)\u003c/a\u003e, which he directed but didn\u0026#39;t appear in.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eEastwood surprised again in the mid-2000s, returning to the top of the A-list with \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0405159/?ls\"\u003eMillion Dollar Baby (2004)\u003c/a\u003e. Also starring \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0005476/?ls\"\u003eHilary Swank\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000151/?ls\"\u003eMorgan Freeman\u003c/a\u003e, the hugely successful drama won four Academy Awards, including Best Picture and Best Director for Eastwood. He scored his second Best Actor nomination, too. His next starring vehicle, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt1205489/?ls\"\u003eGran Torino (2008)\u003c/a\u003e, earned almost $30 million in its opening weekend and was his highest grosser unadjusted for inflation. 2012 saw him in a rare lighthearted movie, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt2083383/?ls\"\u003eTrouble with the Curve (2012)\u003c/a\u003e, as well as a reality show, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt2305717/?ls\"\u003eMrs. Eastwood \u0026amp; Company (2012)\u003c/a\u003e.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eBetween acting jobs, he chalked up an impressive list of credits behind the camera. He directed \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0327056/?ls\"\u003eMystic River (2003)\u003c/a\u003e (in which \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000576/?ls\"\u003eSean Penn\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000209/?ls\"\u003eTim Robbins\u003c/a\u003e gave Oscar-winning performances), \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0418689/?ls\"\u003eFlags of Our Fathers (2006)\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0498380/?ls\"\u003eLetters from Iwo Jima (2006)\u003c/a\u003e (nominated for the Best Picture Oscar), \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0824747/?ls\"\u003eChangeling (2008)\u003c/a\u003e (a vehicle for \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0001401/?ls\"\u003eAngelina Jolie\u003c/a\u003e), \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt1057500/?ls\"\u003eInvictus (2009)\u003c/a\u003e (again with Freeman), \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt1212419/?ls\"\u003eHereafter (2010)\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt1616195/?ls\"\u003eJ. Edgar (2011)\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt1742044/?ls\"\u003eJersey Boys (2014)\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt2179136/?ls\"\u003eAmerican Sniper (2014)\u003c/a\u003e (2014\u0026#39;s top box office champ), \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt3263904/?ls\"\u003eSully (2016)\u003c/a\u003e (starring \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000158/?ls\"\u003eTom Hanks\u003c/a\u003e as hero pilot \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm3314810/?ls\"\u003eChesley Sullenberger\u003c/a\u003e) and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt6802308/?ls\"\u003eThe 15:17 to Paris (2018)\u003c/a\u003e. Back on screens after a considerable absence, he played an unlikely drug courier in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt7959026/?ls\"\u003eThe Mule (2018)\u003c/a\u003e, which reached the top of the box office with a nine-figure gross, then directed \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt3513548/?ls\"\u003eRichard Jewell (2019)\u003c/a\u003e. At age 91, Eastwood made history as the oldest actor to star above the title in a movie with the release of \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt1924245/?ls\"\u003eCry Macho (2021)\u003c/a\u003e.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eAway from the limelight, Eastwood has led an aberrant existence and is described by biographer \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0569292/?ls\"\u003ePatrick McGilligan\u003c/a\u003e as a cunning manipulator of the media. His convoluted slew of partners and children are now somewhat factually acknowledged, but for the first three decades of his celebrity, his personal life was kept top secret, and several of his families were left out of the official narrative. The actor refuses to disclose his exact number of offspring even to this day. He had a longtime relationship with similarly abstruse co-star Locke (who died aged 74 in 2018, though for her entire public life she masqueraded about being younger), and has fathered at least eight children by at least six different women in an unending string of liaisons, many of which overlapped. legendary actor with 50 celebrated years of film, television and producing experience, Michael Douglas is known for his era-defining roles and enduring cultural impact.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eIn addition to his career accomplishments, Douglas has remained a steadfast public servant, activist and philanthropist dedicated to peace and human welfare, democracy, gun control advocacy, support of the arts and support of nuclear disarmament. In 1998, former United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan appointed Douglas as a Messenger of Peace for his commitment on disarmament issues, including nuclear non-proliferation and halting the illicit trade in small arms and light weapons.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eSince his earliest acting work on \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0064399/?ls\"\u003eHail, Hero! (1969)\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0068135/?ls\"\u003eThe Streets of San Francisco (1972)\u003c/a\u003e Douglas has played some of the most memorable and enigmatic American anti-heroes of the last half century. He is most known for his iconic screen roles, like his Academy Award-winning turn as Gordon Gekko \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0094291/?ls\"\u003eWall Street (1987)\u003c/a\u003e as well as the critically and commercially acclaimed films \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0093010/?ls\"\u003eFatal Attraction (1987)\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0112346/?ls\"\u003eThe American President (1995)\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0103772/?ls\"\u003eBasic Instinct (1992)\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0181865/?ls\"\u003eTraffic (2000)\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0088011/?ls\"\u003eRomancing the Stone (1984)\u003c/a\u003e. He is also a prolific producer with credits on politically relevant and socially influential motion pictures like \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0073486/?ls\"\u003eOne Flew Over the Cuckoo\u0026#39;s Nest (1975)\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0078966/?ls\"\u003eThe China Syndrome (1979)\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0181865/?ls\"\u003eTraffic (2000)\u003c/a\u003e the television series: \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt7255502/?ls\"\u003eThe Kominsky Method (2018)\u003c/a\u003e and an upcoming limited series where Douglas portrays Benjamin \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt18351584/?ls\"\u003eFranklin (2024)\u003c/a\u003e during his nine years in France lobbying for French aid for the American Revolution.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eWith a passion for complex protagonists and darkly humorous undercurrents, Douglas has received numerous accolades for his work, including two Academy Awards, five Golden Globe Awards, a Primetime Emmy Award, AFI Life Achievement Award, two French César Awards for Career Achievement and, most recently, the Palme d\u0026#39;or d\u0026#39;honneur for lifetime achievement at the 76th Annual Festival de Cannes as well as the Satyajit Ray Lifetime Achievement Award for Excellence in Cinema at the Goa Film Festival in India.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eMichael Douglas was born in New Brunswick, New Jersey, to actors \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0235022/?ls\"\u003eDiana Douglas\u003c/a\u003e (Diana Love Dill) and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000018/?ls\"\u003eKirk Douglas\u003c/a\u003e (born Issur Danielovitch). His paternal grandparents were Belarusian Jewish immigrants, while his mother was born in Bermuda, the daughter of a local Attorney General, Lieutenant Colonel Thomas Melville Dill; Diana\u0026#39;s family had long been established in both Bermuda and the United States. Douglas\u0026#39;s parents divorced when he was six, and he went to live with his mother and her new husband. Only seeing Kirk on holidays, Michael attended Eaglebrook School in Deerfield, Massachusetts, where he was about a year younger than all of his classmates.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eDouglas attended the elite preparatory Choate School and spent his summers with his father on movie sets. Although accepted at Yale, Douglas attended the University of California, Santa Barbara. Deciding he wanted to be an actor in his teenage years, Michael often asked his father about getting a \u0026quot;foot in the door\u0026quot; Kirk was strongly opposed to Michael pursuing an acting career, saying that it was an industry with many downs and few ups, and that he wanted all four of his sons to stay out of it. Michael, however, was persistent, and made his film debut in his father\u0026#39;s film \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0060218/?ls\"\u003eCast a Giant Shadow (1966)\u003c/a\u003e.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eAfter receiving his B.A. degree in 1968, Douglas moved to New York City to continue his dramatic training, studying at the American Place Theatre with \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0359640/?ls\"\u003eWynn Handman\u003c/a\u003e, and at the Neighborhood Playhouse, where he appeared in workshop productions of Pirandello\u0026#39;s Six Characters in Search of an Author (1976) and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0928642/?ls\"\u003eThornton Wilder\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s Happy Journey (1963). A few months after he arrived in New York, Douglas got his first big break, when he was cast in the pivotal role of the free-spirited scientist who compromises his liberal views to accept a lucrative job with a high-tech chemical corporation in the CBS Playhouse production of \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0899225/?ls\"\u003eEllen M. Violett\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s drama, The Experiment, which was televised nationwide on February 25, 1969.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eDouglas\u0026#39; convincing portrayal won him the leading role in the adaptation of John Weston\u0026#39;s controversial novel, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0064399/?ls\"\u003eHail, Hero! (1969)\u003c/a\u003e, which was the initial project of CBS\u0026#39;s newly organized theatrical film production company, Cinema Center Films. Douglas starred as a well-meaning, almost saintly young pacifist determined not only to justify his beliefs to his conservative parents but also to test them under fire in the jungles of Indochina. His second feature, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0065371/?ls\"\u003eAdam at Six A.M. (1970)\u003c/a\u003e concerned a young man\u0026#39;s search for his roots. Douglas next appeared in the film version of \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0184734/?ls\"\u003eRon Cowen\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s play \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0067804/?ls\"\u003eSummertree (1971)\u003c/a\u003e, produced by \u0026#39;Kirk Douglas\u0026#39;\u0026#39; Bryna Company, and then \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0068990/?ls\"\u003eNapoleon and Samantha (1972)\u003c/a\u003e, a sentimental children\u0026#39;s melodrama from the Walt Disney studio.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eIn between film assignments, he worked in summer stock and off-Broadway productions, among them \u0026quot;City Scenes,\u0026quot; \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm3422900/?ls\"\u003eFrank Gagliano\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s surrealistic vignettes of contemporary life in New York, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0788234/?ls\"\u003eJohn Patrick Shanley\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s short-lived romance \u0026quot;Love is a Time of Day\u0026quot; and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0846068/?ls\"\u003eGeorge Tabori\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s \u0026quot;Pinkville,\u0026quot; in which he played a young innocent brutalized by his military training. He also appeared in the made-for-television thriller, \u0026quot;When Michael Calls,\u0026quot; broadcast by ABC-TV on February 5, 1972 and in episodes of the popular series \u0026quot;Medical Center\u0026quot; and \u0026quot;The F.B.I.\u0026quot;\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eImpressed by Douglas\u0026#39; performance in a segment of The F.B.I. Douglas earned three successive Emmy Award nominations for his performance and he directed two episodes of the series.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eDuring the annual breaks in the shooting schedule for The Streets of San Francisco (1972), Douglas devoted most of his time to his film production company, Big Stick Productions, Ltd., which produced several short subjects in the early 1970s. Long interested in producing a film version of \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0450181/?ls\"\u003eKen Kesey\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s grimly humorous novel \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0073486/?ls\"\u003eOne Flew Over the Cuckoo\u0026#39;s Nest (1975)\u003c/a\u003e, Douglas purchased the movie rights from his father and began looking for financial backing. After a number of major motion picture studios turned him down, Douglas formed a partnership with \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0951763/?ls\"\u003eSaul Zaentz\u003c/a\u003e, a record industry executive, and the two set about recruiting the cast and crew. Douglas still had a year to go on his contract for \u0026quot;The Streets of San Francisco,\u0026quot; but the producers agreed to write his character out of the story so that he could concentrate on filming \u0026quot;Cuckoo\u0026#39;s Nest.\u0026quot;\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eA critical and commercial success, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0073486/?ls\"\u003eOne Flew Over the Cuckoo\u0026#39;s Nest (1975)\u003c/a\u003e won five Academy Awards, including Best Picture, Best Director, Best Screenplay, Best Actor and Best Actress, and went on to gross more than $180 million at the box office. Douglas suddenly found himself in demand as an independent producer. One of the many scripts submitted to him for consideration was Mike Gray\u0026#39;s chilling account of the attempted cover-up of an accident at a nuclear power plant. Attracted by the combination of social relevance and suspense, Douglas immediately bought the property. Deemed not commercial by most investors, Douglas teamed up with Jane Fonda and her own motion picture production company, IPC Films.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eA Michael Douglas-IPC Films co-production, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0078966/?ls\"\u003eThe China Syndrome (1979)\u003c/a\u003e starred \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000493/?ls\"\u003eJack Lemmon\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000404/?ls\"\u003eJane Fonda\u003c/a\u003e, and Michael Douglas and received Academy Award nominations for Lemmon and Fonda, as well as for Best Screenplay. The National Board of Review named the film one of the best films of the year.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eDespite his success as a producer, Douglas resumed his acting career in the late 1970s, starring in Michael Crichton\u0026#39;s medical thriller \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0077355/?ls\"\u003eComa (1978)\u003c/a\u003e with Genevieve Bujold, Claudia Weill\u0026#39;s feminist comedy \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0080936/?ls\"\u003eIt\u0026#39;s My Turn (1980)\u003c/a\u003e starring \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0001049/?ls\"\u003eJill Clayburgh\u003c/a\u003e, and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0001382/?ls\"\u003ePeter Hyams\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39; gripping tale of modern-day vigilante justice, \u0026quot;The Star Chamber\u0026quot; (1983). Douglas also starred in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0079832/?ls\"\u003eRunning (1979)\u003c/a\u003e, as a compulsive quitter who sacrifices everything to take one last shot at the Olympics, and as Zach the dictatorial director/choreographer in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000277/?ls\"\u003eRichard Attenborough\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s screen version of the Broadway\u0026#39;s longest running musical \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0088915/?ls\"\u003eA Chorus Line (1985)\u003c/a\u003e.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eDouglas\u0026#39; career as an actor/producer came together again in 1984 with the release of the tongue-in-cheek romantic fantasy \u0026quot;Romancing the Stone.\u0026quot; Douglas had begun developing the project several years earlier, and with Kathleen Turner as Joan Wilder, the dowdy writer of gothic romances, Danny DeVito as the feisty comic foil Ralphie and Douglas as Jack Colton, the reluctant soldier of fortune. \u0026quot;Romancing the Stone\u0026quot; was a resounding hit and grossed more than $100 million at the box office. Douglas was named Producer of the Year in 1984 by the National Association of Theater Owners. Douglas, Turner and DeVito teamed up in 1985 for the successful sequel \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0089370/?ls\"\u003eThe Jewel of the Nile (1985)\u003c/a\u003e.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eIt took Douglas nearly two years to convince Columbia Pictures executives to approve the production of \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0088172/?ls\"\u003eStarman (1984)\u003c/a\u003e, an unlikely tale of romance between an extraterrestrial, played by Jeff Bridges, and a young widow, played by Karen Allen. \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0088172/?ls\"\u003eStarman (1984)\u003c/a\u003e was the sleeper hit of the 1984 Christmas season and earned an Oscar nomination for Best Actor for Jeff Bridges. Tragically, the night before she was to move to Hollywood, she was injured riding in a car hit by a train, ending the possibility of a dancing career.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eIt was a terrible setback, but after taking singing lessons she found a new vocation, and at age 17, she began touring with the \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0114089/?ls\"\u003eLes Brown\u003c/a\u003e Band. She made three films for Warner Bros. in 1950 and five more in 1951. She began to slow down her filmmaking pace in the 1960s, even though she started out the decade with a hit, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0054188/?ls\"\u003ePlease Don\u0026#39;t Eat the Daisies (1960)\u003c/a\u003e.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eIn 1958, her brother Paul died. Avenue Général de Gaulle). The family\nmoved to the United States when she was three. As Claudette grew up,\nshe wanted nothing more than to play to Broadway audiences (in those\ndays, any actress or actor worth their salt went for Broadway, not\nHollywood). After her formal education ended, she enrolled in the Art\nStudents League, where she paid for her dramatic training by working in\na dress shop. She made her Broadway debut in 1923 in the stage\nproduction of \u0026quot;The Wild Wescotts\u0026quot;. Moore starred as Mary Richards, who moves to Minneapolis on the heels of a failed relationship. Mary finds work at the newsroom of WJM-TV, whose news program is the lowest-rated in the city, and establishes fast friendships with her colleagues and her neighbors. The sitcom was a commercial and critical success and for years was a fixture of CBS television\u0026#39;s unbeatable Saturday night line-up. Moore and Tinker were determined from the start to make the sitcom a cut above the average, and it certainly was - instead of going for a barrage of gags, the humor took longer to develop and arose out of the interaction between the characters in more realistic situations. This was also one of the earliest television portrayals of a woman who was happy and successful on her own rather than simply being a man\u0026#39;s wife. \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0065314/?ls\"\u003eMary Tyler Moore Show (1970)\u003c/a\u003e is generally included amongst the finest television series ever produced in America.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eMoore ended the sitcom in 1977, while it was still on a high point, but found it difficult to flee the beloved Mary Richards persona - her subsequent attempts at television series, variety programs, and specials (such as the mortifying disco-era \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0158763/?ls\"\u003eMary\u0026#39;s Incredible Dream (1976)\u003c/a\u003e) usually failed, but even her dramatic work, which is generally excellent, fell under the shadow of Mary Richards. Kim, who had blossomed to a 5\u0026#39; 7\u0026quot; beauty, was offered a contract on the spot with the Ford Modeling Agency. At the age of 20, Kim was a top model commanding $1,000 a day. Throughout the early 1970s, she appeared on dozens of magazine covers and in hundreds of ads, most notably as the Breck girl. Kim took acting classes at the Neighborhood Playhouse, performed in various Greenwich Village clubs, and she sang under the stage name Chelsea. Kim moved to Los Angeles in 1976, ready to conquer Hollywood. Martin was born on August 14, 1945 in Waco, Texas, USA as Stephen Glenn Martin to Mary Lee (née Stewart; 1913-2002) and Glenn Vernon Martin (1914-1997), a real estate salesman and aspiring actor. He was raised in Inglewood and Garden Grove in California. In 1960, he got a job at the Magic shop of Disney\u0026#39;s Fantasyland, and while there he learned magic, juggling, and creating balloon animals. At Santa Ana College, he took classes in drama and English poetry. He also took part in comedies and other productions at the Bird Cage Theatre, and joined a comedy troupe at Knott\u0026#39;s Berry Farm. He attended California State University as a philosophy major, but in 1967 transferred to UCLA as a theatre major.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eHis writing career began on \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0061296/?ls\"\u003eThe Smothers Brothers Comedy Hour (1967)\u003c/a\u003e, winning him an Emmy Award. He also appeared on talk shows and comedy shows in the late 1960s and early 1970s. The twelfth of thirteen children, his mother died while he was a toddler and his father later abandoned the family, leaving him to be raised by an elder sister, Cecilia. An avid fan of Shakespeare, poetry and reading, he once said \u0026quot;home is where the books are\u0026quot;. He received a scholarship to Oxford University to study acting and made his first stage appearance in 1944.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eHis first film appearances were in routine British movies such as \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0041579/?ls\"\u003eThe Last Days of Dolwyn (1949)\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0043121/?ls\"\u003eWaterfront (1950)\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0043601/?ls\"\u003eGreen Grow the Rushes (1951)\u003c/a\u003e. Voight is an American actor of German and Slovak descent. He has won the Academy Award for Best Actor in a Leading Role for his role as paraplegic Vietnam War veteran Luke Martin in the war film \u0026quot;Coming Home\u0026quot; (1978). He has also been nominated for the same award other two times. He was first nominated for his role as aspiring gigolo Joe Buck in \u0026quot;Midnight Cowboy\u0026quot; (1969), He was last nominated for the award for his role as escaped convict Oscar \u0026quot;Manny\u0026quot; Manheim in \u0026quot;Runaway Train\u0026quot; (1985). His paternal grandfather was a Slovak immigrant, as were the parents of his paternal grandmother. His maternal grandfather was a German immigrant, as were the parents of his maternal grandmother. His maternal great-uncle was political activist Joseph P. Kamp (1900-1993), a leader of the anti-communist organization \u0026quot;Constitutional Educational League\u0026quot;.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eVoight has two siblings: volcanologist Barry Voight (1937-) and singer-songwriter James Wesley Voight (pseudonym Chip Taylor, 1940-). Barry is most famous for first predicting and then investigating the eruption of Mount St. Helens (1980). James is most famous for writing the hit songs \u0026quot;Wild Thing\u0026quot; (1965) and \u0026quot;Angel of the Morning\u0026quot; (1967).\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eVoight was educated at Archbishop Stepinac High School, an all-boys Roman Catholic high school located at White Plains, New York. At the time, the school was operated by the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of New York. He took an interest in acting in his high school years, performing a comedic role in the school\u0026#39;s annual musical, \u0026quot;The Song of Norway\u0026quot;. He graduated in 1956, at the age of 18.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eVoight continued his education at The Catholic University of America, located in Washington, D.C.. He then moved to New York City, having decided to pursue an acting career.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eIn the early 1960s, Voight primarily worked as a television actor. Streisand is an American singer, actress, director and producer and one of the most successful personalities in show business. She is the only person ever to receive all of the following: Oscar, Tony, Emmy, Grammy, Golden Globe, Cable Ace, National Endowment for the Arts, and Peabody awards, as well as the Kennedy Center Honor, American Film Institute\u0026#39;s Lifetime Achievement honor and the Film Society of Lincoln Center Chaplin Award.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eShe was born in Brooklyn, New York, in 1942 to \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm3689838/?ls\"\u003eDiana Kind\u003c/a\u003e (née Ida Rosen), a singer turned school secretary, and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm8964156/?ls\"\u003eEmanuel Streisand\u003c/a\u003e, a high school teacher. Her father died when she was 15 months old. She has a brother, Sheldon, and a half-sister, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0454238/?ls\"\u003eRoslyn Kind\u003c/a\u003e, from their mother\u0026#39;s remarriage. As a child she attended the Beis Yakov Jewish School in Brooklyn. She was raised in a middle-class family and grew up dreaming of becoming an actress (or even an actress / conductor, as she happily described her teenage years at one of her concerts).\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eAfter a period as a nightclub singer and off-Broadway performer in New York City she began to attract interest and a fan base, thanks to her original and powerful vocal talent. She debuted on Broadway in the 1962 musical comedy \u0026quot;I Can Get It For You Wholesale\u0026quot; by \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0739173/?ls\"\u003eHarold Rome\u003c/a\u003e, receiving a Tony Award nomination for Best Supporting Actress and a New York Drama Critics Poll award. The following year she reached great commercial success with her first Columbia Records solo releases, \u0026quot;The Barbra Streisand Album\u0026quot; (multiple Grammy winner, including \u0026quot;Best Album of the Year\u0026quot;) and \u0026quot;The Second Barbra Streisand Album\u0026quot; (her first RIAA Gold Album); these albums, mostly devoted to composer \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0002182/?ls\"\u003eHarold Arlen\u003c/a\u003e, brought her critical praise and, most of all, public acclaim all over the US. In almost 50 years of career, Streisand has contributed to the show business industry in a personal and unique way, collecting a multi-generational fan base; she has a powerful and recognize vocal range, and a raucous and often self-deprecating sense of humor, which doesn\u0026#39;t prevent her from showing the serious and dramatic sides of her personality. Her strong political belief in social justice infuses her professional career and personal life, and she makes no bones about what she believes; her willingness to put her money where her mouth is has resulted in some truly vicious attacks by many who hold opposite political views, but that hasn\u0026#39;t stopped her from acting on her beliefs. She has been honored with the Humanitarian Award from the Human Rights Campaign, an Honorary Doctorate in Arts and Humanities from Brandeis University in 1995, an Honorary Doctorate of Philosophy from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem in 2013 and the bestowing by the government of France the title of Commander of the Order of Arts and Letters. She supports many humanitarian causes through the Streisand Foundation and has been a dedicated environmentalist for many years; she endowed a chair in environmental studies in 1987 and donated her 24-acre estate to the Santa Monica Mountains Conservancy. In addition, she was the lead founder for the Clinton Climate Change Initiative. This effort brought together a consortium of major cities around the world to drive down greenhouse gas emissions. She is a leading spokesperson and fund-raiser for social and political causes close to her heart and has often dedicated proceeds from her live concert performances to benefit programs she She is from a Jewish\nfamily (originally from Austria-Hungary and the Russian Empire). Her\nmaternal grandparents called her Mary, while her parents called her\nDebra (her father named her Debra after his favorite actress,\n\u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0656428/?ls\"\u003eDebra Paget\u003c/a\u003e). The\nfamily moved to California when Debra was five. She fell in love with\nacting in high school but kept it a secret from her family. She was a\nprecocious teenager, having graduated high school at an early age of\n15. She enrolled in college, majoring in criminology. She worked\npart-time in the local amusement park when she got thrown from a truck\nand suffered serious injuries and went temporarily blind for several\nmonths. She was in the hospital when she vowed to pursue her passion\nfor acting.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eAfter she recovered, she abandoned college and studied acting. In 2001, Marion starred in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0263496/?ls\"\u003ePretty Things (2001)\u003c/a\u003e as the twin sisters Marie and Lucie, and was nominated for her second César award for Most Promising Actress.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eCotillard\u0026#39;s breakthrough in France came in 2003, when she starred in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm1077168/?ls\"\u003eYann Samuell\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s dark romantic comedy \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0364517/?ls\"\u003eChildren\u0026#39;s Games (2003)\u003c/a\u003e, in which she played Sophie Kowalsky, the daughter of Polish immigrants who lives a love-hate relationship with her childhood friend. In 2004, she won the Chopard Thophy of Female Revelation at the Cannes Film Festival. Director \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0196860/?ls\"\u003eOlivier Dahan\u003c/a\u003e cast Cotillard to play the legendary French singer because to him, her eyes were like those of \u0026quot;Piaf\u0026quot;. The role won Cotillard the Academy Award for Best Actress along with a César, a Lumière Award, a BAFTA Award, and a Golden Globe. That made her only the second actress to win an acting Oscar performing in a language other than English next to \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000047/?ls\"\u003eSophia Loren\u003c/a\u003e (\u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0054749/?ls\"\u003eTwo Women (1960)\u003c/a\u003e). A favorite of film buffs, Del Toro gained mainstream public attention as the conflicted but basically honest Mexican policeman in \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0001752/?ls\"\u003eSteven Soderbergh\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0181865/?ls\"\u003eTraffic (2000)\u003c/a\u003e.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eBenicio was born on February 19, 1967 in Santurce, Puerto Rico, the son of lawyer parents Fausta Genoveva Sanchez Rivera and Gustavo Adolfo Del Toro Bermudez. His mother died when he was young, and his father moved the family to a farm in Pennsylvania. A basketball player with an interest in acting, he decided to follow the family way and study business at the University of California in San Diego. A class in acting resulted in his being bitten by the acting bug, and he subsequently dropped out and began studying with legendary acting teacher \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0012245/?ls\"\u003eStella Adler\u003c/a\u003e in Los Angeles and at the Circle in the Square Acting School in New York City. However, things looked better when he landed the role of Dario, the vicious henchman in the James Bond film \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0097742/?ls\"\u003eLicence to Kill (1989)\u003c/a\u003e. Surprising his co-stars at age 21, Del Toro was the youngest actor ever to portray a Bond villain. However, the potential break was spoiled as the picture turned out to be one of the most disappointing Bond films ever; this was lost amid bigger summer competition.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eBenicio gave creditable performances in many overlooked films for the next several years, such as \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0102116/?ls\"\u003eThe Indian Runner (1991)\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0103962/?ls\"\u003eChristopher Columbus: The Discovery (1992)\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0107594/?ls\"\u003eMoney for Nothing (1993)\u003c/a\u003e. Their act soon gained the reputation as one of the roughest in the country for their wild, physical onstage antics. It was normal for Joe to throw Buster around the stage and participate in elaborate, dangerous stunts to the awe of audiences. After several years on the Vaudeville circuit, \u0026quot;The Three Keatons\u0026quot; toured until Keaton had to break up the act because of his father\u0026#39;s increasing alcohol dependence, making him a show business veteran by age 21.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eWhile he was looking for work in New York, he had a chance run-in with wildly-successful film star and director \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000779/?ls\"\u003eRoscoe \u0026#39;Fatty\u0026#39; Arbuckle\u003c/a\u003e, who invited him to be in his upcoming short \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0007761/?ls\"\u003eThe Butcher Boy (1917)\u003c/a\u003e. This appearance launched Keaton\u0026#39;s film career and spawned a friendship that lasted until Arbuckle\u0026#39;s sudden death in 1933. By 1920, after making several successful shorts together, Arbuckle moved on to features, and Keaton inherited his studio, allowing him the opportunity to begin producing his own films. By September 1921, tragedy touched Arbuckle\u0026#39;s life by way of a scandal, where he was tried three times for the murder of Virginia Rapp. Although he was not guilty of the charges, and never convicted, he was unable to regain his status, and the viewing public would no longer tolerate his presence in film. entertainment world has enjoyed a six-decade love affair with comedienne/singer Carol Burnett. A peerless sketch performer and delightful, self-effacing personality who rightfully succeeded \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000840/?ls\"\u003eLucille Ball\u003c/a\u003e as the carrot-topped \u0026quot;Queen of Television Comedy,\u0026quot; it was Burnett\u0026#39;s traumatic childhood that set the stage for her comedy.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eCarol\u0026#39;s rags-to-riches story started out in San Antonio, Texas, on April 26, 1933, where she was born to Ina Louise (Creighton) and Joseph Thomas \u0026quot;Jodie\u0026quot; Burnett, both of whom suffered from acute alcoholism. As a child, she was left in the care of a beloved grandmother, who shuttled the two of them off to Hollywood, California, where they lived in a boarding house and shared a great passion for the Golden Age of movies. The plaintive, loose-limbed, highly sensitive Carol survived her wallflower insecurities by grabbing attention as a cut-up at Hollywood High School. A natural talent, she attended the University of California and switched majors from journalism to theater. Scouting out comedy parts on TV and in the theater, she first had them rolling in the aisles in the mid-1950s performing a lovelorn novelty song called \u0026quot;I Made a Fool of Myself Over John Foster Dulles\u0026quot; (then Secretary of State) in a nightclub act. This led to night-time variety show appearances with \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0654967/?ls\"\u003eJack Paar\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0838047/?ls\"\u003eEd Sullivan\u003c/a\u003e and where the career ball really started rolling.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eCarol\u0026#39;s first big TV breaks came at age 22 and 23 as a foil to a ventriloquist\u0026#39;s dummy on the already-established \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0300836/?ls\"\u003eThe Paul Winchell and Jerry Mahoney Show (1950)\u003c/a\u003e in 1955, and as \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0004983/?ls\"\u003eBuddy Hackett\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#39;s gawky girlfriend on the short-lived sitcom \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0048898/?ls\"\u003eStanley (1956)\u003c/a\u003e. She also developed an affinity for game shows and appeared as a regular on one of TV earliest, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0042130/?ls\"\u003ePantomime Quiz (1947)\u003c/a\u003e in 1958. While TV would bring Carol fans by the millions, it was Broadway that set her on the road to stardom. She began as the woebegone Princess Winnifred in the 1959 Broadway musical \u0026quot;Once Upon a Mattress\u0026quot; which earned her first Tony Award nomination. [She would later appear in three TV adaptations - \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0424325/?ls\"\u003eOnce Upon a Mattress (1964)\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0374926/?ls\"\u003eOnce Upon a Mattress (1972)\u003c/a\u003e and\n\u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0426148/?ls\"\u003eOnce Upon a Mattress (2005)\u003c/a\u003e.] This, in turn, led to the first of an armful of Emmy Awards as a repertoire player on the popular variety series \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0051276/?ls\"\u003eThe Garry Moore Show (1958)\u003c/a\u003e in 1959. Burnett invented a number of scene-stealing characters during this time, most notably her charwoman character. With the phenomenal household success of the Moore show, she moved up quickly from second banana to headliner and appeared in a 1962 Emmy-winning special \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0280799/?ls\"\u003eJulie and Carol at Carnegie Hall (1962)\u003c/a\u003e co-starring close friend \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000267/?ls\"\u003eJulie Andrews\u003c/a\u003e. (1963)\u003c/a\u003e.\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003eNot surprisingly, fellow redhead \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000840/?ls\"\u003eLucille Ball\u003c/a\u003e, who had been Carol\u0026#39;s treasured idol growing up, subsequently became a friend and mentor to the rising funny girl. Hilarious as a guest star on \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0055686/?ls\"\u003eThe Lucy Show (1962)\u003c/a\u003e, Carol appeared as a painfully shy (natch) wallflower type who suddenly blooms in jaw-dropping fashion. Ms. Ball was so convinced of Carol\u0026#39;s talent that she offered Carol her own Desilu-produced sitcom, but Burnett had her heart set on fronting a variety show. With her own team of second bananas, including character crony \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0466327/?ls\"\u003eHarvey Korman\u003c/a\u003e, handsome foil \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0905741/?ls\"\u003eLyle Waggoner\u003c/a\u003e, and lookalike \u0026quot;kid sister\u0026quot; type \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0493069/?ls\"\u003eVicki Lawrence\u003c/a\u003e, the \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/title/tt0061240/?ls\"\u003eThe Carol Burnett Show (1967)\u003c/a\u003e became an instant sensation, and earned 22 Emmy Awards during its 11-year run. It allowed Carol to fire off her wide range of comedy and musical ammunition--whether running amok in broad sketch comedy, parodying movie icons such as \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0841797/?ls\"\u003eGloria Swanson\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000073/?ls\"\u003eShirley Temple\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0000046/?ls\"\u003eVivien Leigh\u003c/a\u003e or \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0001076/?ls\"\u003eJoan Crawford\u003c/a\u003e, or singing/gushing alongside favorite vocalists \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0001561/?ls\"\u003eJim Nabors\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0493031/?ls\"\u003eSteve Lawrence\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0498007/?ls\"\u003ePeggy Lee\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0002035/?ls\"\u003eSammy Davis Jr.\u003c/a\u003e, \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0280228/?ls\"\u003eElla Fitzgerald\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca class=\"ipc-md-link ipc-md-link--entity\" href=\"/name/nm0868123/?ls\"\u003eMel Tormé\u003c/a\u003e. Carol took on new challenges to display her unseen dramatic mettle, and accomplished this amazingly in TV-movie showcases.
